advice-51242cca143176f23d88d4c2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-51242cca143176f23d88d4c2.body:
(On how virtue is acquired) We are right then in saying, that these virtues are formed in a man by his doing the actions; but no one, if he should leave them undone, would be even in the way to become a good man.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book II, chapter III, paragraph 4 (Chase edition)

advice-b9dcec78c11ec02044a1e90d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b9dcec78c11ec02044a1e90d.body:
(On moral choices within our power) But if it is in our power to do and to forbear doing what is creditable or the contrary, and these respectively constitute the being good or bad, then the being good or vicious characters is in our power.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter VII, paragraph 3 (Chase edition)

advice-ae71b4982ee7b3d13e59286b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ae71b4982ee7b3d13e59286b.body:
(On generosity in the use of wealth) And again, it is they who give that are denominated Liberal, while they who forbear to receive are commended, not on the score of Liberality but of just dealing, while for receiving men are not, in fact, praised at all.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter I, paragraph 7 (Chase edition)

advice-f524389f6b485b6245301de7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f524389f6b485b6245301de7.body:
(On truth and friends: truth takes priority) Still perhaps it may appear better, nay to be our duty where the safety of the truth is concerned, to upset if need be even our own theories, specially as we are lovers of wisdom: for since both are dear to us, we are bound to prefer the truth.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book I, chapter III, paragraph 8 (Chase edition)

advice-fe4f6f592146263cc737707d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fe4f6f592146263cc737707d.body:
(On educating moral feelings) Then, as for Words and Precept, they, it is to be feared, will not avail with all; but it may be necessary for the mind of the disciple to have been previously prepared for liking and disliking as he ought; just as the soil must, to nourish the seed sown.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter VIII, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-eb0ae86a1ab328dbf0143e3a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-eb0ae86a1ab328dbf0143e3a.body:
(On extremes misjudging a person who holds the mean) And so the extreme characters push away, so to speak, towards each other the man in the mean state; the brave man is called a rash man by the coward, and a coward by the rash man, and in the other cases accordingly.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book II, chapter VIII, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-8f4f0abd18daaed9feebe706.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8f4f0abd18daaed9feebe706.body:
(On judgments grounded in experience) And so one should attend to the undemonstrable dicta and opinions of the skilful, the old and the Practically-Wise, no less than to those which are based on strict reasoning, because they see aright, having gained their power of moral vision from experience.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VI, chapter XI, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-0e4e9582f481cc574e9820b3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0e4e9582f481cc574e9820b3.body:
(On the starting points of reasoning) And again, you must not demand the reason either in all things alike, because in some it is sufficient that the fact has been well demonstrated, which is the case with first principles; and the fact is the first step, i.e. starting-point or principle.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book I, chapter V, paragraph 8 (Chase edition)

advice-1bb9e100efcf286d7cd869bd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1bb9e100efcf286d7cd869bd.body:
(On choosing against passion and appetite) Next; the man who fails of self-control acts from Lust but not from Moral Choice; the man of self-control, on the contrary, from Moral Choice, not from Lust.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter IV, paragraph 3 (Chase edition)

advice-003b168f035d75650ab3f660.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-003b168f035d75650ab3f660.body:
(On bringing desires under reason) In short, as the child ought to live with constant regard to the orders of its educator, so should the appetitive principle with regard to those of Reason.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter XIV, paragraph 7 (Chase edition)

advice-321d81ad965117d9ff634e98.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-321d81ad965117d9ff634e98.body:
(On friendship and one's relationship with oneself) Now the friendly feelings which are exhibited towards our friends, and by which Friendships are characterised, seem to have sprung out of those which we entertain toward ourselves.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter IV, paragraph 1 (Chase edition)

advice-1bd078b5fc2271fe143608f4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1bd078b5fc2271fe143608f4.body:
(On pleasure accompanying activity) Furthermore, Pleasure perfects the act of Working not in the way of an inherent state but as a supervening finish, such as is bloom in people at their prime.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter IV, paragraph 4 (Chase edition)

advice-b79457c9c3acaabf1db9b806.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b79457c9c3acaabf1db9b806.body:
(On bringing desires under reason) So then in the man of Perfected Self-Mastery, the appetitive principle must be accordant with Reason: for what is right is the mark at which both principles aim: that is to say, the man of perfected self-mastery desires what he ought in right manner and at right times, which is exactly what Reason directs.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter XIV, paragraph 8 (Chase edition)

advice-5141b03335a8d03df53cd92f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5141b03335a8d03df53cd92f.body:
(On friends agreeing in shared affairs) Unity of Sentiment is also plainly connected with Friendship, and therefore is not the same as Unity of Opinion, because this might exist even between people unacquainted with one another.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter VI, paragraph 1 (Chase edition)

advice-f209e84a93a4a943fcc8cb0a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f209e84a93a4a943fcc8cb0a.body:
(On equitable correction of a general law) What causes the difficulty is this; the Equitable is Just, but not the Just which is in accordance with written law, being in fact a correction of that kind of Just.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book V, chapter XV, paragraph 3 (Chase edition)

advice-575defa1179b59ed403ccec6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-575defa1179b59ed403ccec6.body:
(On friendship as the capacity to love) Since then Friendship stands rather in the entertaining, than in being the object of, the sentiment, and they are praised who are fond of their friends, it seems that entertaining the sentiment is the Excellence of friends; and so, in whomsoever this exists in due proportion these are stable friends and their Friendship is permanent.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter VIII, paragraph 10 (Chase edition)

advice-7b898e1e5ba646987578f96e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7b898e1e5ba646987578f96e.body:
(On moral choice and opinion) Further, Moral Choice is commended rather for having a right object than for being judicious, but Opinion for being formed in accordance with truth.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter IV, paragraph 11 (Chase edition)

advice-4873511472872257f30ac92c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4873511472872257f30ac92c.body:
(On magnanimity and justified self-worth) Whereas the Great-minded man despises on good grounds (for he forms his opinions truly), but the mass of men do it at random.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter IV, paragraph 11 (Chase edition)

advice-79e765d70ddc921e6863982d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-79e765d70ddc921e6863982d.body:
(On shameful actions and moral character) And for a man to be such that he would feel Shame if he should do anything disgraceful, and to think that this constitutes him a good man, is absurd: because Shame is felt at voluntary actions only, and a good man will never voluntarily do what is base.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter XI, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-d744d4dd28a73efb4d00bbef.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d744d4dd28a73efb4d00bbef.body:
(On disputes between unequal friends) Quarrels arise also in those Friendships in which the parties are unequal because each party thinks himself entitled to the greater share, and of course, when this happens, the Friendship is broken up.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter XIV, paragraph 1 (Chase edition)

advice-c3a041579a861c2f04d9b2e3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c3a041579a861c2f04d9b2e3.body:
(On virtue as a mean between extremes) Now Virtue is concerned with feelings and actions, in which the excess is wrong and the defect is blamed but the mean is praised and goes right; and both these circumstances belong to Virtue.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book II, chapter V, paragraph 8 (Chase edition)

advice-a2f76015f21d4d5e05638520.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a2f76015f21d4d5e05638520.body:
(On activities competing for our attention) Much the same kind of thing takes place in other cases, when a person is engaged in two different Workings at the same time: that is, the pleasanter of the two keeps pushing out the other, and, if the disparity in pleasantness be great, then more and more till a man even ceases altogether to work at the other.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter IV, paragraph 10 (Chase edition)

advice-db1f8b7d9750ee92d6da3506.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-db1f8b7d9750ee92d6da3506.body:
(On voluntary and involuntary actions) Involuntary actions then are thought to be of two kinds, being done either on compulsion, or by reason of ignorance.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter I, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-a43007ded8eb17f8b9771f57.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a43007ded8eb17f8b9771f57.body:
(On trust between proven friends) And further, the Friendship of the good is alone superior to calumny; it not being easy for men to believe a third person respecting one whom they have long tried and proved: there is between good men mutual confidence, and the feeling that one’s friend would never have done one wrong, and all other such things as are expected in Friendship really worthy the name; but in the other kinds there is nothing to prevent all such suspicions.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter V, paragraph 9 (Chase edition)

advice-2d4a425acc12accef678424c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2d4a425acc12accef678424c.body:
(On happiness and the place of amusement) Happiness then stands not in amusement; in fact the very notion is absurd of the End being amusement, and of one’s toiling and enduring hardness all one’s life long with a view to amusement: for everything in the world, so to speak, we choose with some further End in view, except Happiness, for that is the End comprehending all others.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter V, paragraph 7 (Chase edition)

advice-2a75e154663355edc47d338c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2a75e154663355edc47d338c.body:
(On friends quarrelling over expected benefits) Now this results from the fact, that all men, or the generality at least, wish what is honourable, but, when tested, choose what is profitable; and the doing kindnesses disinterestedly is honourable while receiving benefits is profitable.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter XIII, paragraph 7 (Chase edition)

advice-a87fcd3a081760d4f0a33b6b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a87fcd3a081760d4f0a33b6b.body:
(On managing wealth) Whatever things are for use may be used well or ill, and Wealth belongs to this class.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter I, paragraph 4 (Chase edition)

advice-6907b18a6ed4c9fb4efea416.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6907b18a6ed4c9fb4efea416.body:
(On self-control and enduring difficulty) Furthermore, to the character of Imperfect Self-Control is opposed that of Self-Control, and to that of Softness that of Endurance: because Endurance consists in continued resistance but Self-Control in actual mastery, and continued resistance and actual mastery are as different as not being conquered is from conquering; and so Self-Control is more choice-worthy than Endurance.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VII, chapter VII, paragraph 4 (Chase edition)

advice-6261df639f1d4403ea29f034.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6261df639f1d4403ea29f034.body:
(On the difficulty of changing settled habits) No, indeed! it is either actually impossible, or a task of no mean difficulty, to alter by words what has been of old taken into men’s very dispositions: and, it may be, it is a ground for contentment if with all the means and appliances for goodness in our hands we can attain to Virtue.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter VIII, paragraph 3 (Chase edition)

advice-e101432b6712189a38186286.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e101432b6712189a38186286.body:
(On mildness and measured anger) I mean, it is no easy matter to define how, and with what persons, and at what kind of things, and how long one ought to be angry, and up to what point a person is right or is wrong.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter VII, paragraph 9 (Chase edition)

advice-fe1c26907bb085deaa321304.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fe1c26907bb085deaa321304.body:
(On how virtue is acquired) Or, in one word, the habits are produced from the acts of working like to them: and so what we have to do is to give a certain character to these particular acts, because the habits formed correspond to the differences of these.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book II, chapter I, paragraph 7 (Chase edition)

advice-be26cf4782d3ff009ecba1a5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-be26cf4782d3ff009ecba1a5.body:
(On rest and amusement) Yet some pause and amusement in life are generally judged to be indispensable.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter X, paragraph 9 (Chase edition)

advice-053846a796cdc7791aaee71f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-053846a796cdc7791aaee71f.body:
(On valuing the fruits of one's labour) Once more: all people value most what has cost them much labour in the production; for instance, people who have themselves made their money are fonder of it than those who have inherited it: and receiving kindness is, it seems, unlaborious, but doing it is laborious.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter VII, paragraph 12 (Chase edition)

advice-e6e2ea8240745b82fdb01089.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e6e2ea8240745b82fdb01089.body:
(On moderation and tact in humour) Now they who exceed in the ridiculous are judged to be Buffoons and Vulgar, catching at it in any and every way and at any cost, and aiming rather at raising laughter than at saying what is seemly and at avoiding to pain the object of their wit.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter X, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-9c77420dcc4a2a67611de79a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9c77420dcc4a2a67611de79a.body:
(On friendship between good people) Equality, then, and similarity are a tie to Friendship, and specially the similarity of goodness, because good men, being stable in themselves, are also stable as regards others, and neither ask degrading services nor render them, but, so to say, rather prevent them: for it is the part of the good neither to do wrong themselves nor to allow their friends in so doing.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter VIII, paragraph 11 (Chase edition)

advice-27a4d43a3d145c45bcded97f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-27a4d43a3d145c45bcded97f.body:
(On guiding one's actions by reason) In the case of the bad man, what he ought to do and what he does are at variance, but the good man does what he ought to do, because all Intellect chooses what is best for itself and the good man puts himself under the direction of Intellect.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter VIII, paragraph 10 (Chase edition)

advice-262933c4b0356f75b7207e2e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-262933c4b0356f75b7207e2e.body:
(On friends sharing life, thoughts and conversation) Therefore one ought to be thoroughly conscious of one’s friend’s existence, which will result from living with him, that is sharing in his words and thoughts: for this is the meaning of the term as applied to the human species, not mere feeding together as in the case of brutes.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter IX, paragraph 14 (Chase edition)

advice-c4c6951f35ceb4f345d289c4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c4c6951f35ceb4f345d289c4.body:
(On what is good in itself) By choice-worthy in themselves are meant those from which nothing is sought beyond the act of Working: and of this kind are thought to be the actions according to Virtue, because doing what is noble and excellent is one of those things which are choice-worthy for their own sake alone.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter V, paragraph 3 (Chase edition)

advice-8fde275df470f65a48b16a40.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8fde275df470f65a48b16a40.body:
(On bringing desires under reason) Unless then the appetite be obedient and subjected to the governing principle it will become very great: for in the fool the grasping after what is pleasant is insatiable and undiscriminating; and every acting out of the desire increases the kindred habit, and if the desires are great and violent in degree they even expel Reason entirely; therefore they ought to be moderate and few, and in no respect to be opposed to Reason.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter XIV, paragraph 6 (Chase edition)

advice-cecc0b9e1b732e1bcd016d7d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cecc0b9e1b732e1bcd016d7d.body:
(On moral choices within our power) Now since the End is the object of Wish, and the means to the End of Deliberation and Moral Choice, the actions regarding these matters must be in the way of Moral Choice, i.e. voluntary: but the acts of working out the virtues are such actions, and therefore Virtue is in our power.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter VII, paragraph 1 (Chase edition)

advice-f9bd352ab3d78f284b6ef3a4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f9bd352ab3d78f284b6ef3a4.body:
(On three friendships: advantage, pleasure and virtue) And Friendship having been divided into these kinds, bad men will be friends by reason of pleasure or profit, this being their point of resemblance; while the good are friends for one another’s sake, that is, in so far as they are good.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter V, paragraph 11 (Chase edition)

advice-3ee486a2ade59272649044ec.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3ee486a2ade59272649044ec.body:
(On practical wisdom in choosing actions) And again, it is not knowledge merely, but aptitude for action, which constitutes Practical Wisdom: and of this aptitude the man of Imperfect Self-Control is destitute.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VII, chapter IX, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-f8e51e8ffafca953897e1457.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f8e51e8ffafca953897e1457.body:
(On a happy person's need for friends) The man therefore who is to come up to our notion “Happy” will need good Friends.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter IX, paragraph 15 (Chase edition)

advice-306e9f746f2bf97b885e7bc9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-306e9f746f2bf97b885e7bc9.body:
(On vice as conflict within oneself) If then to be thus is exceedingly wretched it is a man’s duty to flee from wickedness with all his might and to strive to be good, because thus may he be friends with himself and may come to be a friend to another.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter IV, paragraph 10 (Chase edition)

advice-1c75572fc65590afd8ab9c26.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1c75572fc65590afd8ab9c26.body:
(On testing accounts of happiness against life) And thus the opinions of the Wise seem to be accordant with our account of the matter: of course such things carry some weight, but truth, in matters of moral action, is judged from facts and from actual life, for herein rests the decision.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter VII, paragraph 6 (Chase edition)

advice-2b30665732cb5c7f8c1f1e66.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2b30665732cb5c7f8c1f1e66.body:
(On courage in the face of danger) So honour is the motive from which the Brave man withstands things fearful and performs the acts which accord with Courage.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter X, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-64f6861e3a05b81e09b76a58.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-64f6861e3a05b81e09b76a58.body:
(On virtue as human excellence) We must observe then that all excellence makes that whereof it is the excellence both to be itself in a good state and to perform its work well.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book II, chapter V, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-132808c0a5484bb4decdabf5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-132808c0a5484bb4decdabf5.body:
(On friendship among parents, children and siblings) The Friendship of Kindred is likewise of many kinds, and appears in all its varieties to depend on the Parental: parents, I mean, love their children as being a part of themselves, children love their parents as being themselves somewhat derived from them.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter XII, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-f462294b240b827c2dba11ed.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f462294b240b827c2dba11ed.body:
(On the judgments of a good person) For there are fair and pleasant things peculiar to, and so varying with, each state; and perhaps the most distinguishing characteristic of the good man is his seeing the truth in every instance, he being, in fact, the rule and measure of these matters.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter VI, paragraph 4 (Chase edition)

advice-959cb1e0dc3cdc7358d97ca4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-959cb1e0dc3cdc7358d97ca4.body:
(On practical wisdom in choosing actions) Whereas to have deliberated well is thought to be a good, because Good Counsel is Rightness of deliberation of such a nature as is apt to attain good.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VI, chapter IX, paragraph 6 (Chase edition)

advice-afb9992f499d1d3b2c9880e6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-afb9992f499d1d3b2c9880e6.body:
(On law and distinguishing justice from injustice) For Just implies mutually acknowledged law, and law the possibility of injustice, for adjudication is the act of distinguishing between the Just and the Unjust.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book V, chapter X, paragraph 4 (Chase edition)

advice-5e3ee0d413c829f00a2fc056.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5e3ee0d413c829f00a2fc056.body:
(On friendship and one's relationship with oneself) Furthermore, the good man wishes to continue to live with himself; for he can do it with pleasure, in that his memories of past actions are full of delight and his anticipations of the future are good and such are pleasurable.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter IV, paragraph 6 (Chase edition)

advice-20593f2302268ef7458848a4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-20593f2302268ef7458848a4.body:
(On friendship in adversity and prosperity) For the very presence of friends is pleasant even in adversity: since men when grieved are comforted by the sympathy of their friends.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter XI, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-4096a86363466df7c862062c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4096a86363466df7c862062c.body:
(On how virtue is acquired) The Virtues then come to be in us neither by nature, nor in despite of nature, but we are furnished by nature with a capacity for receiving them and are perfected in them through custom.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book II, chapter I, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-d85ec9d09f3a3a5c1a916328.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d85ec9d09f3a3a5c1a916328.body:
(On moral choice and opinion) However, nobody perhaps maintains its identity with Opinion simply; but it is not the same with opinion of any kind, because by choosing good and bad things we are constituted of a certain character, but by having opinions on them we are not.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter IV, paragraph 9 (Chase edition)

advice-fb8b79793a9b0b34a0cbb83c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fb8b79793a9b0b34a0cbb83c.body:
(On shameful actions and moral character) To speak of Shame as a Virtue is incorrect, because it is much more like a feeling than a moral state.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter XI, paragraph 1 (Chase edition)

advice-a6dd42078120a53f2aa6fa4c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a6dd42078120a53f2aa6fa4c.body:
(On shameful actions and moral character) And, granted that impudence and the not being ashamed to do what is disgraceful is base, it does not the more follow that it is good for a man to do such things and feel Shame.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter XI, paragraph 3 (Chase edition)

advice-5a676f8196c5af79dfe178bf.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5a676f8196c5af79dfe178bf.body:
(On moderation in seeking honour) Further: as in giving and receiving of wealth there is a mean state, an excess, and a defect, so likewise in grasping after Honour there is the more or less than is right, and also the doing so from right sources and in right manner.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter VI, paragraph 1 (Chase edition)

advice-505e8c40fecd53234e710fce.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-505e8c40fecd53234e710fce.body:
(On learning statesmanship through practice) Practice, however, seems to contribute no little to its acquisition; merely breathing the atmosphere of politics would never have made Statesmen of them, and therefore we may conclude that they who would acquire a knowledge of Statesmanship must have in addition practice.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter VIII, paragraph 18 (Chase edition)

advice-63731be6d2cf8392f019a012.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-63731be6d2cf8392f019a012.body:
(On appropriate precision in ethical reasoning) We must be content then, in speaking of such things and from such data, to set forth the truth roughly and in outline; in other words, since we are speaking of general matter and from general data, to draw also conclusions merely general.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book I, chapter I, paragraph 9 (Chase edition)

advice-ddebdbb9aef5a971823289c9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ddebdbb9aef5a971823289c9.body:
(On happiness and the soul's highest faculty) Now if Happiness is a Working in the way of Excellence of course that Excellence must be the highest, that is to say, the Excellence of the best Principle.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter VI, paragraph 1 (Chase edition)

advice-f64e1e9e459d4f97a44f0e07.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f64e1e9e459d4f97a44f0e07.body:
(On conflicting views of self-love) Perhaps then, in respect of theories of this kind, the proper course is to distinguish and define how far each is true, and in what way.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter VIII, paragraph 3 (Chase edition)

advice-e5459a80d59687e524188729.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e5459a80d59687e524188729.body:
(On wishing for ends and choosing means) Further: Wish has for its object the End rather, but Moral Choice the means to the End; for instance, we wish to be healthy but we choose the means which will make us so; or happiness again we wish for, and commonly say so, but to say we choose is not an appropriate term, because, in short, the province of Moral Choice seems to be those things which are in our own power.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter IV, paragraph 7 (Chase edition)

advice-523ee87649486c5210af9736.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-523ee87649486c5210af9736.body:
(On living by our highest rational faculty) Yet must we not give ear to those who bid one as man to mind only man’s affairs, or as mortal only mortal things; but, so far as we can, make ourselves like immortals and do all with a view to living in accordance with the highest Principle in us, for small as it may be in bulk yet in power and preciousness it far more excels all the others.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter VI, paragraph 10 (Chase edition)

advice-e4439b1fec062b536a0eda56.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e4439b1fec062b536a0eda56.body:
(On generosity in the use of wealth) In fact generally, doing well by others is more characteristic of virtue than being done well by, and doing things positively honourable than forbearing to do things dishonourable; and any one may see that the doing well by others and doing things positively honourable attaches to the act of giving, but to that of receiving only the being done well by or forbearing to do what is dishonourable.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter I, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-99a71144cd8a859afe22f196.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-99a71144cd8a859afe22f196.body:
(On gratitude and disinterested goodwill) I mean, he who has received a kindness requites it by Kindly Feeling towards his benefactor, and is right in so doing: but he who wishes another to be prosperous, because he has hope of advantage through his instrumentality, does not seem to be kindly disposed to that person but rather to himself; just as neither is he his friend if he pays court to him for any interested purpose.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter V, paragraph 3 (Chase edition)

advice-25cd7edb9010a781dd7bbfca.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-25cd7edb9010a781dd7bbfca.body:
(On how virtue is acquired) Well: human Excellence is of two kinds, Intellectual and Moral: now the Intellectual springs originally, and is increased subsequently, from teaching (for the most part that is), and needs therefore experience and time; whereas the Moral comes from custom, and so the Greek term denoting it is but a slight deflection from the term denoting custom in that language.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book II, chapter I, paragraph 1 (Chase edition)

advice-a53bd5b2adcd222ce5384197.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a53bd5b2adcd222ce5384197.body:
(On war as a means to an end) Now all the Practical Virtues require either society or war for their Working, and the actions regarding these are thought to exclude rest; those of war entirely, because no one chooses war, nor prepares for war, for war’s sake: he would indeed be thought a bloodthirsty villain who should make enemies of his friends to secure the existence of fighting and bloodshed.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter VI, paragraph 7 (Chase edition)

advice-db817290825fd5d6ddf71da8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-db817290825fd5d6ddf71da8.body:
(On equal treatment when redressing harm) Because it makes no difference whether a robbery, for instance, is committed by a good man on a bad or by a bad man on a good, nor whether a good or a bad man has committed adultery: the law looks only to the difference created by the injury and treats the men as previously equal, where the one does and the other suffers injury, or the one has done and the other suffered harm.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book V, chapter VII, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-b650bec4469969c4acd27002.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b650bec4469969c4acd27002.body:
(On measuring a benefit between virtuous friends) In Friendships based on goodness, the question, of course, is never raised, but herein the motive of the doer seems to be the proper standard, since virtue and moral character depend principally on motive.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter XIII, paragraph 11 (Chase edition)

advice-8181b523cfa9bac483b01761.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8181b523cfa9bac483b01761.body:
(On generosity in the use of wealth) But the man who gives to improper people, or not from a motive of honour but from some other cause, shall be called not Liberal but something else.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IV, chapter I, paragraph 10 (Chase edition)

advice-743dfd9f97016d84fba442e1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-743dfd9f97016d84fba442e1.body:
(On worthy and base pleasures) So it is not every one who acts from the motive of pleasure who is utterly destitute of Self-Control or base or of Imperfect Self-Control, only he who acts from the impulse of a base pleasure.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VII, chapter VIII, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-0a2c6a2eba3ef25cdbb3e433.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0a2c6a2eba3ef25cdbb3e433.body:
(On novelty, pleasure and fading attention) But there are some things which please when new, but afterwards not in the like way, for exactly the same reason: that at first the mind is roused and works on these Objects with its powers at full tension; just as they who are gazing stedfastly at anything; but afterwards the act of Working is not of the kind it was at first, but careless, and so the Pleasure too is dulled.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter IV, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-e23f01df9fd378e6d7423eef.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e23f01df9fd378e6d7423eef.body:
(On learning through prior knowledge) And all teaching is based upon previous knowledge; (a statement you will find in the Analytics also,) for there are two ways of teaching, by Syllogism and by Induction.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VI, chapter III, paragraph 4 (Chase edition)

advice-d0a2f6c747f61b0eeaae2b45.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d0a2f6c747f61b0eeaae2b45.body:
(On friendship for advantage or pleasure) Now surely in respect of those whose motive to Friendship is utility or pleasure there can be nothing wrong in breaking up the connection when they no longer have those qualities; because they were friends [not of one another, but] of those qualities: and, these having failed, it is only reasonable to expect that they should cease to entertain the sentiment.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book IX, chapter III, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-6e9369da6727da8536b3032f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6e9369da6727da8536b3032f.body:
(On happiness as virtuous activity) Let this then be taken for a rough sketch of the Chief Good: since it is probably the right way to give first the outline, and fill it in afterwards.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book I, chapter V, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-c395cfe03a601cdbb6b4912c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c395cfe03a601cdbb6b4912c.body:
(On deliberate indulgence and weakness of will) For the man who has lost all Self-Control is led on with deliberate moral choice, holding that it is his line to pursue pleasure as it rises: while the man of Imperfect Self-Control does not think that he ought to pursue it, but does pursue it all the same.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VII, chapter III, paragraph 2 (Chase edition)

advice-5535b7637cc7e2e1541c390d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5535b7637cc7e2e1541c390d.body:
(On friendship based on mutual advantage) Where people do not interchange pleasure but profit in matters of Love, the Friendship is both less intense in degree and also less permanent: in fact, they who are friends because of advantage commonly part when the advantage ceases; for, in reality, they never were friends of one another but of the advantage.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter V, paragraph 7 (Chase edition)

advice-4d9e33436ae1b19c9a1dce3d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4d9e33436ae1b19c9a1dce3d.body:
(On differences in what people enjoy) Yet in the case of human creatures they differ not a little: for the very same things please some and pain others: and what are painful and hateful to some are pleasant to and liked by others.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book X, chapter IV, paragraph 17 (Chase edition)

advice-0f8a797f1d79df0d36622b91.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0f8a797f1d79df0d36622b91.body:
(On courage in the face of danger) And, again, a man is not a coward for fearing insult to his wife or children, or envy, or any such thing; nor is he a Brave man for being bold when going to be scourged.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book III, chapter IX, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-b1e4b048ae075d39ea16970b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b1e4b048ae075d39ea16970b.body:
(On friendship among parents, children and siblings) Then again the being brought up together, and the nearness of age, are a great help towards Friendship, for a man likes one of his own age and persons who are used to one another are companions, which accounts for the resemblance between the Friendship of Brothers and that of Companions.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book VIII, chapter XII, paragraph 5 (Chase edition)

advice-d77c82d2de090a19322bc31a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d77c82d2de090a19322bc31a.body:
(On justice as a good for others) If virtue is a faculty of beneficence, the highest kinds of it must be those which are most useful to others, and for this reason men honour most the just and the courageous, since courage is useful to others in war, justice both in war and in peace.
Aristotle

advice-5bd64f7bfc0b5825ad21029b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5bd64f7bfc0b5825ad21029b.body:
(On wishing a friend well for their own sake) The terms 'possession of many friends' and 'possession of good friends' need no explanation; for we define a 'friend' as one who will always try, for your sake, to do what he takes to be good for you.
Aristotle

advice-38d818b3f7dc346073b0d5db.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-38d818b3f7dc346073b0d5db.body:
(On the pleasure of learning and wonder) Learning things and wondering at things are also pleasant as a rule; wondering implies the desire of learning, so that the object of wonder is an object of desire; while in learning one is brought into one's natural condition.
Aristotle

advice-e633151ed9deaa2619f0b348.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e633151ed9deaa2619f0b348.body:
(On the value of friendship) Friends and friendship: for a friend is desirable in himself and also productive of many other good things.
Aristotle

advice-60b747802ef5814183d4fb03.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-60b747802ef5814183d4fb03.body:
(On qualities that make people likable) We also like temperate men, because they are not unjust to others; and, for the same reason, those who mind their own business.
Aristotle

advice-d0fbb01f7b763ab253612606.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d0fbb01f7b763ab253612606.body:
(On happiness as virtuous activity) Let us therefore be well assured, that every one enjoys as much happiness as he possesses virtue and wisdom, and acts according to their dictates; since for this we have the example of GOD Himself, who is completely happy, not from any external good, but in Himself, and because such is His nature.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book VII, chapter I, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-039df24ff5d564573fc7a979.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-039df24ff5d564573fc7a979.body:
(On clarity and the expression of thought) Style to be good must be clear, as is proved by the fact that speech which fails to convey a plain meaning will fail to do just what speech has to do.
Aristotle

advice-2cf095dfe8b6482c6ee133f9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2cf095dfe8b6482c6ee133f9.body:
(On virtue as human excellence) The virtues, too, must be something good; for it is by possessing these that we are in a good condition, and they tend to produce good works and good actions.
Aristotle

advice-ade5aa83c5fe800aab0d8691.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ade5aa83c5fe800aab0d8691.body:
(On exercising virtue rather than merely possessing it) To prefer doing of nothing to virtuous activity is also wrong, for happiness consists in action, and many noble ends are produced by the actions of the just and wise.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book VII, chapter III, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-fb9ed661951390d3eacae437.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fb9ed661951390d3eacae437.body:
(On honour as recognition of virtue) Honour is the token of a man's being famous for doing good. It is chiefly and most properly paid to those who have already done good; but also to the man who can do good in future.
Aristotle

advice-cec14f800813d316ff568f81.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cec14f800813d316ff568f81.body:
(On trust in a speaker's character) There are three things which inspire confidence in the orator's own character-the three, namely, that induce us to believe a thing apart from any proof of it: good sense, good moral character, and goodwill.
Aristotle

advice-f286d7abc9ead6be967dbbe1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f286d7abc9ead6be967dbbe1.body:
(On anger, resentment and the desire for revenge) Anger may be defined as an impulse, accompanied by pain, to a conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous slight directed without justification towards what concerns oneself or towards what concerns one's friends.
Aristotle

advice-b9e659325f250fe8d4453b20.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b9e659325f250fe8d4453b20.body:
(On goals revealing the character of government) We shall learn the qualities of governments in the same way as we learn the qualities of individuals, since they are revealed in their deliberate acts of choice; and these are determined by the end that inspires them.
Aristotle

advice-793abc73b13b9df7eea21aa1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-793abc73b13b9df7eea21aa1.body:
(On the judgments of a good person) And that is a greater good which would be chosen by a better man, either absolutely, or in virtue of his being better: for instance, to suffer wrong rather than to do wrong, for that would be the choice of the juster man.
Aristotle

advice-562a61232954cc774f75c1d5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-562a61232954cc774f75c1d5.body:
(On help at a time of special need) Kindness is great if shown to one who is in great need, or who needs what is important and hard to get, or who needs it at an important and difficult crisis; or if the helper is the only, the first, or the chief person to give the help.
Aristotle

advice-59b69183692ae12036602013.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-59b69183692ae12036602013.body:
(On the pleasure of familiarity) Habits also are pleasant; for as soon as a thing has become habitual, it is virtually natural; habit is a thing not unlike nature; what happens often is akin to what happens always, natural events happening always, habitual events often.
Aristotle

advice-0f61d54d561e20859be609ee.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0f61d54d561e20859be609ee.body:
(On truth and probability) Hence the man who makes a good guess at truth is likely to make a good guess at probabilities.
Aristotle

advice-7f99c458ec309cbda2616b1d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7f99c458ec309cbda2616b1d.body:
(On the difference between anger and hatred) And anger is accompanied by pain, hatred is not; the angry man feels pain, but the hater does not.
Aristotle

advice-6c27cfa0fdc2dd5a12ada6f2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6c27cfa0fdc2dd5a12ada6f2.body:
(On desire and pleasure) Everything, too, is pleasant for which we have the desire within us, since desire is the craving for pleasure.
Aristotle

advice-c6f057ccda94c3662ae75eba.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c6f057ccda94c3662ae75eba.body:
(On fear of future harm) Fear may be defined as a pain or disturbance due to a mental picture of some destructive or painful evil in the future.
Aristotle

advice-06bdcf9ea4d5a228ebc8af77.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-06bdcf9ea4d5a228ebc8af77.body:
(On the causes of human actions) Thus every action must be due to one or other of seven causes: chance, nature, compulsion, habit, reasoning, anger, or appetite.
Aristotle

advice-1ea66a8d99e7cd6f948f4444.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1ea66a8d99e7cd6f948f4444.body:
(On grounding arguments in facts) Thus, in handling the question whether justice is or is not a good, we must start with the real facts about justice and goodness.
Aristotle

advice-e40810ab400744a361dab4ae.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e40810ab400744a361dab4ae.body:
(On fame and recognition) Fame means being respected by everybody, or having some quality that is desired by all men, or by most, or by the good, or by the wise.
Aristotle

advice-1667c66fc20a7036b6a80fd5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1667c66fc20a7036b6a80fd5.body:
(On happiness as the final goal of action) For all advice to do things or not to do them is concerned with happiness and with the things that make for or against it; whatever creates or increases happiness or some part of happiness, we ought to do; whatever destroys or hampers happiness, or gives rise to its opposite, we ought not to do.
Aristotle

advice-55ea8593b3ce99b8fedc4277.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-55ea8593b3ce99b8fedc4277.body:
(On justice as a good for others) And those qualities are noble which give more pleasure to other people than to their possessors; hence the nobleness of justice and just actions.
Aristotle

advice-4c9be01165b1dc2462f8a509.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4c9be01165b1dc2462f8a509.body:
(On allocating goods by relevant merit) But that this is evidently absurd is clear from other arts and sciences; for with respect to musicians who play on the flute together, the best flute is not given to him who is of the best family, for he will play never the better for that, but the best instrument ought to be given to him who is the best artist.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book III, chapter XII, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-6f599e6050d9e849546c68ab.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6f599e6050d9e849546c68ab.body:
(On happiness as virtuous activity) Now it is evident that all persons are desirous to live well and be happy; but that some have the means thereof in their own power, others not; and this either through nature or fortune; for many ingredients are necessary to a happy life; but fewer to those who are of a good than to those who are of a bad disposition.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book VII, chapter XIII, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-1644bbb66faa7369aa3f8f5a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1644bbb66faa7369aa3f8f5a.body:
(On metaphor as a way to learn) Good riddles do, in general, provide us with satisfactory metaphors: for metaphors imply riddles, and therefore a good riddle can furnish a good metaphor.
Aristotle

advice-9bea720afff9930ed8b47aaf.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9bea720afff9930ed8b47aaf.body:
(On the difference between anger and hatred) Now whereas anger arises from offences against oneself, enmity may arise even without that; we may hate people merely because of what we take to be their character.
Aristotle

advice-cc34ca658792ff39b8b11f03.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cc34ca658792ff39b8b11f03.body:
(On a gift as a sign of honour) For a present is not only the bestowal of a piece of property, but also a token of honour; which explains why honour-loving as well as money-loving persons desire it.
Aristotle

advice-fa8088d0cdd3362b790c6465.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fa8088d0cdd3362b790c6465.body:
(On desires arising from beliefs) Rational desires are those which we are induced to have; there are many things we desire to see or get because we have been told of them and induced to believe them good.
Aristotle

advice-1c2edaf718305fa2b3384cce.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1c2edaf718305fa2b3384cce.body:
(On trust in a speaker's character) You may use any means you choose to make your hearer receptive; among others, giving him a good impression of your character, which always helps to secure his attention.
Aristotle

advice-027a33fcfccb5deb10c40913.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-027a33fcfccb5deb10c40913.body:
(On qualities that make people likable) And we also feel friendly towards those who praise such good qualities as we possess, and especially if they praise the good qualities that we are not too sure we do possess.
Aristotle

advice-8bbf62cae648264927599c21.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8bbf62cae648264927599c21.body:
(On love and missing an absent person) Indeed, it is always the first sign of love, that besides enjoying some one's presence, we remember him when he is gone, and feel pain as well as pleasure, because he is there no longer.
Aristotle

advice-5ece6785a5e8caa91b6a1319.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5ece6785a5e8caa91b6a1319.body:
(On a listener's prejudices) For just as our minds refuse a favourable reception to a person against whom they are prejudiced, so they refuse it to a speech when they have been favourably impressed by the speech on the other side.
Aristotle

advice-9bb4970b0efc46d4b88c97c0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9bb4970b0efc46d4b88c97c0.body:
(On anger and one's state of mind) Hence people who are afflicted by sickness or poverty or love or thirst or any other unsatisfied desires are prone to anger and easily roused: especially against those who slight their present distress.
Aristotle

advice-718dd31202cfc8d3022c7ceb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-718dd31202cfc8d3022c7ceb.body:
(On how virtue is acquired) Men are worthy and good three ways; by nature, by custom, by reason.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book VII, chapter XIII, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-51629579aafea4da6d2142e7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-51629579aafea4da6d2142e7.body:
(On indignation at another's undeserved good fortune) Indignation is pain caused by the sight of undeserved good fortune.
Aristotle

advice-5185f1e3b4ee19b381abc46e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5185f1e3b4ee19b381abc46e.body:
(On the strength and duration of pleasure) One pleasure is greater than another if it is more unmixed with pain, or more lasting.
Aristotle

advice-11a6bae799dd35737f7ea17d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-11a6bae799dd35737f7ea17d.body:
(On justice as a good for others) Since in every art and science the end aimed at is always good, so particularly in this, which is the most excellent of all, the founding of civil society, the good wherein aimed at is justice; for it is this which is for the benefit of all.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book III, chapter XII, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-140c1f6e7b7bc38a5c0c2b2b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-140c1f6e7b7bc38a5c0c2b2b.body:
(On pity for undeserved misfortune) Pity may be defined as a feeling of pain caused by the sight of some evil, destructive or painful, which befalls one who does not deserve it, and which we might expect to befall ourselves or some friend of ours, and moreover to befall us soon.
Aristotle

advice-04998311ee4f2d9a89355188.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-04998311ee4f2d9a89355188.body:
(On how virtue is acquired) Besides, as in every business and art there are some things which men are to learn first and be made accustomed to, which are necessary to perform their several works; so it is evident that the same thing is necessary in the practice of virtue.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book VIII, chapter I, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-6ede3e923f775c18fac17f9a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6ede3e923f775c18fac17f9a.body:
(On honour as recognition of virtue) Again, those actions are noble for which the reward is simply honour, or honour more than money.
Aristotle

advice-e0ee7328afe671756ced9d13.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e0ee7328afe671756ced9d13.body:
(On desires arising from beliefs) Rational craving is a craving for good, i.e. a wish-nobody wishes for anything unless he thinks it good.
Aristotle

advice-82254726600b5ab8ba320da2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-82254726600b5ab8ba320da2.body:
(On things valued only for public display) We may define what aims at appearance as what a man will not choose if nobody is to know of his having it.
Aristotle

advice-8ed03c88aa36e73a5869d3c9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8ed03c88aa36e73a5869d3c9.body:
(On justice as a good for others) Justice, for instance, is a virtue, and so necessary to society, that all others must yield her the precedence.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book III, chapter XIII, paragraph 2 (Ellis translation)

advice-241bae01ef5e2483d027faad.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-241bae01ef5e2483d027faad.body:
(On consistency in actions and decisions) Another line is, when a contemplated action is inconsistent with any past action, to examine them both together.
Aristotle

advice-200af598ed24ec06fd088ecd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-200af598ed24ec06fd088ecd.body:
(On trust in a speaker's character) Persuasion is achieved by the speaker's personal character when the speech is so spoken as to make us think him credible.
Aristotle

advice-5dd3a8bea84f6b9d5bcb126a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5dd3a8bea84f6b9d5bcb126a.body:
(On defending oneself through speech and reason) Again, it is absurd to hold that a man ought to be ashamed of being unable to defend himself with his limbs, but not of being unable to defend himself with speech and reason, when the use of rational speech is more distinctive of a human being than the use of his limbs.
Aristotle

advice-d31022002e3614f8704ac6b9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d31022002e3614f8704ac6b9.body:
(On moderation in bodily pleasures) Temperance is the virtue that disposes us to obey the law where physical pleasures are concerned; incontinence is the opposite.
Aristotle

advice-7c859e89fdbd874123962006.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7c859e89fdbd874123962006.body:
(On anger over disappointed expectations) Again, we are angrier with our friends than with other people, since we feel that our friends ought to treat us well and not badly.
Aristotle

advice-7e9992aaf6f0a0e02bc33182.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7e9992aaf6f0a0e02bc33182.body:
(On how emotions affect judgment) The Emotions are all those feelings that so change men as to affect their judgements, and that are also attended by pain or pleasure.
Aristotle

advice-7a3167ce71d5c889e3e16649.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7a3167ce71d5c889e3e16649.body:
(On educating moral feelings) Moreover, as music is one of those things which are pleasant, and as virtue itself consists in rightly enjoying, loving, and hating, it is evident that we ought not to learn or accustom ourselves to anything so much as to judge right and rejoice in honourable manners and noble actions.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book VIII, chapter V, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-a96a714f74c6fe884551da4b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a96a714f74c6fe884551da4b.body:
(On studying other peoples' laws and customs) From this we can see that books of travel are useful aids to legislation, since from these we may learn the laws and customs of different races.
Aristotle

advice-c4a7316e12d890d913fa24f0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c4a7316e12d890d913fa24f0.body:
(On what is good in itself) The Noble is that which is both desirable for its own sake and also worthy of praise; or that which is both good and also pleasant because good.
Aristotle

advice-8ae103f6923a765addb70d25.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8ae103f6923a765addb70d25.body:
(On knowing how to lead and obey) But it is a great recommendation to know how to command as well as to obey; and to do both these things well is the virtue of an accomplished citizen.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book III, chapter IV, paragraph 2 (Ellis translation)

advice-33c7ef0474759f62618e6476.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-33c7ef0474759f62618e6476.body:
(On managing wealth) Wealth as a whole consists in using things rather than in owning them; it is really the activity-that is, the use-of property that constitutes wealth.
Aristotle

advice-6d981ec5501fec7ffded3e44.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6d981ec5501fec7ffded3e44.body:
(On metaphor as a way to learn) Now strange words simply puzzle us; ordinary words convey only what we know already; it is from metaphor that we can best get hold of something fresh.
Aristotle

advice-76629b5210d96e71a2acc55c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-76629b5210d96e71a2acc55c.body:
(On choosing under changing circumstances) For it is about our actions that we deliberate and inquire, and all our actions have a contingent character; hardly any of them are determined by necessity.
Aristotle

advice-385ab65e9d3ecb42a1c2018c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-385ab65e9d3ecb42a1c2018c.body:
(On the audience's role in shaping a speech) For of the three elements in speech-making--speaker, subject, and person addressed--it is the last one, the hearer, that determines the speech's end and object.
Aristotle

advice-c7cca6eda879ecfe0972c429.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c7cca6eda879ecfe0972c429.body:
(On consistency in actions and decisions) Another line of argument is based on the fact that men do not always make the same choice on a later as on an earlier occasion, but reverse their previous choice.
Aristotle

advice-13f7e374c9c7347394a59f47.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-13f7e374c9c7347394a59f47.body:
(On clarity and the expression of thought) For it is not enough to know what we ought to say; we must also say it as we ought; much help is thus afforded towards producing the right impression of a speech.
Aristotle

advice-a540b05af3ac162c0c65d131.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a540b05af3ac162c0c65d131.body:
(On difficulty as pain or time spent) Things are done 'easily' when they are done either without pain or quickly: the 'difficulty' of an act lies either in its painfulness or in the long time it takes.
Aristotle

advice-465ce9a94bf55008adeb2ece.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-465ce9a94bf55008adeb2ece.body:
(On pity for undeserved misfortune) In order to feel pity we must also believe in the goodness of at least some people; if you think nobody good, you will believe that everybody deserves evil fortune.
Aristotle

advice-afa6cad33b9e8529cbe8970d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-afa6cad33b9e8529cbe8970d.body:
(On choosing an active or contemplative life) And yet it is of no little consequence on which side the truth lies; for a man of sense must naturally incline to the better choice; both as an individual and a citizen.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book VII, chapter II, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-d37908eba8bb03f44c35c1cb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d37908eba8bb03f44c35c1cb.body:
(On courage in the face of danger) Courage is the virtue that disposes men to do noble deeds in situations of danger, in accordance with the law and in obedience to its commands; cowardice is the opposite.
Aristotle

advice-475e3fac834074a5fd2bc76d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-475e3fac834074a5fd2bc76d.body:
(On virtue as human excellence) Virtue is, according to the usual view, a faculty of providing and preserving good things; or a faculty of conferring many great benefits, and benefits of all kinds on all occasions.
Aristotle

advice-0df492ca1bc60253b3d84301.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0df492ca1bc60253b3d84301.body:
(On clarity and the expression of thought) We can now see that a good writer can produce a style that is distinguished without being obtrusive, and is at the same time clear, thus satisfying our definition of good oratorical prose.
Aristotle

advice-d30ddac4fbe3b28514125832.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d30ddac4fbe3b28514125832.body:
(On comparing utility, nobility and justice) To go further than this, and try to establish abstract laws of greatness and superiority, is to argue without an object; in practical life, particular facts count more than generalizations.
Aristotle

advice-0dd4b6a6397e51bbdb8e4f83.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0dd4b6a6397e51bbdb8e4f83.body:
(On using familiar maxims as arguments) Even hackneyed and commonplace maxims are to be used, if they suit one's purpose: just because they are commonplace, every one seems to agree with them, and therefore they are taken for truth.
Aristotle

advice-a67c3b00befff6ef641c0edf.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a67c3b00befff6ef641c0edf.body:
(On recognising one's own inclinations) Further, a man of a given disposition makes chiefly for the corresponding things: lovers of victory make for victory, lovers of honour for honour, money-loving men for money, and so with the rest.
Aristotle

advice-508bc81221468d0d5e9095f2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-508bc81221468d0d5e9095f2.body:
(On anger over disappointed expectations) Further, we are angered if we happen to be expecting a contrary result: for a quite unexpected evil is specially painful, just as the quite unexpected fulfilment of our wishes is specially pleasant.
Aristotle

advice-faeb8fe3eed20cadcf3e8ec2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-faeb8fe3eed20cadcf3e8ec2.body:
(On anger, resentment and the desire for revenge) To passion and anger are due all acts of revenge.
Aristotle

advice-fb9df2b165cdd8b79a6020bd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fb9df2b165cdd8b79a6020bd.body:
(On persuasion, style and a speech's structure) In making a speech one must study three points: first, the means of producing persuasion; second, the style, or language, to be used; third, the proper arrangement of the various parts of the speech.
Aristotle

advice-4031a7ec005bde0aa75d7580.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4031a7ec005bde0aa75d7580.body:
(On law and distinguishing justice from injustice) Justice is the virtue through which everybody enjoys his own possessions in accordance with the law; its opposite is injustice, through which men enjoy the possessions of others in defiance of the law.
Aristotle

advice-a90a9f0e9fd7b1544387c479.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a90a9f0e9fd7b1544387c479.body:
(On wishing a friend well for their own sake) We may describe friendly feeling towards any one as wishing for him what you believe to be good things, not for your own sake but for his, and being inclined, so far as you can, to bring these things about.
Aristotle

advice-e612eddb0d84865fb88a40ae.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e612eddb0d84865fb88a40ae.body:
(On the difference between anger and hatred) Moreover, anger can be cured by time; but hatred cannot.
Aristotle

advice-0bf26cff17885ab8ad8cf4d1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0bf26cff17885ab8ad8cf4d1.body:
(On the pleasure of familiarity) Habit, whether acquired by mere familiarity or by effort, belongs to the class of pleasant things, for there are many actions not naturally pleasant which men perform with pleasure, once they have become used to them.
Aristotle

advice-2bb73ce507680f7b9cd69ecc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2bb73ce507680f7b9cd69ecc.body:
(On habits formed by repeated actions) Acts are done from habit which men do because they have often done them before.
Aristotle

advice-27d2bc080ae6f702e78a947d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-27d2bc080ae6f702e78a947d.body:
(On generosity in the use of wealth) Liberality disposes us to spend money for others' good; illiberality is the opposite.
Aristotle

advice-2396a6be1c2931160735087b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2396a6be1c2931160735087b.body:
(On anger and one's state of mind) Each man is predisposed, by the emotion now controlling him, to his own particular anger.
Aristotle

advice-2e5c7ed68e8725fca5c53669.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2e5c7ed68e8725fca5c53669.body:
(On ambiguous words that mislead listeners) Words of ambiguous meaning are chiefly useful to enable the sophist to mislead his hearers.
Aristotle

advice-d80060eb09bf837896e0f7f4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d80060eb09bf837896e0f7f4.body:
(On moderation and excess) Further: that which is not in excess is good, and that which is greater than it should be is bad.
Aristotle

advice-bf447d0c08a6812978b6a345.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bf447d0c08a6812978b6a345.body:
(On how emotions affect judgment) Our judgements when we are pleased and friendly are not the same as when we are pained and hostile.
Aristotle

advice-2a07e3f266f9b81ea05eafb4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2a07e3f266f9b81ea05eafb4.body:
(On choosing under changing circumstances) For we turn a thing over in our mind until we have reached the point of seeing whether we can do it or not.
Aristotle

advice-d5468bc4171242e774a48b6f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d5468bc4171242e774a48b6f.body:
(On managing wealth) For men become richer not only by increasing their existing wealth but also by reducing their expenditure.
Aristotle

advice-a5f81dfc1f721af926686996.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a5f81dfc1f721af926686996.body:
(On judgments grounded in experience) We respect, as true, the views of sensible people, such as our elders and those who have been well educated.
Aristotle

advice-38f82b5bcf17086637fa69bd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-38f82b5bcf17086637fa69bd.body:
(On clarity and the expression of thought) Your language will be appropriate if it expresses emotion and character, and if it corresponds to its subject.
Aristotle

advice-fba07059bf201fc1fabe1848.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fba07059bf201fc1fabe1848.body:
(On clarity and the expression of thought) We see, then, that both speech and reasoning are lively in proportion as they make us seize a new idea promptly.
Aristotle

advice-3b07521b077d9bfabef72770.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3b07521b077d9bfabef72770.body:
(On moderation and tact in humour) In all these jokes, whether a word is used in a second sense or metaphorically, the joke is good if it fits the facts.
Aristotle

advice-8830e752bddf104fd049967f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8830e752bddf104fd049967f.body:
(On fear for oneself and pity for others) Speaking generally, anything causes us to feel fear that when it happens to, or threatens, others causes us to feel pity.
Aristotle

advice-38bc46f670d16b21bb3f62e9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-38bc46f670d16b21bb3f62e9.body:
(On supporting claims that are not self-evident) Where a statement, without being paradoxical, is not obviously true, the reason should be added as concisely as possible.
Aristotle

advice-1eca3325f3e71b6612ae231d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1eca3325f3e71b6612ae231d.body:
(On wishing for ends and choosing means) In every art and science, therefore, we should be master of this knowledge, namely, the proper end, and the means to obtain it.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book VII, chapter XIII, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-2cac79c5eca4abd5c6e64b94.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2cac79c5eca4abd5c6e64b94.body:
(On the difference between emulation and envy) Emulation makes us take steps to secure the good things in question, envy makes us take steps to stop our neighbour having them.
Aristotle

advice-c6ca3c2e4f266694ad721bf4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c6ca3c2e4f266694ad721bf4.body:
(On vices that cause no felt pain) All painful things are felt; but the greatest evils, injustice and folly, are the least felt, since their presence causes no pain.
Aristotle

advice-dd586655ca37c892869cdd2b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-dd586655ca37c892869cdd2b.body:
(On persuasion through proof) Persuasion is clearly a sort of demonstration, since we are most fully persuaded when we consider a thing to have been demonstrated.
Aristotle

advice-9b9e78b92c37da5c93087170.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9b9e78b92c37da5c93087170.body:
(On shameful actions and moral character) And we feel more shame when we are likely to be continually seen by, and go about under the eyes of, those who know of our disgrace.
Aristotle

advice-c4f6dd1b4d555c429d7884f3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c4f6dd1b4d555c429d7884f3.body:
(On grounding arguments in facts) The facts must be admitted before you can discuss how important they are; just as the body cannot grow except from something already present.
Aristotle

advice-517ad1893161823063ffe106.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-517ad1893161823063ffe106.body:
(On the audience's role in shaping a speech) Moreover, before some audiences not even the possession of the exactest knowledge will make it easy for what we say to produce conviction.
Aristotle

advice-3e9ea2c63f96b78167f8b924.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3e9ea2c63f96b78167f8b924.body:
(On written and spoken language) The written style is the more finished: the spoken better admits of dramatic delivery-like the kind of oratory that reflects character and the kind that reflects emotion.
Aristotle

advice-8343bb3ffe1ab9df9c9bbdc3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8343bb3ffe1ab9df9c9bbdc3.body:
(On moderation in using epithets) But we must aim at the due mean, or the result will be worse than if we took no trouble at all; we shall get something actually bad instead of something merely not good.
Aristotle

advice-713ee33367b5a50f7b0fe7b9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-713ee33367b5a50f7b0fe7b9.body:
(On emotional appeals to a judge) The arousing of prejudice, pity, anger, and similar emotions has nothing to do with the essential facts, but is merely a personal appeal to the man who is judging the case.
Aristotle

advice-303defe6e953eb4d81b893d9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-303defe6e953eb4d81b893d9.body:
(On choosing under changing circumstances) Clearly counsel can only be given on matters about which people deliberate; matters, namely, that ultimately depend on ourselves, and which we have it in our power to set going.
Aristotle

advice-e2e0fc6a2b43972c0b280d65.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e2e0fc6a2b43972c0b280d65.body:
(On truth and probability) The true and the approximately true are apprehended by the same faculty; it may also be noted that men have a sufficient natural instinct for what is true, and usually do arrive at the truth.
Aristotle

advice-1f8d5b657a49764d5074a095.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1f8d5b657a49764d5074a095.body:
(On speech as a basis of human society) The gift of speech also evidently proves that man is a more social animal than the bees, or any of the herding cattle: for nature, as we say, does nothing in vain, and man is the only animal who enjoys it.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Politics, Book I, chapter II, paragraph 1 (Ellis translation)

advice-c7f8e7001a2e7e486eb12231.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c7f8e7001a2e7e486eb12231.body:
(On defining terms in an argument) Another line of proof is secured by defining your terms.
Aristotle

advice-4948560b362a1214c6513026.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4948560b362a1214c6513026.body:
(On law and distinguishing justice from injustice) We may describe 'wrong-doing' as injury voluntarily inflicted contrary to law.
Aristotle

advice-155e5c8b2cdfff0af1eaa82d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-155e5c8b2cdfff0af1eaa82d.body:
(On brevity: naming rather than describing) To achieve conciseness, do the opposite-put the name instead of the description.
Aristotle

advice-c0530e273ebe846a13ea3bad.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c0530e273ebe846a13ea3bad.body:
(On truth and probability) We should also base our arguments upon probabilities as well as upon certainties.
Aristotle

advice-a41517b5e172de8837000390.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a41517b5e172de8837000390.body:
(On wishing for ends and choosing means) And of two things that which leads more directly to the end in view is the better.
Aristotle

advice-386c1be9ac92493ba5e6fbb6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-386c1be9ac92493ba5e6fbb6.body:
(On clarity and the expression of thought) Clearness is secured by using the words (nouns and verbs alike) that are current and ordinary.
Aristotle

advice-fe8abe20d0b9a93a5311e7fd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fe8abe20d0b9a93a5311e7fd.body:
(On intention as a basis of moral judgment) The worse of two acts of wrong done to others is that which is prompted by the worse disposition.
Aristotle

advice-ec12f67adbf17f74aad1ea35.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ec12f67adbf17f74aad1ea35.body:
(On ambiguous words that mislead listeners) In replying, you must meet ambiguous questions by drawing reasonable distinctions, not by a curt answer.
Aristotle

advice-5ec8c85e712d340fb422c4ce.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5ec8c85e712d340fb422c4ce.body:
(On mistaking a single example for proof) Another line is to use a 'Sign', or single instance, as certain evidence; which, again, yields no valid proof.
Aristotle

advice-f5b599850bffb226c362afc7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f5b599850bffb226c362afc7.body:
(On mockery and confidence in one's qualities) For when we are convinced that we excel in the qualities for which we are jeered at, we can ignore the jeering.
Aristotle

advice-baf25b421a5ded26656b0146.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-baf25b421a5ded26656b0146.body:
(On metaphor as a way to learn) The materials of metaphor must be beautiful to the ear, to the understanding, to the eye or some other physical sense.
Aristotle

advice-06def729e6382ff5b89fffb6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-06def729e6382ff5b89fffb6.body:
(On moderation in self-praise and criticism) With regard to the element of moral character: there are assertions which, if made about yourself, may excite dislike, appear tedious, or expose you to the risk of contradiction; and other things which you cannot say about your opponent without seeming abusive or ill-bred.
Aristotle

advice-aa6072bbeeb471b9002c9301.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-aa6072bbeeb471b9002c9301.body:
(On grounding arguments in facts) So, too, in a court of law: whether we are prosecuting or defending, we must pay attention to the existing facts of the case.
Aristotle

advice-a39fcbc977fb9665a3017c58.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a39fcbc977fb9665a3017c58.body:
(On moderation and tact in humour) Irony better befits a gentleman than buffoonery; the ironical man jokes to amuse himself, the buffoon to amuse other people.
Aristotle

advice-57f7989d3266df1fd2bcc56a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-57f7989d3266df1fd2bcc56a.body:
(On choosing under changing circumstances) Concerning things which exist or will exist inevitably, or which cannot possibly exist or take place, no counsel can be given.
Aristotle

advice-3286927bf27ff76fb3ae39d3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3286927bf27ff76fb3ae39d3.body:
(On choosing under changing circumstances) Most of the things about which we make decisions, and into which therefore we inquire, present us with alternative possibilities.
Aristotle

advice-04839a584bb72f3ccbe3bc73.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-04839a584bb72f3ccbe3bc73.body:
(On affection for oneself and one's creations) And because we are all fond of ourselves, it follows that what is our own is pleasant to all of us, as for instance our own deeds and words.
Aristotle

advice-b29f5e5539276e59635bf548.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b29f5e5539276e59635bf548.body:
(On accounts of the past guiding future choices) If there is narration at all, it will be of past events, the recollection of which is to help the hearers to make better plans for the future.
Aristotle

advice-a8758c92ba928d8901d610c3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a8758c92ba928d8901d610c3.body:
(On exercising virtue rather than merely possessing it) For we do not wish to know what bravery is but to be brave, nor what justice is but to be just, just as we wish to be in health rather than to know what being in health is, and to have our body in good condition rather than to know what good condition is.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book I, chapter 5, Bekker 1215b–1216b (Solomon 1915)

advice-05d42a4b2692a37faf9e1cb9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-05d42a4b2692a37faf9e1cb9.body:
(On friendship for advantage or pleasure) Some friends wrong one another; they love rather the things than the possessor of them; and so they love the persons much as they choose wine because it is pleasant, or wealth because it is useful; for wealth is more useful than its owner.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 11, Bekker 1244a–1244a (Solomon 1915)

advice-fd256efd80db4e01b83082c3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fd256efd80db4e01b83082c3.body:
(On friendliness between hostility and flattery) Friendliness is a mean between animosity and flattery; for the man who readily accommodates himself in all respects to another's desires is a flatterer; the man who opposes every desire is prone to enmity; the man who neither accommodates himself to nor resists every one's pleasure, but only accommodates himself to what seems to be best, is friendly.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 7, Bekker 1233b–1234b (Solomon 1915)

advice-76080cf0e60fb3687b30f7a2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-76080cf0e60fb3687b30f7a2.body:
