(On friendship between good people) Further, all say that justice and injustice are specially exhibited towards friends; the same man seems both good and a friend, and friendship seems a sort of moral habit; and if one wishes to act without injustice, it is enough to make friends, for genuine friends do not act unjustly.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 1, Bekker 1234b–1235b (Solomon 1915)

advice-8c600c4451aae1f9a7028b9a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8c600c4451aae1f9a7028b9a.body:
(On friends quarrelling over expected benefits) The reason of the quarrel is that moral friendship is more noble, but useful friendship more necessary; men come, then, proposing to be moral friends, i.e. friends through virtue; but when some private interest stands in the way, they show clearly they were not so.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 10, Bekker 1242a–1243b (Solomon 1915)

advice-ea83d8dfe15dc3e5572d0490.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ea83d8dfe15dc3e5572d0490.body:
(On happiness as virtuous activity) But happiness, we saw, was the best of things; therefore happiness is the activity of a good soul.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 1, Bekker 1218b–1220a (Solomon 1915)

advice-79a6290667f068093683d4cc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-79a6290667f068093683d4cc.body:
(On happiness over a complete life) But since happiness was something complete, and living is either complete or incomplete and so also virtue—one virtue being a whole, the other a part—and the activity of what is incomplete is itself incomplete, therefore happiness would be the activity of a complete life in accordance with complete virtue.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 1, Bekker 1218b–1220a (Solomon 1915)

advice-7b148ad869b7a336ba117615.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7b148ad869b7a336ba117615.body:
(On possessing knowledge and using it) But since science or knowledge is of two sorts, one the possession, the other the use of knowledge, the man who has, but does not use knowledge may in a sense be justly called ignorant, but in another sense not justly, e.g. if he had not used his knowledge owing to carelessness.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 9, Bekker 1225a–1225b (Solomon 1915)

advice-8bcc763990f7d9561ea7d563.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8bcc763990f7d9561ea7d563.body:
(On wishing a friend well for their own sake) But since active loving is to treat the loved qua loved, and the friend is loved by the friend qua friend and not qua musician or doctor, the pleasure coming from him merely as being himself is the pleasure of friendship; for he loves the object as himself and not for being something else.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-a912c890dbffc2c30ebb2ce6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a912c890dbffc2c30ebb2ce6.body:
(On courage in the face of danger) For bravery consists in following reason, and reason bids one choose the noble.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 1, Bekker 1228a–1230a (Solomon 1915)

advice-9a49ccb1f999b5b96f2ff3e8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9a49ccb1f999b5b96f2ff3e8.body:
(On wishing for ends and choosing means) And in general, in choosing we show both what we choose and for what we choose it, the latter being that for which we choose something else, the former that which we choose for something else.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 10, Bekker 1225b–1227b (Solomon 1915)

advice-4d632a7a93ce975160a4fdb1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4d632a7a93ce975160a4fdb1.body:
(On a friend as a second self) Further, we say about friendship such things as that friendship is equality, and true friends a single soul.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 6, Bekker 1240a–1240b (Solomon 1915)

advice-7dc4b960dd3d53deb1f429f9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7dc4b960dd3d53deb1f429f9.body:
(On choosing a goal to guide one's life) First then about these things we must enjoin every one that has the power to live according to his own choice to set up for himself some object for the beautiful life to aim at, (whether honour or reputation or wealth or culture), with reference to which he will then do all his acts, since not to have one's life organized in view of some end is a mark of much folly.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book I, chapter 2, Bekker 1214b–1214b (Solomon 1915)

advice-d14d52df4975fac2d7be5732.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d14d52df4975fac2d7be5732.body:
(On flattery that feeds self-love) Therefore with some the flatterer is more valued than the friend, for he procures the appearance of both love and superiority for the object of his flattery.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 4, Bekker 1239a–1239b (Solomon 1915)

advice-79769beca71401e50c1b0cf2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-79769beca71401e50c1b0cf2.body:
(On how virtue is acquired) Now to know anything that is noble is itself noble; but regarding virtue, at least, not to know what it is, but to know out of what it arises is most precious.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book I, chapter 5, Bekker 1215b–1216b (Solomon 1915)

advice-bcc078005f17a2f0aa95d95a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bcc078005f17a2f0aa95d95a.body:
(On friends sharing life, thoughts and conversation) Sometimes we wish the object of our love to be happy away from us, sometimes to share the same fortune as ourselves; the wish to be together is characteristic of friendship.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 12, Bekker 1244b–1246a (Solomon 1915)

advice-47d08146e74e46b718457bc1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-47d08146e74e46b718457bc1.body:
(On practical wisdom in choosing actions) For choice is not simply taking but taking one thing before another; and this is impossible without consideration and deliberation; therefore choice arises out of deliberate opinion.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 10, Bekker 1225b–1227b (Solomon 1915)

advice-8666247317c5484945058818.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8666247317c5484945058818.body:
(On virtue as a mean between extremes) In all the mean in relation to us is the best; for this is as knowledge and reason direct us.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 3, Bekker 1220b–1221b (Solomon 1915)

advice-2c24b7e4c95667fee7b7e43b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2c24b7e4c95667fee7b7e43b.body:
(On loving the dead without love in return) Therefore we praise those who persist in their love towards the dead; for they know but are not known.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 4, Bekker 1239a–1239b (Solomon 1915)

advice-bab4bd9c3398e0afdabe82df.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bab4bd9c3398e0afdabe82df.body:
(On goodwill as the beginning of friendship) For goodwill is the beginning of friendship; every friend has goodwill, but not all who have goodwill are friends.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 7, Bekker 1240b–1241a (Solomon 1915)

advice-00fe548ab312751f24f4d760.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-00fe548ab312751f24f4d760.body:
(On friendship between good people) But neither will men act unjustly if they are just; therefore justice and friendship are either the same or not far different.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 1, Bekker 1234b–1235b (Solomon 1915)

advice-16c141651c185e72345ef81b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-16c141651c185e72345ef81b.body:
(On friendship as a bond of community) For justice involves a number of individuals who are partners, and the friend is a partner either in family or in one's scheme of life.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 10, Bekker 1242a–1243b (Solomon 1915)

advice-e20240c84982a8fbdb102b96.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e20240c84982a8fbdb102b96.body:
(On voluntary and involuntary actions) Now, we all admit that of acts that are voluntary and done from the deliberate choice of each man he is the cause, but of involuntary acts he is not himself the cause; and all that he does from deliberate choice he clearly does voluntarily.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 6, Bekker 1222b–1223a (Solomon 1915)

advice-b7940b654fd73cc4e8ff7aa8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b7940b654fd73cc4e8ff7aa8.body:
(On confidence grounded in skill) But those who know how to ascend masts are confident not because they know what is terrible, but because they know how to help themselves in dangers.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 1, Bekker 1228a–1230a (Solomon 1915)

advice-eccaac92adf54de60d5daf03.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-eccaac92adf54de60d5daf03.body:
(On courage and reckless boldness) But reason does not bid a man to endure what is very painful or destructive unless it is noble; now the confident is confident about such things even if reason does not bid him be so, while the coward is not confident even if it does; the brave man alone is confident about them only if reason bids him.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 1, Bekker 1228a–1230a (Solomon 1915)

advice-bc2b50c6266e00fad432a39b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bc2b50c6266e00fad432a39b.body:
(On happiness as virtuous activity) For to do well and to live well is held to be identical with being happy, but each of these— living and doing—is an employment, an activity; for the practical life is one of using or employing, e.g. the smith produces a bridle, the good horseman uses it.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 1, Bekker 1218b–1220a (Solomon 1915)

advice-16a7becbe61bf466dcf54c5d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-16a7becbe61bf466dcf54c5d.body:
(On the meaning of a happy life) About many other things it is difficult to judge well, but most difficult about that on which judgement seems to all easiest and the knowledge of it in the power of any man—viz. what of all that is found in living is desirable, and what, if attained, would satisfy our desire.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book I, chapter 5, Bekker 1215b–1216b (Solomon 1915)

advice-a2ed35621037e6f437f26d47.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a2ed35621037e6f437f26d47.body:
(On the good appropriate to each thing) And to say that all existing things desire some one good is not true; for each seeks its own special good, the eye vision, the body health, and so on.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book I, chapter 8, Bekker 1217b–1218b (Solomon 1915)

advice-4b6a39d0f94db8502a73f847.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4b6a39d0f94db8502a73f847.body:
(On the value of friendship) Further, men believe a friend to be among the greatest of goods, and friendlessness and solitude to be most terrible, because all life and voluntary association is with friends; for we spend our days with our family, kinsmen, or comrades, children, parents, or wife.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 1, Bekker 1234b–1235b (Solomon 1915)

advice-4fa527b2160560b2546b1e15.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4fa527b2160560b2546b1e15.body:
(On likable qualities even in bad people) A man might be pleasant, not as bad but as partaking in some common property, e.g. as being musical, or again, so far as there is something good in all (for which reason some might be glad to associate even with the good), or in so far as they suit each individual; for all have something of the good.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-dfd3ac01e4de965c4a73592b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-dfd3ac01e4de965c4a73592b.body:
(On friendship between good people) The like is brought both under the pleasant and under the good, for the good is simple, but the bad various in form; and the good man is ever like himself and does not change in character; but the bad and the foolish are quite different in the evening from what they were in the morning.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 5, Bekker 1239b–1240a (Solomon 1915)

advice-96c74e0cd5ab1e8508514223.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-96c74e0cd5ab1e8508514223.body:
(On bringing desires under reason) But appetite leads without persuading, being devoid of reason.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 8, Bekker 1223b–1225a (Solomon 1915)

advice-f63a6835a89bf1b6147b6153.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f63a6835a89bf1b6147b6153.body:
(On responsibility for ignorance caused by neglect) Similarly, one might be blamed for not having the knowledge, if it were something easy or necessary and he does not have it because of carelessness or pleasure or pain.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 9, Bekker 1225a–1225b (Solomon 1915)

advice-4063fda0ebae0acac5121596.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4063fda0ebae0acac5121596.body:
(On trust between proven friends) There is no stable friendship without confidence, but confidence needs time.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-845515365a79150ea51e2dc2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-845515365a79150ea51e2dc2.body:
(On trust between proven friends) But it happens with friendship as with other things; as man is not in health merely because he wishes to be so, neither are men at once friends as soon as they wish to be friends.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-3265b03ccf8ef293294397c7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3265b03ccf8ef293294397c7.body:
(On goodwill as the beginning of friendship) So that it is clear that goodwill is concerned with the friendship that depends on character; but goodwill shows itself in merely wishing, friendship in also doing what one wishes.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 7, Bekker 1240b–1241a (Solomon 1915)

advice-095e7987d0167b28f2d341c4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-095e7987d0167b28f2d341c4.body:
(On the trustfulness of good people) Therefore the good are more easily deceived unless experience has taught them distrust.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-fc3f2adcf7935cd35ae06736.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fc3f2adcf7935cd35ae06736.body:
(On desire and deliberate choice) But we do many things from wish suddenly, but no one deliberately chooses an act suddenly.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 8, Bekker 1223b–1225a (Solomon 1915)

advice-a4ff94affba160e7293d7019.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a4ff94affba160e7293d7019.body:
(On friendship and one's relationship with oneself) Therefore to perceive a friend must be in a way to perceive one's self and to know one's self.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 12, Bekker 1244b–1246a (Solomon 1915)

advice-f4b2f25af98b2cde3731e8f8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f4b2f25af98b2cde3731e8f8.body:
(On wishing for ends and choosing means) For the man deliberating deliberates if he has considered, from the point of view of the end, what conduces to bringing the end within his own action, or what he at present can do towards the object.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 10, Bekker 1225b–1227b (Solomon 1915)

advice-30f67e107ad5771871f8d1a9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-30f67e107ad5771871f8d1a9.body:
(On friendship based on mutual advantage) But misfortune shows those who are not really friends, but friends only for some accidental utility.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-2d3aa8a788d2b15ee9ce6e97.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2d3aa8a788d2b15ee9ce6e97.body:
(On moral choices within our power) Hence, it follows that both vice and virtue are voluntary; for there is no necessity to do what is wicked.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 11, Bekker 1227b–1228a (Solomon 1915)

advice-efa5b155751e1b401c188aa6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-efa5b155751e1b401c188aa6.body:
(On friendship as mutual, acknowledged love) And a man becomes a friend when he is loved and returns that love, and this is recognized by the two men in question.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-8891649dad834f11abd077ff.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8891649dad834f11abd077ff.body:
(On intention as a basis of moral judgment) Further, we praise and blame all men with regard to their choice rather than their acts (though activity is more desirable than virtue), because men may do bad acts under compulsion, but no one chooses them under compulsion.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 11, Bekker 1227b–1228a (Solomon 1915)

advice-b2e46c69e26ccad2a5a4c748.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b2e46c69e26ccad2a5a4c748.body:
(On friendliness between hostility and flattery) To act in everything so as to give another pleasure is servility, but to give pleasure seldom and reluctantly is stubbornness.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 3, Bekker 1220b–1221b (Solomon 1915)

advice-24f8213ba2ab217393187585.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-24f8213ba2ab217393187585.body:
(On intention as a basis of moral judgment) Further, it is only because it is not easy to see the nature of a man's choice that we are forced to judge of his character by his acts.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 11, Bekker 1227b–1228a (Solomon 1915)

advice-85e0353965362ea18d835ad0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-85e0353965362ea18d835ad0.body:
(On responding well to pleasure and pain) For by whatever things a soul tends to become better or worse, it is with regard to and in relation to these things that it finds pleasure.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 4, Bekker 1221b–1222a (Solomon 1915)

advice-f6519d8c3301bb3cdcb1770d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f6519d8c3301bb3cdcb1770d.body:
(On trust between proven friends) For a friend is not to be had without trial nor in a single day, but there is need of time and so 'the bushel of salt' has become proverbial.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-61bf020cd40d036591284697.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-61bf020cd40d036591284697.body:
(On friends agreeing in shared affairs) Friendly agreement is not about all things, but only about things that may be done by those in agreement and what relates to their common life.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 7, Bekker 1240b–1241a (Solomon 1915)

advice-2fc6b586fb5d293de4c5de46.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2fc6b586fb5d293de4c5de46.body:
(On moral choices within our power) If, then, a man, having it in his power to do the honourable and abstain from the base, does the opposite, it is clear that this man is not good.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 11, Bekker 1227b–1228a (Solomon 1915)

advice-d4b8e8de916462251e32214f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d4b8e8de916462251e32214f.body:
(On intention as a basis of moral judgment) And therefore it is from a man's choice that we judge his character—that is from the object for the sake of which he acts, not from the act itself.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 11, Bekker 1227b–1228a (Solomon 1915)

advice-5e1096b5f12e54642d9ac9b6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5e1096b5f12e54642d9ac9b6.body:
(On the limits of close friendship) But the need of active loving also prevents one from being at the same time a friend to many; for one cannot be active towards many at the same time.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-3cacb94a839df60335236e9a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3cacb94a839df60335236e9a.body:
(On envy and malicious joy) For, to consider the habits to which they owe their names, envy is pain felt at deserved good fortune, while the feeling of the man who rejoices at misfortunes has itself no name, but such a man shows his nature by rejoicing over undeserved ill fortune.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 7, Bekker 1233b–1234b (Solomon 1915)

advice-895aa20e0aab3a7cb251cc3b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-895aa20e0aab3a7cb251cc3b.body:
(On happiness and its necessary conditions) Then above all we must first define to ourselves without hurry or carelessness in which of our belongings the happy life is lodged, and what are the indispensable conditions of its attainment—for health is not the same as the indispensable conditions of health; and so it is with many other things, e.g. the beautiful life and its indispensable conditions are not identical.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book I, chapter 2, Bekker 1214b–1214b (Solomon 1915)

advice-cc83f7caa20ed806f26f6e27.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cc83f7caa20ed806f26f6e27.body:
(On measuring a benefit between virtuous friends) But that moral friendship is based on purpose is clear, since even if after receiving great benefits one does not repay them through inability, but repays only to the extent of his ability, he acts honourably; and God is satisfied at getting sacrifices as good as our power allows.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 10, Bekker 1242a–1243b (Solomon 1915)

advice-13fc390afcb17b1e2602ce7f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-13fc390afcb17b1e2602ce7f.body:
(On trust between proven friends) Yet in all things it seems the mark of a sensible man to choose the better of two alternatives; and if one has used the worse garment for a long time and not the better, the better is to be chosen, but not in place of an old friend one of whom you do not know whether he is better.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-77e04a14573c964f86688a87.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-77e04a14573c964f86688a87.body:
(On inner goods and external possessions) All goods are either outside or in the soul, and of these those in the soul are more desirable; this distinction we make even in our popular discussions.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 1, Bekker 1218b–1220a (Solomon 1915)

advice-30be92545c3d8fbbaadb143b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-30be92545c3d8fbbaadb143b.body:
(On enjoyment shared with friends) But since both well-being and participation are desirable, it is clear that participation with a smaller good is more desirable than to enjoy a greater good in solitude.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 12, Bekker 1244b–1246a (Solomon 1915)

advice-662eaf640b9a6b60936c2c62.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-662eaf640b9a6b60936c2c62.body:
(On choosing a goal to guide one's life) Therefore, those who have no aim fixed have no inclination to deliberate.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 10, Bekker 1225b–1227b (Solomon 1915)

advice-ea8667d82983ab86ed1822ef.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ea8667d82983ab86ed1822ef.body:
(On exercising virtue rather than merely possessing it) Further, our judging the character of a man by his acts is a confirmation.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 1, Bekker 1218b–1220a (Solomon 1915)

advice-81cc2f39957d30cd2787d7f0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-81cc2f39957d30cd2787d7f0.body:
(On virtue as a mean between extremes) Therefore moral virtue must have to do with the mean and be a sort of mediety.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 3, Bekker 1220b–1221b (Solomon 1915)

advice-5ff2738eecd18e78cd7c203a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5ff2738eecd18e78cd7c203a.body:
(On three friendships: advantage, pleasure and virtue) To speak, then, of friendship in the primary sense only is to do violence to facts, and makes one assert paradoxes; but it is impossible for all friendships to come under one definition.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-7dc6b75854f7b96c884e0833.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7dc6b75854f7b96c884e0833.body:
(On vices that resemble virtues) Therefore, sometimes men really opposite lay claim to the same character, e.g. the lavish to that of the liberal, the self-willed to that of the dignified, the confident to that of the brave.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 5, Bekker 1232a–1233a (Solomon 1915)

advice-5ed0ffaf673eb6c55e464584.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5ed0ffaf673eb6c55e464584.body:
(On friendship among parents, children and siblings) And so fathers love their children—and still more mothers—more than they are loved by them.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 8, Bekker 1241a–1241b (Solomon 1915)

advice-7d1e717f7e54ef59e9e34559.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7d1e717f7e54ef59e9e34559.body:
(On moral choices within our power) So that this is clear, that the object of choice must be one of the things in our own power.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 10, Bekker 1225b–1227b (Solomon 1915)

advice-1c1c907119b854ee4ef22a96.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1c1c907119b854ee4ef22a96.body:
(On courage in the face of danger) The brave endures even what is very formidable, the coward not even what is slightly formidable.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 1, Bekker 1228a–1230a (Solomon 1915)

advice-0be69e816e367e2ced696ffd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0be69e816e367e2ced696ffd.body:
(On choices distorted by pleasure or pain) And the cause is pleasantness or painfulness; for we are so constituted that the pleasant appears good to the soul and the more pleasant better, while the painful appears bad and the more painful worse.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 10, Bekker 1225b–1227b (Solomon 1915)

advice-ae7b52dec0c7f0f4bdafc9d0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ae7b52dec0c7f0f4bdafc9d0.body:
(On voluntary and involuntary actions) For the involuntary if base or bad is not blamable, if good is not praiseworthy, but only the voluntary.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 11, Bekker 1227b–1228a (Solomon 1915)

advice-9cc2e58add995be1045ce6ca.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9cc2e58add995be1045ce6ca.body:
(On fame and recognition) For honour, great or small, is of two kinds; for it may be given by a crowd of ordinary men or by those worthy of consideration; and, again, there is a difference according to the ground on which honour is given.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 5, Bekker 1232a–1233a (Solomon 1915)

advice-5225d68c1cd7f4a37e2f5df3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5225d68c1cd7f4a37e2f5df3.body:
(On wishing for ends and choosing means) The end aimed at is, then, the starting-point of our thought, the end of our thought the starting-point of action.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 11, Bekker 1227b–1228a (Solomon 1915)

advice-bbefb3c3119923bab5b1bcc1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bbefb3c3119923bab5b1bcc1.body:
(On choosing friends free from need and calculation) And we judge better when independent than when in want, and most of all we then seek friends worthy to be lived with.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 12, Bekker 1244b–1246a (Solomon 1915)

advice-c1ee10754d25b7ed5434ee8d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c1ee10754d25b7ed5434ee8d.body:
(On assessing one's own merits fairly) The vain man is he who thinks himself worthy of more than he is, while the poor-spirited thinks himself worthy of less.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 3, Bekker 1220b–1221b (Solomon 1915)

advice-f9883bb17546e6973df50365.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f9883bb17546e6973df50365.body:
(On friendship as the capacity to love) Loving, rather than being loved, depends on lovingness; being loved rather depends on the nature of the object of love.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 4, Bekker 1239a–1239b (Solomon 1915)

advice-46cadc058f9f6ab0f7149804.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-46cadc058f9f6ab0f7149804.body:
(On friendliness between hostility and flattery) The man who is more ready than is proper to join in praise is a flatterer; the man who is less ready is prone to dislike.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 3, Bekker 1220b–1221b (Solomon 1915)

advice-94e9970df043561cd117f51b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-94e9970df043561cd117f51b.body:
(On bias towards one's own advantage) But men judge wrongly what is small; for their own good by its nearness seems great, that of another by its distance small.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 4, Bekker 1239a–1239b (Solomon 1915)

advice-c2b495576388acbdf0738d81.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c2b495576388acbdf0738d81.body:
(On the limits of close friendship) The primary friendship then is not found between many, for it is hard to test many men, for one would have to live with each.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-ef058b0280282674d8995111.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ef058b0280282674d8995111.body:
(On virtue as a mean between extremes) Also magnanimity, magnificence, and liberality are mean states—liberality being shown in the acquisition or expenditure of wealth.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 4, Bekker 1231b–1232a (Solomon 1915)

advice-8a22f03a12a13a9f26da5a1b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8a22f03a12a13a9f26da5a1b.body:
(On contractual friendship and companionship) When, then, friendship proceeds by contract, it is of the civic and strictly legal kind; but when each of the two parties leaves the return for his services to be fixed by the other, we have the moral friendship, that of comrades.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 10, Bekker 1242a–1243b (Solomon 1915)

advice-73bee47a3d3645b8d2fe2d27.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-73bee47a3d3645b8d2fe2d27.body:
(On enjoyment shared with friends) For when we need nothing, then we all seek others to share our enjoyment, those whom we may benefit rather than those who will benefit us.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 12, Bekker 1244b–1246a (Solomon 1915)

advice-509f0b35fcf19ec37e9f5085.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-509f0b35fcf19ec37e9f5085.body:
(On wastefulness and refusing to reckon expenses) And similarly one class of spendthrift is a waster by his disorderly expenditure, the other a fool who cannot bear the pain of calculation.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 4, Bekker 1231b–1232a (Solomon 1915)

advice-1867c8a05f4d6004f75c11d2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1867c8a05f4d6004f75c11d2.body:
(On courage and reckless boldness) The coward, then, fears even what he ought not, the confident is confident even when he ought not to be; the brave man both fears and is confident when he ought to be, and is in this sense a mean, for he is confident or fears as reason bids him.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 1, Bekker 1228a–1230a (Solomon 1915)

advice-b1095c086e661fd750724cec.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b1095c086e661fd750724cec.body:
(On courage and reckless boldness) The cowardly, then, and the confident are misled by their habits; for to the coward what is not terrible seems terrible, and what is slightly terrible greatly so, while in the opposite way, to the confident the terrible seems safe and the very terrible but slightly so; but the brave man thinks things what they truly are.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 1, Bekker 1228a–1230a (Solomon 1915)

advice-eb39438010015ec01525987e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-eb39438010015ec01525987e.body:
(On boasting, pretence and sincerity) For the man who knowingly and falsely depreciates himself is a dissembler; the man who exalts himself is a charlatan; the man who represents himself as he is, is sincere, and in the Homeric phrase 'intelligent'; in general the one loves truth, the other a lie.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 7, Bekker 1233b–1234b (Solomon 1915)

advice-52a7d43325bf485f1da510b5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-52a7d43325bf485f1da510b5.body:
(On the wish to love and to be recognised) By nature some grow up loving, and others ambitious; the former is one who delights rather in loving than in being loved, the other is rather fond of honour.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 4, Bekker 1239a–1239b (Solomon 1915)

advice-95222c20f356a481a87aa06d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-95222c20f356a481a87aa06d.body:
(On judging the value of goods) For to distinguish correctly great goods from small is laudable.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 5, Bekker 1232a–1233a (Solomon 1915)

advice-b49b864a1966c205e244c88b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b49b864a1966c205e244c88b.body:
(On disregarding things only apparently important) But this characteristic seems to belong to the magnanimous man because he cares about few things only, and those great, and not because some one else thinks them so.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 5, Bekker 1232a–1233a (Solomon 1915)

advice-c2483bb7030e091e0b612b1a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c2483bb7030e091e0b612b1a.body:
(On generosity in the use of wealth) The lavish runs short of necessaries; but the liberal man gives his superfluities.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 4, Bekker 1231b–1232a (Solomon 1915)

advice-e52b11e534b3333f8681b3e4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e52b11e534b3333f8681b3e4.body:
(On moderation and tact in humour) Wittiness also is a mean, the witty being a mean between the boorish or stiff and the buffoon.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 7, Bekker 1233b–1234b (Solomon 1915)

advice-5cb5117594fa32aeaaf8c48b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5cb5117594fa32aeaaf8c48b.body:
(On choosing under changing circumstances) For some things are possible, but the production of them is not in our power, some being due to nature, others to other causes; and about these none would attempt to deliberate except in ignorance.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 10, Bekker 1225b–1227b (Solomon 1915)

advice-997a2f59d88d5207f945bdd2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-997a2f59d88d5207f945bdd2.body:
(On choosing a friend after mature reflection) For a formed decision is stable, and where we do not act quickly or easily, we get the decision right.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-f015fde8ffd8028c489fb29f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f015fde8ffd8028c489fb29f.body:
(On exercising virtue rather than merely possessing it) And we crown the actual conquerors, not those who have the power to conquer but do not actually conquer.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 1, Bekker 1218b–1220a (Solomon 1915)

advice-7b09915100434d8e47a05a2d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7b09915100434d8e47a05a2d.body:
(On boasting, pretence and sincerity) The braggart is one who pretends to more than he possesses, the self-depreciator is one who pretends to less.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 3, Bekker 1220b–1221b (Solomon 1915)

advice-bd2cc339506df0db8079838f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bd2cc339506df0db8079838f.body:
(On shame between shamelessness and timidity) Shame is a mean between shamelessness and shyness; for the man who thinks of no one's opinion is shameless, he who thinks of every one's alike is shy, he who thinks only of that of apparently good men is modest.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 7, Bekker 1233b–1234b (Solomon 1915)

advice-9c2cecb33c3ce4935ae6dac8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9c2cecb33c3ce4935ae6dac8.body:
(On moral choices within our power) But of what it depends on him to do or not to do, he is himself the cause; and what he is the cause of depends on him.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 6, Bekker 1222b–1223a (Solomon 1915)

advice-e7bd679f611c4d964e9e184c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e7bd679f611c4d964e9e184c.body:
(On the strength and duration of pleasure) For the absolutely pleasant must be determined as such by the end it realizes and the time for which it continues pleasant.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-a2151ebca34de923d8d0531e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a2151ebca34de923d8d0531e.body:
(On friendship as a bond of community) Civic friendship has been established mainly in accordance with utility; for men seem to have come together because each is not sufficient for himself, though they would have come together anyhow for the sake of living in company.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 10, Bekker 1242a–1243b (Solomon 1915)

advice-ab20cf6e083d3588cd7d58e2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ab20cf6e083d3588cd7d58e2.body:
(On the limits of close friendship) For if it is possible to live with and share the perceptions of many at the same time, it is most desirable that these should be as numerous as possible; but since this is most difficult, the activity of joint perception must exist among fewer.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 12, Bekker 1244b–1246a (Solomon 1915)

advice-d4afc605d9ac17e09e640e5c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d4afc605d9ac17e09e640e5c.body:
(On friends balancing opposite characters) Therefore some delight in what is unlike themselves, the rigid in the witty, the energetic in the lazy; for they reduce each other to the mean state.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 5, Bekker 1239b–1240a (Solomon 1915)

advice-2dd7105f6d5010c8c831c6e2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2dd7105f6d5010c8c831c6e2.body:
(On dignity between wilfulness and servility) Dignity is a mean between self-will and too great obligingness; for the contemptuous man who lives with no consideration for another is self-willed; the man who adapts his whole life to another and is submissive to everybody is too obliging; but he who acts thus in certain cases but not in others, and only to those worthy, is dignified.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book III, chapter 7, Bekker 1233b–1234b (Solomon 1915)

advice-f84f24c714129322cfc7cafc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f84f24c714129322cfc7cafc.body:
(On a friend wishing to share another's pain) For the friend wants, if possible, not merely to feel pain along with his friend, but to feel the same pain, e.g. to feel thirsty when he is thirsty, if that were possible, and if not, then to feel a pain as like as possible.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 6, Bekker 1240a–1240b (Solomon 1915)

advice-8b56002eaff703502340cec2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8b56002eaff703502340cec2.body:
(On the changeable friendships of youth) But the friendship based on pleasure is that of the young, for they are sensitive to pleasure; therefore also their friendship easily changes; for with a change in their characters as they grow up there is also a change in their pleasures.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book VII, chapter 2, Bekker 1235b–1238b (Solomon 1915)

advice-713019dbab52e83dc7d90365.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-713019dbab52e83dc7d90365.body:
(On activities of the soul that form virtue) Virtue too, then, is that sort of condition which is produced by the best movements in the soul, and from which are produced the soul's best works and feelings; and by the same things, if they happen in one way, it is produced, but if they happen in another, it is destroyed.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book II, chapter 1, Bekker 1218b–1220a (Solomon 1915)

advice-69146e877e283c9493516975.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-69146e877e283c9493516975.body:
(On clarifying true but confused judgments) For by advancing from true but obscure judgements he will arrive at clear ones, exchanging ever the usual confused statement for more real knowledge.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Eudemian Ethics, Book I, chapter 6, Bekker 1216b–1217a (Solomon 1915)

advice-b16e1721129a6cb90f4db38c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b16e1721129a6cb90f4db38c.body:
(On happiness over a complete life) For as it is not one swallow or one fine day that makes a spring, so it is not one day or a short time that makes a man blessed and happy.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book I, chapter V, paragraph 4 (Chase edition)

advice-db6d6ce1d279ab90f3f0cc9e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-db6d6ce1d279ab90f3f0cc9e.body:
(On the starting points of reasoning) It is thought, I mean, that the starting-point or principle is more than half the whole matter, and that many of the points of enquiry come simultaneously into view thereby.
Aristotle

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.reference: Book I, chapter V, paragraph 9 (Chase edition)

advice-390899724332a3f338572284.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-390899724332a3f338572284.body:
To understand nature as a whole, learn to bring the individual facts you have studied together in a clear, concise account.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 2

advice-fb79d0a51a125e00565142c3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fb79d0a51a125e00565142c3.body:
(Herodotus: recipient of a letter on precise concepts) First of all, then, Herodotus, one must determine with exactness the notion comprehended under each separate word, in order to be able to refer to it, as to a certain criterion, the conceptions which emanate from ourselves, the ulterior researches and the difficulties; otherwise the judgment has no foundation.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 3

advice-a9f4fa0cb55282d34f8769b5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a9f4fa0cb55282d34f8769b5.body:
(Herodotus: recipient of a letter on precise concepts) In fact, it is absolutely necessary that in every word we should perceive directly, and without the assistance of any demonstration, the fundamental notion which it expresses, if we wish to have any foundation to which we may refer our researches, our difficulties, and our personal judgments, whatever in other respects may be the criterion which we adopt, whether we take as our standard the impressions produced on our senses, or the actual impression in general; or whether we cling to the idea by itself, or to any other criterion.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 3

advice-77ee1d64308ceb948372bfbc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-77ee1d64308ceb948372bfbc.body:
(On matter’s eternity in Epicurean physics) And, first of all, we must admit that nothing can come of that which does not exist; for, were the fact otherwise, then every thing would be produced from everything, and there would be no need of any seed.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 5

advice-961e4052b6102c5f5e329b58.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-961e4052b6102c5f5e329b58.body:
(On matter’s eternity in Epicurean physics) And if that which disappeared were so absolutely destroyed as to become non-existent, then every thing would soon perish, as the things with which they would be dissolved would have no existence.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 5

advice-45dd3d4dd4e57895920a65f0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-45dd3d4dd4e57895920a65f0.body:
(On matter’s eternity in Epicurean physics) But, in truth, the universal whole always was such as it now is, and always will be such. For there is nothing into which it can change; for there is nothing beyond this universal whole which can penetrate into it, and produce any change in it.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 5

advice-1ca3a92d898ddc0fe5a867b6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1ca3a92d898ddc0fe5a867b6.body:
(On the infinite universe having no outer boundary) The universe is infinite. For that which is finite has an extreme, and that which has an extreme is looked at in relation to something else. Consequently, that which has not an extreme, has no boundary; and if it has no boundary, it must be infinite, and not terminated by any limit.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 7

advice-b69740276d9902e4ecb13698.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b69740276d9902e4ecb13698.body:
(Epicurus’s atoms are indivisible moving particles) The atoms are in a continual state of motion.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 9

advice-784750e17bbf26743f30b147.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-784750e17bbf26743f30b147.body:
(On the Epicurean doctrine of countless worlds) But, again, the worlds also are infinite, whether they resemble this one of ours or whether they are different from it.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 11

advice-4a7dbbc5f07fcf892e6a5cd7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4a7dbbc5f07fcf892e6a5cd7.body:
(On a moving body’s position in Epicurean physics) At all events, a body in motion does not find itself, at any moment imaginable, in two places at the same time; that is quite inconceivable.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 12

advice-96302398f0fb80e96ce78f20.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-96302398f0fb80e96ce78f20.body:
(On distinguishing sensory evidence from opinions requiring verification) Error and false judgments always depend upon the supposition that a preconceived idea will be confirmed, or at all events will not be overturned, by evidence.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 16

advice-6a494bbdb3b6d9895ccaa6bd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6a494bbdb3b6d9895ccaa6bd.body:
(On the infinite universe having no outer boundary) Moreover, we must not say (while speaking of the infinite), that such or such a point is the highest point of it, or the lowest. For height and lowness must not be predicated of the infinite.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 25

advice-54c8e1218371379ab26ee970.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-54c8e1218371379ab26ee970.body:
(The soul: fine matter resembling breath and heat) Let us now return to the study of the affections, and of the sensations; for this will be the best method of proving that the soul is a bodily substance composed of slight particles, diffused over all the members of the body, and presenting a great analogy to a sort of spirit, having an admixture of heat, resembling at one time one, and at another time the other of those two principles.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 29

advice-2ac017da31f6c5bb61121a71.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2ac017da31f6c5bb61121a71.body:
(The soul: fine matter resembling breath and heat) We must admit that it is in the soul most especially that the principle of sensation resides.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 29

advice-676795541c7e52b71e864891.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-676795541c7e52b71e864891.body:
(Void in Epicurean physics makes the movement of material bodies possible) Now, nothing can be conceived in itself as incorporeal except the vacuum; but the vacuum cannot be either passive or active; it is only the condition and the place of movement.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 32

advice-f0ae3fd12e81f43d58e02383.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f0ae3fd12e81f43d58e02383.body:
(The soul: fine matter resembling breath and heat) Accordingly, they who pretend that the soul is incorporeal, utter words destitute of sense; for, if it had this character, it would not be able either to do or to suffer anything; but, as it is, we see plainly enough that it is liable to both these circumstances.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 32

advice-d0e3916112bb1d8695015821.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d0e3916112bb1d8695015821.body:
(On time observed through movement, rest, and changes) It is, in fact, evident, that we speak of time as composed of days and nights, and parts of days and nights; passiveness and impassibility, movement and repose, are equally comprised in time.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 36

advice-cd83bf7e074827ff2d191a28.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cd83bf7e074827ff2d191a28.body:
(On human skills developing through nature and experience) Again, we must admit that in many and various respects, nature is both instructed and constrained by circumstances themselves; and that reason subsequently makes perfect and enriches with additional discoveries the things which it has borrowed from nature; in some cases rapidly, and in others more slowly.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 41

advice-9680381bed0c619d5a49a358.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9680381bed0c619d5a49a358.body:
(On explaining the heavens without divine management) As to the heavenly phænomena, such as the motion and course of the stars, the eclipses, their rising and setting, and all other appearances of the same kind, we must beware of thinking that they are produced by any particular being which has regulated, or whose business it is to regulate, for the future, the order of the world, a being immortal and perfectly happy; for the cares and anxieties, the benevolence and the anger, far from being compatible with felicity, are, on the contrary, the consequence of weakness, of fear, and of the want which a thing has of something else.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 42

advice-3b04618895280a1a3b2db28a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3b04618895280a1a3b2db28a.body:
(Celestial phenomena: several possible natural explanations) These heavenly phænomena admit of several explanations; they have no reason of a necessary character, and one may explain them in different manners.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 43

advice-af45ba86c80254882e892532.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-af45ba86c80254882e892532.body:
(On understanding the heavens through observations on Earth) Let us content ourselves with examining how it is that similar phænomena are brought about under our own eyes, and let us apply these observations to the heavenly objects and to everything which is not known but indirectly.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 44

advice-616b1860edd5a01deb25f7e3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-616b1860edd5a01deb25f7e3.body:
(On distinguishing one necessary explanation from several possible explanations) Let us despise those people who are unable to distinguish facts susceptible of different explanations from others which can only exist and be explained in one single way.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 44

advice-eeb0c50509abbe399a018264.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-eeb0c50509abbe399a018264.body:
(On sensory evidence as the basis of Epicurean knowledge) Accordingly, it is well to pay a scrupulous attention to existing phænomena and to the sensations, to the general sensations for general things, and to the particular sensations for particular things.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Herodotus; source paragraph 45

advice-4cde304dcb047c3c59194721.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4cde304dcb047c3c59194721.body:
(On philosophy as lifelong care for the soul) Let no one delay to study philosophy while he is young, and when he is old let him not become weary of the study; for no man can ever find the time unsuitable or too late to study the health of his soul. And he who asserts either that it is not yet time to philosophize, or that the hour is passed, is like a man who should say that the time is not yet come to be happy, or that it is too late.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 1

advice-5207a317a2949c02462b9f6a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5207a317a2949c02462b9f6a.body:
(Happiness as the aim of philosophical reflection) It is right then for a man to consider the things which produce happiness, since, if happiness is present, we have everything, and when it is absent, we do everything with a view to possess it.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 2

advice-7ebba7fe3a137f31ad983a72.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7ebba7fe3a137f31ad983a72.body:
(Epicurus’s gods: immortal and free from disturbing passions) And that man is not impious who discards the Gods believed in by the many, but he who applies to the Gods the opinions entertained of them by the many.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 2

advice-99019c642d015c9fd1a28052.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-99019c642d015c9fd1a28052.body:
(On fear of death: after death there is no sensation) For it is very absurd that that which does not distress a man when it is present, should afflict him when only expected.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 3

advice-8efb963647532ecc046eedb9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8efb963647532ecc046eedb9.body:
(On the quality of life rather than its length) Nor is the not living a thing feared, since living is not connected with it: nor does the wise man think not living an evil; but, just as he chooses food, not preferring that which is most abundant, but that which is nicest; so too, he enjoys time, not measuring it as to whether it is of the greatest length, but as to whether it is most agreeable.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 3

advice-3273d81a4aa9c0d6ab0ca7fa.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3273d81a4aa9c0d6ab0ca7fa.body:
(Learning to live well and to face death is one and the same task) And he who enjoins a young man to live well, and an old man to die well, is a simpleton, not only because of the constantly delightful nature of life, but also because the care to live well is identical with the care to die well.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 3

advice-12a77c2de6ca3dc39e5e83ba.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-12a77c2de6ca3dc39e5e83ba.body:
(On reasonable choices when the future is unknown) We must recollect, that the future is not our own, nor, on the other hand, is it wholly not our own, I mean so that we can never altogether await it with a feeling of certainty that it will be, nor altogether despair of it as what will never be.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 4

advice-8c5f95047c196b0378b482f6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8c5f95047c196b0378b482f6.body:
(Choosing pleasures wisely and accepting necessary pains) Every pleasure is therefore a good on account of its own nature, but it does not follow that every pleasure is worthy of being chosen; just as every pain is an evil, and yet every pain must not be avoided.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 6

advice-818aa18a30effcc625b6de56.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-818aa18a30effcc625b6de56.body:
(Epicurean simplicity of life and modest needs) And, we think, contentment a great good, not in order that we may never have but a little, but in order that, if we have not much, we may make use of a little, being genuinely persuaded that those men enjoy luxury most completely who are the best able to do without it; and that everything which is natural is easily provided, and what is useless is not easily procured.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 6

advice-5bc52172f5310b59c60286f1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5bc52172f5310b59c60286f1.body:
(Epicurean simplicity of life and modest needs) And simple flavours give as much pleasure as costly fare, when everything that can give pain, and every feeling of want, is removed; and corn and water give the most extreme pleasure when any one in need eats them.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 6

advice-780fb4d7aa185d389dc15752.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-780fb4d7aa185d389dc15752.body:
(Epicurean simplicity of life and modest needs) To accustom one’s self, therefore, to simple and inexpensive habits is a great ingredient in the perfecting of health, and makes a man free from hesitation with respect to the necessary uses of life.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 6

advice-76de8f75225221e84eebc819.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-76de8f75225221e84eebc819.body:
(Epicurean pleasure: absence of pain and mental disturbance) When, therefore, we say that pleasure is a chief good, we are not speaking of the pleasures of the debauched man, or those which lie in sensual enjoyment, as some think who are ignorant, and who do not entertain our opinions, or else interpret them perversely; but we mean the freedom of the body from pain, and of the soul from confusion.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 6

advice-c419bf3a0230b40feaeb07f1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c419bf3a0230b40feaeb07f1.body:
(Sober reasoning rather than pursuit of sensual excess) For it is not continued drinkings and revels, or the enjoyment of female society, or feasts of fish and other such things, as a costly table supplies, that make life pleasant, but sober contemplation, which examines into the reasons for all choice and avoidance, and which puts to flight the vain opinions from which the greater part of the confusion arises which troubles the soul.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 6

advice-b0d1c079387b5e288fb5f2dc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b0d1c079387b5e288fb5f2dc.body:
(Prudence and virtue as conditions of a pleasant life) Now, the beginning and the greatest good of all these things is prudence, on which account prudence is something more valuable than even philosophy, inasmuch as all the other virtues spring from it, teaching us that it is not possible to live pleasantly unless one also lives prudently, and honourably, and justly; and that one cannot live prudently, and honestly, and justly, without living pleasantly; for the virtues are connate with living agreeably, and living agreeably is inseparable from the virtues.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 7

advice-080eb7ca12d206ae7cb99796.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-080eb7ca12d206ae7cb99796.body:
(On Epicurus’s rejection of absolute predestination) Since it would be better to follow the fables about the Gods than to be a slave to the fate of the natural philosopher; for the fables which are told give us a sketch, as if we could avert the wrath of God by paying him honour; but the other presents us with necessity who is inexorable.
Epicurus

sources.author: Epicurus
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius X; Letter to Menoeceus; source paragraph 7

advice-a21daf93467abc22bec68bb4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a21daf93467abc22bec68bb4.body:
(Epicurus’s gods: immortal and free from disturbing passions) That which is happy and imperishable, neither has trouble itself, nor does it cause it to anything; so that it is not subject to the feelings of either anger or gratitude; for these feelings only exist in what is weak.
Epicurus

advice-f8ccb1c8028c3bb007e9fb0f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f8ccb1c8028c3bb007e9fb0f.body:
(On fear of death: after death there is no sensation) Death is nothing to us; for that which is dissolved is devoid of sensation, and that which is devoid of sensation is nothing to us.
Epicurus

advice-d7c5831055cd751d0fadc78d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d7c5831055cd751d0fadc78d.body:
(Epicurean pleasure: absence of pain and mental disturbance) The limit of the greatness of the pleasures is the removal of everything which can give pain. And where pleasure is, as long as it lasts, that which gives pain, or that which feels pain, or both of them, are absent.
Epicurus

advice-5a77186b929c56ed8d65c491.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5a77186b929c56ed8d65c491.body:
(Epicurus’s ancient argument about the duration of pain) Pain does not abide continuously in the flesh, but in its extremity it is present only a very short time. That pain which only just exceeds the pleasure in the flesh, does not last many days. But long diseases have in them more that is pleasant than painful to the flesh.
Epicurus

advice-9c0f940a55015f390e472be7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9c0f940a55015f390e472be7.body:
(Prudence and virtue as conditions of a pleasant life) It is not possible to live pleasantly without living prudently, and honourably, and justly; nor to live prudently, and honourably, and justly, without living pleasantly. But he to whom it does not happen to live prudently, honourably, and justly, cannot possibly live pleasantly.
Epicurus

advice-0091f0af50e9232dd9582cc1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0091f0af50e9232dd9582cc1.body:
(Political power as a means of security, not an end) For the sake of feeling confidence and security with regard to men, and not with reference to the nature of government and kingly power being a good, some men have wished to be eminent and powerful, in order that others might attain this feeling by their means; thinking that so they would secure safety as far as men are concerned. So that, if the life of such men is safe, they have attained to the nature of good; but if it is not safe, then they have failed in obtaining that for the sake of which they originally desired power according to the order of nature.
Epicurus

advice-5c7970f984a9530dff0ff1b8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5c7970f984a9530dff0ff1b8.body:
(Choosing pleasures wisely and accepting necessary pains) No pleasure is intrinsically bad: but the efficient causes of some pleasures bring with them a great many perturbations of pleasure.
Epicurus

advice-1098c1305fa28a53d57abf7f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1098c1305fa28a53d57abf7f.body:
(A thought experiment: pleasure throughout the body and time) If every pleasure were condensed, if one may so say, and if each lasted long, and affected the whole body, or the essential parts of it, then there would be no difference between one pleasure and another.
Epicurus

advice-cb1f3fb4433a59555697d715.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cb1f3fb4433a59555697d715.body:
(On pleasures considered under the condition of eliminating fear) If those things which make the pleasures of debauched men, put an end to the fears of the mind, and to those which arise about the heavenly bodies, and death, and pain; and if they taught us what ought to be the limit of our desires, we should have no pretence for blaming those who wholly devote themselves to pleasure, and who never feel any pain or grief (which is the chief evil) from any quarter.
Epicurus

advice-32e91a850e0ee1b9c2e48e5d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-32e91a850e0ee1b9c2e48e5d.body:
(Here “physiology” means studying nature to dispel fear) If apprehensions relating to the heavenly bodies did not disturb us, and if the terrors of death have no concern with us, and if we had the courage to contemplate the boundaries of pain and of the desires, we should have no need of physiological studies.
Epicurus

advice-41b047955ec4a3c487bb1439.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-41b047955ec4a3c487bb1439.body:
(Here “physiology” means studying nature to dispel fear) It would not be possible for a person to banish all fear about those things which are called most essential, unless he knew what is the nature of the universe, or if he had any idea that the fables told about it could be true; and therefore, it is, that a person cannot enjoy unmixed pleasure without physiological knowledge.
Epicurus

advice-6c6276ef970419c064aad3fd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6c6276ef970419c064aad3fd.body:
(On safety from people and fear of the cosmos) It would be no good for a man to secure himself safety as far as men are concerned, while in a state of apprehension as to all the heavenly bodies, and those under the earth, and in short, all those in the infinite.
Epicurus

advice-cd008a1be36bde72185bfed6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cd008a1be36bde72185bfed6.body:
(Security through tranquility and freedom from ambition) Irresistible power and great wealth may, up to a certain point, give us security as far as men are concerned; but the security of men in general depends upon the tranquillity of their souls, and their freedom from ambition.
Epicurus

advice-cac804fbd0026c1d653f698b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cac804fbd0026c1d653f698b.body:
(Epicurean simplicity of life and modest needs) The riches of nature are defined and easily procurable; but vain desires are insatiable.
Epicurus

advice-e2a6e0a73591b9d0557873bc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e2a6e0a73591b9d0557873bc.body:
(On rational direction of life taking precedence over luck) Chance has little influence on the wise person; reason has directed, directs, and will direct the greatest and most important matters throughout life.
Epicurus

advice-3e3b4e6898b2bfb82e25ec56.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3e3b4e6898b2bfb82e25ec56.body:
(Justice and peace of conscience) The just man is the freest of all men from disquietude; but the unjust man is a perpetual prey to it.
Epicurus

advice-58b580866b73eec8530bbf8c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-58b580866b73eec8530bbf8c.body:
(Epicurean pleasure: absence of pain and mental disturbance) Pleasure in the flesh is not increased, when once the pain arising from want is removed; it is only diversified. The most perfect happiness of the soul depends on these reflections, and on opinions of a similar character on all those questions which cause the greatest alarm to the mind.
Epicurus

advice-a9b2d44defc3fc3da0d64d45.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a9b2d44defc3fc3da0d64d45.body:
(On the limits of pleasure and accepting finite life) Infinite and finite time both have equal pleasure, if any one measures its limits by reason.
Epicurus

advice-7557f792332bdef87248b07e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7557f792332bdef87248b07e.body:
(On the limits of pleasure and accepting finite life) If the flesh could experience boundless pleasure, it would want to dispose of eternity. But reason, enabling us to conceive the end and dissolution of the body, and liberating us from the fears relative to eternity, procures for us all the happiness of which life is capable, so completely that we have no further occasion to include eternity in our desires. In this disposition of mind, man is happy even when his troubles engage him to quit life; and to die thus, is for him only to interrupt a life of happiness.
Epicurus

advice-08112b4ca8cb46f1c6d319df.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-08112b4ca8cb46f1c6d319df.body:
(Epicurean simplicity of life and modest needs) He who is acquainted with the limits of life knows, that that which removes the pain which arises from want, and which makes the whole of life perfect, is easily procurable; so that he has no need of those things which can only be attained with trouble.
Epicurus

advice-7ceb98cbedcf373de8d01546.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7ceb98cbedcf373de8d01546.body:
(The ultimate goal here is tranquil life without pain) But as to the subsisting end, we ought to consider it with all the clearness and evidence which we refer to whatever we think and believe; otherwise, all things will be full of confusion and uncertainty of judgment.
Epicurus

advice-ea74560b1dc3fb0c92ddb8eb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ea74560b1dc3fb0c92ddb8eb.body:
(On sensory evidence as the basis of Epicurean knowledge) If you resist all the senses, you will not even have anything left to which you can refer, or by which you may be able to judge of the falsehood of the senses which you condemn.
Epicurus

advice-b29ae23d96e1da0805720139.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b29ae23d96e1da0805720139.body:
(On distinguishing sensory evidence from opinions requiring verification) If you simply discard one sense, and do not distinguish between the different elements of the judgment, so as to know on the one hand, the induction which goes beyond the actual sensation, or, on the other, the actual and immediate notion; the affections, and all the conceptions of the mind which lean directly on the sensible representation, you will be imputing trouble into the other sense, and destroying in that quarter every species of criterion. If you allow equal authority to the ideas, which, being only inductive, require to be verified, and to those which bear about them an immediate certainty, you will not escape error; for you will be confounding doubtful opinions with those which are not doubtful, and true judgments with those of a different character.
Epicurus

advice-ef55bfd586332b977d5d63a2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ef55bfd586332b977d5d63a2.body:
(The ultimate goal here is tranquil life without pain) If, on every occasion, we do not refer every one of our actions to the chief end of nature, if we turn aside from that to seek or avoid some other object, there will be a want of agreement between our words and our actions.
Epicurus

advice-4d5d4c5705d9a0f5d8cab5fd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4d5d4c5705d9a0f5d8cab5fd.body:
(On friendship as protection and support for happiness) Of all the things which wisdom provides for the happiness of the whole life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friendship. The same opinion encourages man to trust that no evil will be everlasting, or even of long duration; as it sees that, in the space of life allotted to us, the protection of friendship is most sure and trustworthy.
Epicurus

advice-9a136e941ffc3d1b10edc580.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9a136e941ffc3d1b10edc580.body:
(On necessary, natural, and empty desires) Of the desires, some are natural and necessary, some natural, but not necessary, and some are neither natural nor necessary, but owe their existence to vain opinions.
Epicurus

advice-fe91e937f1ac549d94eaf1ad.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fe91e937f1ac549d94eaf1ad.body:
(On necessary, natural, and empty desires) Those desires which do not lead to pain, if they are not satisfied, are not necessary. It is easy to impose silence on them when they appear difficult to gratify, or likely to produce injury.
Epicurus

advice-d124bc0a3c90f7cfadb782e7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d124bc0a3c90f7cfadb782e7.body:
(On necessary, natural, and empty desires) When the natural desires, the failing to satisfy which is, nevertheless, not painful, are violent and obstinate, it is a proof that there is an admixture of vain opinion in them; for then energy does not arise from their own nature, but from the vain opinions of men.
Epicurus

advice-16ff0f9ed2b8e4ffd5c344bd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-16ff0f9ed2b8e4ffd5c344bd.body:
(Justice as an agreement not to harm one another) Natural justice is a covenant of what is suitable, leading men to avoid injuring one another, and being injured.
Epicurus

advice-89bc553aaf23b9881147af2f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-89bc553aaf23b9881147af2f.body:
(Justice as an agreement not to harm one another) For animals incapable of making mutual agreements neither to harm nor to be harmed, there is neither justice nor injustice. The same holds for peoples who are unable or unwilling to make such agreements.
Epicurus

advice-ea4aa9a46efcbe5eccfe9953.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ea4aa9a46efcbe5eccfe9953.body:
(Justice as an agreement not to harm one another) Justice has no independent existence; it results from mutual contracts, and establishes itself wherever there is a mutual engagement to guard against doing or sustaining mutual injury.
Epicurus

advice-6a7bd76c90ef4853cbebb72e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6a7bd76c90ef4853cbebb72e.body:
(On injustice and fear of punishment) Injustice is not intrinsically bad; it has this character only because there is joined with it a fear of not escaping those who are appointed to punish actions marked with that character.
Epicurus

advice-c011a1f9ba19cec77dddb21a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c011a1f9ba19cec77dddb21a.body:
(On injustice and fear of punishment) It is not possible for a man who secretly does anything in contravention of the agreement which men have made with one another, to guard against doing, or sustaining mutual injury, to believe that he shall always escape notice, even if he have escaped notice already ten thousand times; for, till his death, it is uncertain whether he will not be detected.
Epicurus

advice-7b34b9b13296db3bce3a2161.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7b34b9b13296db3bce3a2161.body:
(On laws being just through their usefulness for coexistence) In a general point of view, justice is the same thing to every one; for there is something advantageous in mutual society. Nevertheless, the difference of place, and divers other circumstances, make justice vary.
Epicurus

advice-c2ae732705e21cee6bc2da6b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c2ae732705e21cee6bc2da6b.body:
(On laws being just through their usefulness for coexistence) From the moment that a thing declared just by the law is generally recognized as useful for the mutual relations of men, it becomes really just, whether it is universally regarded as such or not. But if, on the contrary, a thing established by law is not really useful for the social relations, then it is not just; and if that which was just, inasmuch as it was useful, loses this character, after having been for some time considered so, it is not less true that, during that time, it was really just, at least for those who do not perplex themselves about vain words, but who prefer, in every case, examining and judging for themselves.
Epicurus

advice-bc023f446ca2014d95ddcf05.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bc023f446ca2014d95ddcf05.body:
