advice-af6d9625208982d4669facf7.body:
(Learning, experience, and wise guidance) Education is an ornament in prosperity and a refuge in adversity.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-a0395ebac93018f04f1d4d2b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a0395ebac93018f04f1d4d2b.body:
(Reasoned persuasion instead of compulsion) Encouragement and reasoned persuasion are better guides to virtue than law and compulsion. Someone restrained only by law may do wrong in secret; someone persuaded of what is right is unlikely to do wrong, openly or secretly.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-5f600121ec4323ae07a1359b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5f600121ec4323ae07a1359b.body:
(Learning, experience, and wise guidance) Education gains noble things through effort; shameful things grow by themselves, without effort.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-0b05422d68498f22b71ad4f4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0b05422d68498f22b71ad4f4.body:
(Learning, experience, and wise guidance) Young people can have understanding and old people can lack it. Time alone does not teach wisdom; timely education and nature do.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-f9aea70df129f12fdb48834b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f9aea70df129f12fdb48834b.body:
(The influence of bad company) Constant company with bad people strengthens a bad disposition.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-f65c8d99fa193607f013cc0a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f65c8d99fa193607f013cc0a.body:
(Learning, experience, and wise guidance) The hopes of educated people are better than the wealth of the uneducated.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-073925a6128a529fc3dabca3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-073925a6128a529fc3dabca3.body:
(True friendship and how it is tested) Shared understanding creates friendship.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-9d5832fc3325b15518c1d342.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9d5832fc3325b15518c1d342.body:
(Moderation in desires and pleasures) Pleasure and displeasure mark the boundary between what benefits us and what harms us.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-5faf673212859cd80bfa5f5c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5faf673212859cd80bfa5f5c.body:
(Inner joy and the value of the present) The best life has as much cheerfulness and as little grief as possible. This comes from refusing to place our pleasures in things that perish.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-c25d29eef52315cc1e673ef0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c25d29eef52315cc1e673ef0.body:
(Rejecting talk about shameful conduct) Reject even talk about shameful deeds.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-0d3130ae39f4730ea1d03220.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0d3130ae39f4730ea1d03220.body:
(Moderation in desires and pleasures) Cheerfulness comes through moderation in pleasure and a balanced life. Deficiency and excess tend to change and stir up great disturbances in the soul.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-b3723b0eb6129336e5e06d8a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b3723b0eb6129336e5e06d8a.body:
(Praise, flattery, and fair assessment) It is easy to praise or blame what does not deserve it; both reveal a bad character.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-ef44c8d8c4dce7acf37d0aea.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ef44c8d8c4dce7acf37d0aea.body:
(Foresight before trouble occurs) It is wisdom to guard against a wrong before it happens; it is insensibility not to defend oneself after it has happened.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-edd18b414fc817df610ba512.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-edd18b414fc817df610ba512.body:
(Pleasure in a virtuous life) Great pleasures come from contemplating noble deeds.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-a957cb1c5262ed6bc8862147.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a957cb1c5262ed6bc8862147.body:
(Correcting one’s own faults) Forgetting your own faults gives rise to arrogance.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-edadeb5a047639e61ac50da8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-edadeb5a047639e61ac50da8.body:
(Wisdom acquired through adversity) The foolish are shaped by the gains of fortune; those with understanding are shaped by the gains of wisdom.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-4bbe9146cd40ffea4dbe1259.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4bbe9146cd40ffea4dbe1259.body:
(Fear of death and the limits of knowledge) The foolish hate their lives, yet wish to live because they fear the world below.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-dc198259e42230e39bd71864.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-dc198259e42230e39bd71864.body:
(Inner joy and the value of the present) The foolish live without enjoying life.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-3cd67bcdb3d5b1f47a326a40.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3cd67bcdb3d5b1f47a326a40.body:
(Inner joy and the value of the present) The foolish desire a long life without taking pleasure in the life they have.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-11d2ae88b90656e23ee275bd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-11d2ae88b90656e23ee275bd.body:
(Inner joy and the value of the present) The foolish long for what is absent and waste what is present, though the present is more valuable than what has passed.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-6f9de230982dfc377bb9e5f6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6f9de230982dfc377bb9e5f6.body:
(Fear of death and the limits of knowledge) People sometimes flee death by running after it.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-e174d2238a60ccbbefa72f45.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e174d2238a60ccbbefa72f45.body:
(Fear of death and the limits of knowledge) The foolish want old age because they fear death.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-a8f23877b3a77401c6100b31.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a8f23877b3a77401c6100b31.body:
(Pleasure in a virtuous life) Choose not every pleasure, but the pleasure found in what is noble.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-73ba51d774b3fb406023b81c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-73ba51d774b3fb406023b81c.body:
(Family and the upbringing of children) A father’s self-restraint is the greatest lesson for his children.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-c4e36abc92d3c30165746d9c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c4e36abc92d3c30165746d9c.body:
(Moderation in desires and pleasures) Fortune provides a lavish table; self-restraint provides a sufficient one.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-9fa471412e17df2d7a7edfa5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9fa471412e17df2d7a7edfa5.body:
(Moderation in desires and pleasures) Moderation increases delight and makes pleasure greater.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-7b0d89e80f204091561c1f6b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7b0d89e80f204091561c1f6b.body:
(Cultivating courage and overcoming fear) Courage makes misfortunes small.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-6a2f301d08446ae45c4c111c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6a2f301d08446ae45c4c111c.body:
(Cultivating courage and overcoming fear) The courageous person is the one who conquers not only enemies but also pleasures.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-73b4f171ba1b3b08ad63510d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-73b4f171ba1b3b08ad63510d.body:
(Justice and moral conduct) Justice brings honor and confidence; injustice brings fear of misfortune.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-ac995dac5f0a9a0d11499c80.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ac995dac5f0a9a0d11499c80.body:
(Cultivating courage and overcoming fear) Wisdom without fear is worth everything.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-f8c23755c685efb341532801.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f8c23755c685efb341532801.body:
(Justice and moral conduct) Only those who hate injustice are dear to the gods.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-2c16682f2712eacda3c4c57e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2c16682f2712eacda3c4c57e.body:
(Wealth, wisdom, and virtue) Wealth acquired through evil deeds makes the disgrace more conspicuous.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-9bae1e9e021fdab395cc792a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9bae1e9e021fdab395cc792a.body:
(Wealth, poverty, and moderate desires) An unlimited desire for wealth is worse than extreme poverty: greater desires create greater needs.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-86daa68ea3e7835715a26270.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-86daa68ea3e7835715a26270.body:
(Wealth, wisdom, and virtue) Dishonorable gains cost us virtue.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-7a4f336475e5f79840c49eb4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7a4f336475e5f79840c49eb4.body:
(Wealth, wisdom, and virtue) The hope of dishonest profit is the beginning of loss.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-64d9bea35132450069c1ec03.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-64d9bea35132450069c1ec03.body:
(Greed and the pursuit of wealth) Excessive wealth gathered for children is a pretext for personal greed.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-0260d7dbdb4a772ae18257a7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0260d7dbdb4a772ae18257a7.body:
(Contentment with little) The needs of the body are readily satisfied without great trouble. The wants that demand toil and make life painful arise from opinion, not from the body.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-331c09a525048a52fe6e2941.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-331c09a525048a52fe6e2941.body:
(Aesop’s fable: the dog loses its food chasing a reflection) Wanting more can make us lose what we already have, like the dog in Aesop’s fable.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-eeb6d6347db601e68c338656.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-eeb6d6347db601e68c338656.body:
(Free and frank speech) Freedom of speech belongs to freedom; the danger lies in judging the proper occasion.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-5ca758bbfefdfc5befdfc3dd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5ca758bbfefdfc5befdfc3dd.body:
(Greed and the pursuit of wealth) The miser lives the life of a bee, working as though he will live forever.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-d5df8c9992e808a4c02e4ca5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d5df8c9992e808a4c02e4ca5.body:
(Frugality and timely spending) Frugality and hunger can be useful, but spending at the right moment is useful too. Good judgment recognizes the occasion.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-f387466ef7a72bfb2b2938b5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f387466ef7a72bfb2b2938b5.body:
(Festivals as rest on life’s journey) A life without festivals is a long road without an inn.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-666c05b79766b52202c0b6b0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-666c05b79766b52202c0b6b0.body:
(Inner joy and the value of the present) The sensible person does not grieve over what is missing, but rejoices in what is present.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-8f0e247711c0b2275bc6604f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8f0e247711c0b2275bc6604f.body:
(Moderation in desires and pleasures) Pleasures that come rarely give the greatest delight.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-ee01781b6c8e9043d7b26a5d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ee01781b6c8e9043d7b26a5d.body:
(Moderation in desires and pleasures) If you exceed the proper measure, the most pleasant things become unpleasant.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-1f81db2329cc14e7eed9b9ba.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1f81db2329cc14e7eed9b9ba.body:
(Moderation and care for health) People ask the gods for health without realizing that they have power over it themselves. Through lack of self-restraint they betray their health to their desires.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-6224c061f0f1a4c5b9753f7d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6224c061f0f1a4c5b9753f7d.body:
(Moderation in desires and pleasures) Those who seek their pleasures in excessive eating, drinking, or sex have only brief pleasures and many pains. The desire quickly returns after the pleasure has gone.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-8682bf096ef768c0e51bc895.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8682bf096ef768c0e51bc895.body:
(Anger, mockery, and quarrels) It is hard to fight anger, but a person of reason masters it.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-94f434ad0b617dca50c21425.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-94f434ad0b617dca50c21425.body:
(Anger, mockery, and quarrels) Every quarrel is foolish: while looking for an opponent’s harm, we neglect our own benefit.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-1a65fb6cc8755b93b4f17ae7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1a65fb6cc8755b93b4f17ae7.body:
(Quarreling with someone more powerful) Contending against someone more powerful ends in disgrace.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-1bc3aaa83586be693b3e6cbc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1bc3aaa83586be693b3e6cbc.body:
(Promises made in hardship) Bad people break the promises they made in hardship once they have escaped it.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-f24102d1feb070bcb4be65f2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f24102d1feb070bcb4be65f2.body:
(Cultivating courage and overcoming fear) Hardships freely chosen prepare us to bear hardships we cannot choose.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-854bf42d35a3365abdf0ba0f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-854bf42d35a3365abdf0ba0f.body:
(Practice, effort, and perseverance) Continuous work becomes easier through habit.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-71d1e23e3554f728e695c174.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-71d1e23e3554f728e695c174.body:
(Effort and willingness to become better) More people become good through practice than through nature.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-df9f04b9f582266e906acdf6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-df9f04b9f582266e906acdf6.body:
(Practice, effort, and perseverance) Work is more pleasant than rest when people obtain, or expect to obtain, the goal of their efforts. Failure makes toil painful.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-43da9c07e0ea63ec54240b94.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-43da9c07e0ea63ec54240b94.body:
(Shame, conscience, and self-respect) Even when you are alone, say and do nothing shameful. Learn to respect yourself more than others.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-e1e91111a2b57bc903b5773d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e1e91111a2b57bc903b5773d.body:
(The need for laws in shared life) Laws would not prevent people from living as they wished if people did not harm one another. Envy begins civil conflict.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-76b2c7a389a64a8b047eef83.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-76b2c7a389a64a8b047eef83.body:
(Contentment with little) Travel teaches self-sufficiency: barley bread and a bed of straw are sweet remedies for hunger and weariness.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-99ef2de85c21865c1d6e928b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-99ef2de85c21865c1d6e928b.body:
(The world as the wise person’s homeland) Every land is open to the wise person; the whole world is the homeland of a good soul.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-7e25e47e7cd58f452e8b01e9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7e25e47e7cd58f452e8b01e9.body:
(The need for laws in shared life) Law aims to benefit human life, but it can do so only when people themselves wish to accept its benefit.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-97f7de20ad05cd1956e0d602.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-97f7de20ad05cd1956e0d602.body:
(Peace and civic concord) Civil conflict harms both sides: the ruin of the victors is the same as that of the defeated.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-c77aa52dce85d79a6f0cbf4b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c77aa52dce85d79a6f0cbf4b.body:
(Peace and civic concord) Concord enables cities to accomplish great deeds and to carry wars through. Without it, neither is possible.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-b7e4372ba7674e3abf30f1d3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b7e4372ba7674e3abf30f1d3.body:
(Freedom under democracy and dependence on a ruler) Poverty under democracy is preferable to prosperity under a ruler, just as freedom is preferable to slavery.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-032597f1247c683636f39beb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-032597f1247c683636f39beb.body:
(The common good and the order of the state) The affairs of the city should come before everything else. No one should pursue unfair rivalry or seek power against the common good: when the city is safe, everything is safe; when it is ruined, everything is ruined.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-7dde50a0a51bb6ed3254818e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7dde50a0a51bb6ed3254818e.body:
(Compassion for others’ misfortunes and mistakes) Mistakes are inevitable, yet it is not easy for people to forgive them.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-1d88539e72bd1de32c582103.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1d88539e72bd1de32c582103.body:
(Praise, flattery, and fair assessment) Undeserved honors make people more reckless and foolish.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-4596bdf6e9c691f35cfa3133.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4596bdf6e9c691f35cfa3133.body:
(The common good and the order of the state) When those with resources help and support those in need, they create compassion, fellowship, mutual assistance, concord among citizens, and many other benefits.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-7051e97023621dbe5d39b1b3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7051e97023621dbe5d39b1b3.body:
(Justice and moral conduct) Justice is doing what should be done; injustice is failing to do it.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-c6fe800c4ccd181398dc2e7b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c6fe800c4ccd181398dc2e7b.body:
(Justice and moral conduct) Help those who suffer injustice as far as you can, and do not stand aside. This is just and good.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-5d80ea968dd712a900de2c5a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5d80ea968dd712a900de2c5a.body:
(The corrective purpose of punishment) Those who deserve exile, imprisonment, or a penalty should be punished, not released contrary to law for profit or pleasure.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-a7467f622e1c0e66fb619f3b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a7467f622e1c0e66fb619f3b.body:
(Justice and moral conduct) Do not respect other people more than yourself, or do wrong merely because no one will know. Set this law in your soul: do nothing shameful.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-17ac64799ecede13efdabba1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-17ac64799ecede13efdabba1.body:
(People’s memory of others’ failings) People remember our failings more than our good deeds. Someone who returns a deposit receives no praise, but someone who fails to return it is blamed and punished.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-b8835e80abf1b8d0767ca3b7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b8835e80abf1b8d0767ca3b7.body:
(Flattery and its dangers) Fear produces flattery, not goodwill.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-51800a09b8f09ea83a027dbd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-51800a09b8f09ea83a027dbd.body:
(Uncertain fortune and unfounded hopes) Daring is the beginning of action, but fortune controls the outcome.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-317cae0731520ea61e16ab2e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-317cae0731520ea61e16ab2e.body:
(Marriage and family ties) A good son-in-law gives you a son; a bad one costs you a daughter.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-e654373a1d681db5d2b6c663.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e654373a1d681db5d2b6c663.body:
(Family and the upbringing of children) Raising children is a hazardous undertaking: success is full of struggle and care, while failure brings unsurpassed pain.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-f207ae5da4b2540bf70c0f8c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f207ae5da4b2540bf70c0f8c.body:
(Family and the upbringing of children) It is possible to educate children without great expense, while protecting both their possessions and their bodies.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-21ed79501763da307314c3fb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-21ed79501763da307314c3fb.body:
(Wealth, wisdom, and virtue) Wealth used with understanding serves generosity and the public good.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-66e941f5891d7f4396a7cfae.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-66e941f5891d7f4396a7cfae.body:
(Wealth, poverty, and moderate desires) Poverty and wealth are names for need and sufficiency. Someone in need is not rich, and someone who lacks nothing is not poor.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-5b3a0406b9b8be6b4d2497dc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5b3a0406b9b8be6b4d2497dc.body:
(Wealth, poverty, and moderate desires) If you desire little, little will seem much. Small desires make poverty equal to wealth.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-28b88f2288f9f6caa97bde5c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-28b88f2288f9f6caa97bde5c.body:
(Wealth, poverty, and moderate desires) Human life is fragile and brief, mixed with many dangers and difficulties. We should therefore seek moderate possessions, so that our labor is measured by what we need.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-d39590a47b16eb606fe67b62.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d39590a47b16eb606fe67b62.body:
(Wealth, poverty, and moderate desires) The fortunate person has moderate resources and a cheerful spirit; the unfortunate person has abundant resources and a troubled spirit.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-2f4a0e5ae4e1396c202f4c33.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2f4a0e5ae4e1396c202f4c33.body:
(Widespread poverty and the loss of mutual assistance) Poverty shared by everyone is harder than private poverty, because it leaves no hope of assistance.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-8b006ab375ac6e862a0c3a96.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8b006ab375ac6e862a0c3a96.body:
(Disorder in a household and way of life) A household and a way of life can be unhealthy just as a body can.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-8d90e1a76cc81131f98a5efe.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8d90e1a76cc81131f98a5efe.body:
(Accepting what is inevitable in life) It is foolish not to yield to the necessities of life.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-760642ca1954562b7c7f2ad5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-760642ca1954562b7c7f2ad5.body:
(Overcoming excessive grief through reason) Drive unmeasured grief out of your troubled soul through reasoning.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-f9a458c6660e6880b62b82c5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f9a458c6660e6880b62b82c5.body:
(Wealth, poverty, and moderate desires) A person with good sense bears poverty with composure.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-042631b998fb1716dc1d5506.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-042631b998fb1716dc1d5506.body:
(Uncertain fortune and unfounded hopes) The hopes of the foolish have no reason behind them.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-a601edb50d7de074477138ac.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a601edb50d7de074477138ac.body:
(Compassion for others’ misfortunes and mistakes) Those who delight in a neighbor’s misfortunes fail to understand that fortune is common to all, and they lack joys of their own.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-63ececbe5913771547b1c8d0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-63ececbe5913771547b1c8d0.body:
(The strengths and experience of old age) Strength and beauty are the good things of youth; self-restraint is the flower of old age.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-16149c8b7901a98cc4d950ff.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-16149c8b7901a98cc4d950ff.body:
(The strengths and experience of old age) The old were once young, but the young may never reach old age. A completed good is better than one that is still uncertain.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-8be70e15250a66d2c70c04da.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8be70e15250a66d2c70c04da.body:
(Fear of death and the limits of knowledge) Some people, unaware that human nature is mortal but conscious of their own bad actions, spend their lives in fear and confusion, inventing false stories about what comes after death.
Democritus (attributed)

advice-3b7c8d07cd923834a6cf8744.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3b7c8d07cd923834a6cf8744.body:
When Antisthenes raised a stick against Diogenes, Diogenes replied: ‘Strike: as long as you keep speaking, you will never find a stick that can drive me away.’
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §II; source paragraph 2, excerpt 1

advice-4372b2e36c0548bfc5750bdc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4372b2e36c0548bfc5750bdc.body:
(Preferring spectacle to serious reflection) It was also a saying of his that the Dionysian games were a great marvel to fools; and that the demagogues were the ministers of the multitude.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 1

advice-c983b3c4b2b0c19fdb1fdaa4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c983b3c4b2b0c19fdb1fdaa4.body:
(Superstition and unfounded claims to knowledge) He used likewise to say, “that when in the course of his life he beheld pilots, and physicians, and philosophers, he thought man the wisest of all animals; but when again he beheld interpreters of dreams, and soothsayers, and those who listened to them, and men puffed up with glory or riches, then he thought that there was not a more foolish animal than man.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 2

advice-51d579d1678b0e358bc1775e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-51d579d1678b0e358bc1775e.body:
(Reason as a support against despair) Another of his sayings was, “that he thought a man ought oftener to provide himself with a reason than with a halter.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 3

advice-dd453698112752b917e09b8f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-dd453698112752b917e09b8f.body:
(Moderation in desires and pleasures) At another time he was eating dried figs, when Plato met him, and he said to him, “You may have a share of these;” and as he took some and ate them, he said, “I said that you might have a share of them, not that you might eat them all.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 4

advice-9d75f3c2ad299a1c5efa269e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9d75f3c2ad299a1c5efa269e.body:
(Diogenes tramples Plato’s carpets while condemning his pride) But, as others tell the story, Diogenes said, “Thus I trample on the pride of Plato;” and that Plato rejoined, “With quite as much pride yourself, O Diogenes.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 5

advice-65fee03651170ebba54a22e1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-65fee03651170ebba54a22e1.body:
(Replying to Plato about an answer disproportionate to a request) Sotion too, in his fourth book, states, that the Cynic made the following speech to Plato: Diogenes once asked him for some wine, and then for some dried figs; so he sent him an entire jar full; and Diogenes said to him, “Will you, if you are asked how many two and two make, answer twenty? In this way, you neither give with any reference to what you are asked for, nor do you answer with reference to the question put to you.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 6

advice-fb04ee5ba9f8cd88bc896000.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fb04ee5ba9f8cd88bc896000.body:
(Seeking a morally worthy human being) When he was asked where in Greece he saw virtuous men; “Men,” said he, “nowhere; but I see good boys in Lacedæmon.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 7

advice-9305a1e0d9cbc634a2f1ab25.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9305a1e0d9cbc634a2f1ab25.body:
(Preferring spectacle to serious reflection) On one occasion, when no one came to listen to him while he was discoursing seriously, he began to whistle. And then when people flocked round him, he reproached them for coming with eagerness to folly, but being lazy and indifferent about good things.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 8

advice-2d2968672886ea4d0b755484.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2d2968672886ea4d0b755484.body:
(Striving for virtue without envy) One of his frequent sayings was, “That men contended with one another in punching and kicking, but that no one showed any emulation in the pursuit of virtue.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 9

advice-4d35028da53aff1703b20909.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4d35028da53aff1703b20909.body:
(Self-knowledge before other people’s affairs) He used to express his astonishment at the grammarians for being desirous to learn everything about the misfortunes of Ulysses, and being ignorant of their own.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 10

advice-ef352a4645805350c454c1ce.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ef352a4645805350c454c1ce.body:
(Inner harmony and consistency) He used also to say, “That the musicians fitted the strings to the lyre properly, but left all the habits of their soul ill-arranged.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 11

advice-1e842c87902bdbaf99570e6a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1e842c87902bdbaf99570e6a.body:
(Knowledge of the heavens and ignorance of earthly affairs) And, “That mathematicians kept their eyes fixed on the sun and moon, and overlooked what was under their feet.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 12

advice-c86bb099e023e7669da789f6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c86bb099e023e7669da789f6.body:
(The difference between moral words and deeds) “That orators were anxious to speak justly, but not at all about acting so.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 13

advice-9eb328f175bbc6bf356a3130.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9eb328f175bbc6bf356a3130.body:
(The difference between moral words and deeds) Also, “That misers blamed money, but were preposterously fond of it.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 14

advice-1cd71f2c8e447545e3540a18.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1cd71f2c8e447545e3540a18.body:
(The difference between moral words and deeds) He often condemned those who praise the just for being superior to money, but who at the same time are eager themselves for great riches.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 15

advice-5fbe1d23a0300f694dc51dab.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5fbe1d23a0300f694dc51dab.body:
(Moderation and care for health) He was also very indignant at seeing men sacrifice to the Gods to procure good health, and yet at the sacrifice eating in a manner injurious to health.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 16

advice-65362bc329ced747ba1a8ef1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-65362bc329ced747ba1a8ef1.body:
(Giving, help, and gratitude) One of his sayings was, “That one ought to hold out one’s hand to a friend without closing the fingers.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 5, excerpt 17

advice-723af24c40f045dc7efd0b78.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-723af24c40f045dc7efd0b78.body:
(Diogenes in captivity: the sage’s inner freedom) Hermippus, in his Sale of Diogenes, says that he was taken prisoner and put up to be sold, and asked what he could do; and he answered, “Govern men.” And so he bade the crier “give notice that if any one wants to purchase a master, there is one here for him.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 6, excerpt 1

advice-8080e6b70341778966562675.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8080e6b70341778966562675.body:
(Judging a person by their actual qualities) He used to say, that he wondered at men always ringing a dish or jar before buying it, but being content to judge of a man by his look alone.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 6, excerpt 2

advice-bc5574feea48037abe63cb45.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bc5574feea48037abe63cb45.body:
(Diogenes in captivity: the sage’s inner freedom) When Xeniades bought him, he said to him that he ought to obey him even though he was his slave; for that a physician or a pilot would find men to obey them even though they might be slaves.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IV; source paragraph 6, excerpt 3

advice-bf569dadd6af7c6eca5e3ca0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bf569dadd6af7c6eca5e3ca0.body:
(Practice, effort, and perseverance) When some people said to him, “You are an old man, and should rest for the remainder of your life;” “Why so?” replied he, “suppose I had run a long distance, ought I to stop when I was near the end, and not rather press on?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 9, excerpt 1

advice-33c67d245397970829e0c33b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-33c67d245397970829e0c33b.body:
(Diogenes’s deliberate exaggeration as a way of teaching) He used to say, that he imitated the teachers of choruses, for that they spoke too loud, in order that the rest might catch the proper tone.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 9, excerpt 2

advice-8d14b0a7c8ccc3b93c874371.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8d14b0a7c8ccc3b93c874371.body:
(The conventional social meaning of gestures) Another of his sayings, was that most men were within a finger’s breadth of being mad. If, then, any one were to walk along, stretching out his middle finger, he will seem to be mad; but if he puts out his fore finger, he will not be thought so.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 9, excerpt 3

advice-657d4fe9f846ccf2f43bddea.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-657d4fe9f846ccf2f43bddea.body:
(Outward display and real value) Another of his sayings was, that things of great value were often sold for nothing, and vice versâ. Accordingly, that a statue would fetch three thousand drachmas, and a bushel of meal only two obols;
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 9, excerpt 4

advice-4f558e2acc0db59ed93b65ef.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4f558e2acc0db59ed93b65ef.body:
(True friendship and how it is tested) But Diocles tells this story in the following manner; that when some one said to him, “Give me a commission, Diogenes,” he carried him off, and gave him a halfpenny worth of cheese to carry. And as he refused to carry it, “See,” said Diogenes, “a halfpenny worth of cheese has broken off our friendship.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 13, excerpt 1

advice-364a7082942c622145d3183a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-364a7082942c622145d3183a.body:
(Contentment with little) On one occasion he saw a child drinking out of its hands, and so he threw away the cup which belonged to his wallet, saying, “That child has beaten me in simplicity.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 14, excerpt 1

advice-7b0b3d73008a6f184214d4e7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7b0b3d73008a6f184214d4e7.body:
(Sharing possessions among friends) And he used to argue thus,—“Everything belongs to the gods; and wise men are the friends of the gods. All things are in common among friends; therefore everything belongs to wise men.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 14, excerpt 2

advice-6b63fc100c84281f0dcd2786.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6b63fc100c84281f0dcd2786.body:
(Fortitude, nature, and reason as supports of life) And another of his sayings was that he opposed confidence to fortune, nature to law, and reason to suffering.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 16, excerpt 1

advice-c83087231b9a36d6eb7eda2b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c83087231b9a36d6eb7eda2b.body:
(Diogenes’s independence from rulers) Once, while he was sitting in the sun in the Craneum, Alexander was standing by, and said to him, “Ask any favour you choose of me.” And he replied, “Cease to shade me from the sun.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 16, excerpt 2

advice-e6f8979a94931db5811be73d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e6f8979a94931db5811be73d.body:
(The end of a long reading as reaching shore) On one occasion a man was reading some long passages, and when he came to the end of the book and showed that there was nothing more written, “Be of good cheer, my friends,” exclaimed Diogenes, “I see land.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 16, excerpt 3

advice-bcfe7ae0cdcd26ae50d63b2f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bcfe7ae0cdcd26ae50d63b2f.body:
(Testing abstract arguments through direct experience) A man once proved to him syllogistically that he had horns, so he put his hand to his forehead and said, “I do not see them.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 16, excerpt 4

advice-2f8442d4d34cd450e960a64b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2f8442d4d34cd450e960a64b.body:
(Testing abstract arguments through direct experience) And in a similar manner he replied to one who had been asserting that there was no such thing as motion, by getting up and walking away.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 16, excerpt 5

advice-235d8fbee416185f87ff43e4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-235d8fbee416185f87ff43e4.body:
(Superstition and unfounded claims to knowledge) When a man was talking about the heavenly bodies and meteors, “Pray how many days,” said he to him, “is it since you came down from heaven?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 16, excerpt 6

advice-b77ef236779f8322786c04a1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b77ef236779f8322786c04a1.body:
(The practical point of using perfume) After having anointed his feet with perfume, he said that the ointment from his head mounted up to heaven, and that from his feet up to his nose.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 17, excerpt 1

advice-4d35fa2a5ff795629194024c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4d35fa2a5ff795629194024c.body:
(Moral character and outward rites of purification) When the Athenians entreated him to be initiated in the Eleusinian mysteries, and said that in the shades below the initiated had the best seats; “It will,” he replied, “be an absurd thing if Agesilaus and Epaminondas are to live in the mud, and some miserable wretches, who have been initiated, are to be in the islands of the blest.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 17, excerpt 2

advice-4c20456d4edc2500e469a44d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4c20456d4edc2500e469a44d.body:
(Diogenes answers Plato’s description of him as a dog) When Plato called him a dog, he said, “Undoubtedly, for I have come back to those who sold me.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 17, excerpt 3

advice-80404af96aff6f44168f230d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-80404af96aff6f44168f230d.body:
(Testing abstract arguments through direct experience) Plato defined man thus: “Man is a two-footed, featherless animal,” and was much praised for the definition; so Diogenes plucked a cock and brought it into his school, and said, “This is Plato’s man.” On which account this addition was made to the definition, “With broad flat nails.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 18, excerpt 1

advice-d56921678b7957dc9a33f095.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d56921678b7957dc9a33f095.body:
(Food and simple pleasures) A man once asked him what was the proper time for supper, and he made answer, “If you are a rich man, whenever you please; and if you are a poor man, whenever you can.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 18, excerpt 2

advice-16606c95bf053a2de6099ddd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-16606c95bf053a2de6099ddd.body:
(Family and the upbringing of children) When he was at Megara he saw some sheep carefully covered over with skins, and the children running about naked; and so he said, “It is better at Megara to be a man’s ram, than his son.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 18, excerpt 3

advice-8a788786aabadebe8ba539e8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8a788786aabadebe8ba539e8.body:
(Foresight before trouble occurs) A man once struck him with a beam, and then said, “Take care.” “What,” said he, “are you going to strike me again?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 18, excerpt 4

advice-de2e0a378d84002e00c6caca.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-de2e0a378d84002e00c6caca.body:
(Seeking a morally worthy human being) Having lighted a candle in the day time, he said, “I am looking for a man.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 18, excerpt 5

advice-b2d2cac147f60a1d023a6a30.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b2d2cac147f60a1d023a6a30.body:
(Moral character and outward rites of purification) Once he saw a man purifying himself by washing, and said to him, “Oh, wretched man, do not you know that as you cannot wash away blunders in grammar by purification, so, too, you can no more efface the errors of a life in that same manner?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 19, excerpt 1

advice-24bec4c5e9f9a803ab5721f2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-24bec4c5e9f9a803ab5721f2.body:
(Praying for apparent and real goods) He used to say that men were wrong for complaining of fortune; for that they ask of the Gods what appear to be good things, not what are really so.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 20, excerpt 1

advice-431851a4c468270a58de658f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-431851a4c468270a58de658f.body:
(Superstition and unfounded claims to knowledge) And to those who were alarmed at dreams he said, that they did not regard what they do while they are awake, but make a great fuss about what they fancy they see while they are asleep.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 20, excerpt 2

advice-5920b19329efd9882f804d3c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5920b19329efd9882f804d3c.body:
(Diogenes addresses Philip’s appetite for conquest) And Dionysius, the Stoic, says that after the battle of Chæronea he was taken prisoner and brought to Philip; and being asked who he was, replied, “A spy, to spy upon your insatiability.” And Philip marvelled at him and let him go.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 21, excerpt 1

advice-c0992446cbd4a1d05f3cfcbb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c0992446cbd4a1d05f3cfcbb.body:
(Fear of death and the limits of knowledge) When Perdiccas threatened that he would put him to death if he did not come to him, he replied, “That is nothing strange, for a scorpion or a tarantula could do as much: you had better threaten me that, if I kept away, you should be very happy.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 21, excerpt 2

advice-488fb4cc39cd7fb67c3f2b42.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-488fb4cc39cd7fb67c3f2b42.body:
(Contentment with little) He used constantly to repeat with emphasis that an easy life had been given to man by the Gods, but that it had been overlaid by their seeking for honey, cheese-cakes, and unguents, and things of that sort.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 21, excerpt 3

advice-e694872a148ccdad4c528f6e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e694872a148ccdad4c528f6e.body:
(Accusers who are themselves guilty of greater theft) On one occasion, when he had seen the hieromnemones leading off one of the stewards who had stolen a goblet, he said, “The great thieves are carrying off the little thief.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 21, excerpt 4

advice-656d9d0aff0ed29ff8c1b945.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-656d9d0aff0ed29ff8c1b945.body:
(Diogenes’s independence from rulers) When people were speaking of the happiness of Callisthenes, and saying what splendid treatment he received from Alexander, he replied, “The man then is wretched, for he is forced to breakfast and dine whenever Alexander chooses.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 21, excerpt 5

advice-fb47868cd1b9ae1a4f99feaf.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fb47868cd1b9ae1a4f99feaf.body:
(Sharing possessions among friends) When he was in want of money, he said that be reclaimed it from his friends and did not beg for it.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 21, excerpt 6

advice-ce6624228148bca71f0a80e1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ce6624228148bca71f0a80e1.body:
(Wealth, wisdom, and virtue) He said that a rich but ignorant man, was like a sheep with a golden fleece.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 22, excerpt 1

advice-a0ea0c4b7df311cd45311597.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a0ea0c4b7df311cd45311597.body:
(Praise, flattery, and fair assessment) To a young man, who was complaining of the number of people who sought his acquaintance, he said, “Do not make such a parade of your vanity.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 22, excerpt 2

advice-fa81c0b10e4fc34a4294609d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fa81c0b10e4fc34a4294609d.body:
(Mocking a dirty public bath) Having been in a very dirty bath, he said, “I wonder where the people, who bathe here, clean themselves.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 23, excerpt 1

advice-f8768af540cf480ac13c5edd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f8768af540cf480ac13c5edd.body:
(Judging a person by their actual qualities) When all the company was blaming an indifferent harp-player, he alone praised him, and being asked why he did so, he said, “Because, though he is such as he is, he plays the harp and does not steal.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 23, excerpt 2

advice-cf6d95739c0b8f2ab80d8f32.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cf6d95739c0b8f2ab80d8f32.body:
(An unskilled musician whose listeners leave) He saluted a harp player who was always left alone by his hearers, with, “Good morning, cock;” and when the man asked him, “Why so?” he said, “Because you, when you sing, make every one get up.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 23, excerpt 3

advice-5121e68940d17cd9fdc00639.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5121e68940d17cd9fdc00639.body:
(The difference between moral words and deeds) When Hegesias entreated him to lend him one of his books, he said, “You are a silly fellow, Hegesias, for you will not take painted figs, but real ones; and yet you overlook the genuine practice of virtue, and seek for what is merely written.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 23, excerpt 4

advice-de9a8541fb556cf50c111c53.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-de9a8541fb556cf50c111c53.body:
(Wisdom acquired through adversity) A man once reproached him with his banishment, and his answer was, “You wretched man, that is what made me a philosopher.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 23, excerpt 5

advice-328b47f1759b76a4b44e05ca.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-328b47f1759b76a4b44e05ca.body:
(Exile and freedom from attachment to place) And when, on another occasion, some one said to him, “The people of Sinope condemned you to banishment,” he replied, “And I condemned them to remain where they were.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 23, excerpt 6

advice-da3cd0fca3f35b00b007e6b7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-da3cd0fca3f35b00b007e6b7.body:
(Giving, help, and gratitude) Once he was begging of some one (for he did this at first out of actual want), he said, “If you have given to any one else, give also to me; and if you have never given to any one, then begin with me.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 24, excerpt 1

advice-431e268e58c40bbab729f0a8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-431e268e58c40bbab729f0a8.body:
(The tyrant Dionysius uses and discards his friends) When he was asked how Dionysius treats his friends, he said, “Like bags; those which are full he hangs up, and those which are empty he throws away.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 24, excerpt 2

advice-84df49711dd566f9c15111b0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-84df49711dd566f9c15111b0.body:
(Greed and the pursuit of wealth) He used to say that covetousness was the metropolis of all evils.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 24, excerpt 3

advice-c0b88057746d26b66ba39c6b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c0b88057746d26b66ba39c6b.body:
(Virtue and love as an occupation of the idle) One of his apophthegms was, that good men were the images of the Gods; another, that love was the business of those who had nothing to do.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 24, excerpt 4

advice-856c2cffbf613ff743c80994.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-856c2cffbf613ff743c80994.body:
(The informer and flatterer as dangerous “animals”) When asked which creature bites the worst, he replied, “Among wild creatures, the malicious informer; among tame ones, the flatterer.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 24, excerpt 5

advice-c3c3a6544e57cb35acdba753.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c3c3a6544e57cb35acdba753.body:
(Flattery and its dangers) He used to say that a speech, the object of which was solely to please, was a honeyed halter.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 25, excerpt 1

advice-f2971c9836c3e8530d8c0784.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f2971c9836c3e8530d8c0784.body:
(Greed and the pursuit of wealth) When the question was put to him, why gold is of a pale colour, he said, “Because it has so many people plotting against it.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 25, excerpt 3

advice-81b814d5473057167bbbd167.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-81b814d5473057167bbbd167.body:
(Burial and inheritance) When he was asked whether he had any girl or boy to wait on him, he said, “No.” And as his questioner asked further, “If then you die, who will bury you?” He replied, “Whoever wants my house.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 27, excerpt 1

advice-de1c8faef4eb8ada46d9a1b8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-de1c8faef4eb8ada46d9a1b8.body:
(Debating Plato’s Forms and visible objects) When Plato was discoursing about his “ideas,” and using the nouns “tableness” and “cupness;” “I, O Plato!” interrupted Diogenes, “see a table and a cup, but I see no tableness or cupness.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 31, excerpt 1

advice-370f285b0403f653a39361d7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-370f285b0403f653a39361d7.body:
(Marriage and family ties) Another time, the question was put to him, when a man ought to marry? and his reply was, “Young men ought not to marry yet, and old men never ought to marry at all.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 32, excerpt 1

advice-df31878614677d4dfeacdb66.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-df31878614677d4dfeacdb66.body:
(Diogenes is offered payment for allowing someone to strike him) When asked what he would take to let a man give him a blow on the head? he replied, “A helmet.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 32, excerpt 2

advice-9726ecc952d9080a9ee0d6d7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9726ecc952d9080a9ee0d6d7.body:
(Shame, conscience, and self-respect) Once he saw a youth blushing, and addressed him, “Courage, my boy, that is the complexion of virtue.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 32, excerpt 3

advice-61b7dd518c32807fd9dbbd9b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-61b7dd518c32807fd9dbbd9b.body:
(Dishonesty on both sides of a property dispute) Having once listened to two lawyers, he condemned them both; saying, “That the one had stolen the thing in question, and that the other had not lost it.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 32, excerpt 4

advice-22c3adbdf53a8d7783396bd8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-22c3adbdf53a8d7783396bd8.body:
(Food and simple pleasures) When asked what wine he liked to drink, he said, “That which belongs to another.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 32, excerpt 5

advice-a17d33ac2136afab0cf937da.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a17d33ac2136afab0cf937da.body:
(Independence from other people’s ridicule) A man said to him one day, “Many people laugh at you.” “But I,” he replied, “am not laughed down.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 32, excerpt 6

advice-6bdb22fa1e44b19c3247e863.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6bdb22fa1e44b19c3247e863.body:
(The difference between living and living badly) When a man said to him, that it was a bad thing to live; “Not to live,” said he, “but to live badly.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 32, excerpt 7

advice-23903b2f6fcf441b4ccda45c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-23903b2f6fcf441b4ccda45c.body:
(Contentment with little) When some people were advising him to make search for a slave who had run away, he said, “It would be a very absurd thing for Manes to be able to live without Diogenes, but for Diogenes not to be able to live without Manes.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 32, excerpt 8

advice-473af013d0be4ec04f6d6904.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-473af013d0be4ec04f6d6904.body:
(Food and simple pleasures) The question was put to him, whether wise men ate cheese-cakes, and he replied, “They eat everything, just as the rest of mankind.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 36, excerpt 1

advice-a5c15105edcd8083cbe30894.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a5c15105edcd8083cbe30894.body:
(Giving, help, and gratitude) When asked why people give to beggars and not to philosophers, he said, “Because they think it possible that they themselves may become lame and blind, but they do not expect ever to turn out philosophers.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 36, excerpt 2

advice-382ba24da6e02828e976056f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-382ba24da6e02828e976056f.body:
(Asking for food: wordplay on nourishment and burial) He once begged of a covetous man, and as he was slow to give, he said, “Man, I am asking you for something to maintain me (εἰς τροφὴν) and not to bury me (εἰς ταφὴν).”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 36, excerpt 3

advice-2b8d72bc46e06efc8627806a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2b8d72bc46e06efc8627806a.body:
(Replying to reproach for past adulteration of coinage) When some one reproached him for having tampered with the coinage, he said, “There was a time when I was such a person as you are now; but there never was when you were such as I am now, and never will be.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 36, excerpt 4

advice-f1fe274dee9f290b4b5d546a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f1fe274dee9f290b4b5d546a.body:
(Replying to reproach for past adulteration of coinage) And to another person who reproached him on the same grounds, he said, “There were times when I did what I did not wish to, but that is not the case now.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 36, excerpt 5

advice-56896877e7ca04a91ab8c585.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-56896877e7ca04a91ab8c585.body:
(Outward display and real value) When he went to Myndus, he saw some very large gates, but the city was a small one, and so he said, “Oh men of Myndus, shut your gates, lest your city should steal out.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 36, excerpt 6

advice-63a9fce57b471581bdae2aa1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-63a9fce57b471581bdae2aa1.body:
(Diogenes’s independence from rulers) When Craterus entreated him to come and visit him, he said, “I would rather lick up salt at Athens, than enjoy a luxurious table with Craterus.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 38, excerpt 1

advice-53cb68da9067bc6497a5b1d6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-53cb68da9067bc6497a5b1d6.body:
(Natural needs and social conventions) Being once reproached for eating in the market-place, he made answer, “I did, for it was in the market-place that I was hungry.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 38, excerpt 2

advice-d5c82bbef5cbfcae2008984c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d5c82bbef5cbfcae2008984c.body:
(Independence from other people’s ridicule) When a man said to him once, “Most people laugh at you;” “And very likely,” he replied, “the asses laugh at them; but they do not regard the asses, neither do I regard them.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 38, excerpt 3

advice-fc450a81819a4d10718cfd36.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fc450a81819a4d10718cfd36.body:
(Care of the soul and the order of goods) Once he saw a youth studying philosophy, and said to him, “Well done; inasmuch as you are leading those who admire your person to contemplate the beauty of your mind.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 38, excerpt 4

advice-c53e7347e3ce45ae60426ca8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c53e7347e3ce45ae60426ca8.body:
(Seeking a morally worthy human being) Another time he was returning from the Olympic games, and when some one asked him whether there had been a great multitude there, he said, “A great multitude, but very few men.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 39, excerpt 1

advice-a0bd73f68e95feeef0880f3a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a0bd73f68e95feeef0880f3a.body:
(Explaining the Cynic nickname “dog”) And when he was asked to what actions of his it was owing that he was called a dog, he said, “Because I fawn upon those who give me anything, and bark at those who give me nothing, and bite the rogues.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 40, excerpt 1

advice-5386b33c743194a898041196.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5386b33c743194a898041196.body:
(Natural needs and social conventions) On one occasion he was eating his dinner in the market-place, and the bystanders kept constantly calling out “Dog;” but he said, “It is you who are the dogs, who stand around me while I am at dinner.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 41, excerpt 1

advice-0b030e96c77abc1e4e85f27c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0b030e96c77abc1e4e85f27c.body:
(An unsuccessful wrestler who becomes a healer) Seeing an unskilful wrestler professing to heal a man he said, “What are you about, are you in hopes now to overthrow those who formerly conquered you?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 41, excerpt 2

advice-3beab67204ff789900252f94.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3beab67204ff789900252f94.body:
(Giving, help, and gratitude) And when some people were praising a man who had given him something, he said to them, “And do not you praise me who was worthy to receive it?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 41, excerpt 3

advice-2079fb9f10eddd78002c3a85.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2079fb9f10eddd78002c3a85.body:
(Giving, help, and gratitude) He was asked by some one to give him back his cloak; but he replied, “If you gave it me, it is mine; and if you only lent it me, I am using it.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 41, excerpt 4

advice-7f5083e8196a132ab7a9f61d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7f5083e8196a132ab7a9f61d.body:
(Wisdom acquired through adversity) When he was asked what advantage he had derived from philosophy, he replied, “If no other, at least this, that I am prepared for every kind of fortune.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 41, excerpt 5

advice-fa20227817f31fc17b322c6f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fa20227817f31fc17b322c6f.body:
(The world as the wise person’s homeland) The question was put to him what countryman he was, and he replied, “A Citizen of the world.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 41, excerpt 6

advice-4ab07e3a0c676f9594991742.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4ab07e3a0c676f9594991742.body:
(Family and the upbringing of children) Some men were sacrificing to the Gods to prevail on them to send them sons, and he said, “And do you not sacrifice to procure sons of a particular character?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 41, excerpt 7

advice-3b792f1a8be5ba9461531ae2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3b792f1a8be5ba9461531ae2.body:
(Mocking Alexander’s deification by vote) When the Athenians had voted that Alexander was Bacchus, he said to them, “Vote, too, that I am Serapis.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 43, excerpt 1

advice-eb2b92385820aa6be12d3a77.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-eb2b92385820aa6be12d3a77.body:
(Moral integrity when visiting disreputable places) When a man reproached him for going into unclean places, he said, “The sun too penetrates into privies, but is not polluted by them.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 43, excerpt 2

advice-92ce2e319053a46beaaecaa5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-92ce2e319053a46beaaecaa5.body:
(Learning, experience, and wise guidance) A man once brought him a boy, and said that he was a very clever child, and one of an admirable disposition. “What, then,” said Diogenes, “does he want of me?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 43, excerpt 3

advice-2906fb480743a7ec7386b203.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2906fb480743a7ec7386b203.body:
(The difference between moral words and deeds) He used to say, that those who utter virtuous sentiments but do not do them, are no better than harps, for that a harp has no hearing or feeling.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 43, excerpt 4

advice-4b6a5c0c886ef7a4283c2207.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4b6a5c0c886ef7a4283c2207.body:
(Living against the direction of the crowd) Once he was going into a theatre while every one else was coming out of it; and when asked why he did so, “It is,” said he, “what I have been doing all my life.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 43, excerpt 5

advice-2f3b070fd166a7b2a8cc5f27.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2f3b070fd166a7b2a8cc5f27.body:
(The difference between living and living badly) When a man said to him, “I am not calculated for philosophy,” he said, “Why then do you live, if you have no desire to live properly?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 43, excerpt 6

advice-4d896d1e8203f6c8a1acc667.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4d896d1e8203f6c8a1acc667.body:
(Family and the upbringing of children) To a man who treated his father with contempt, he said, “Are you not ashamed to despise him to whom you owe it that you have it in your power to give yourself airs at all?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 43, excerpt 7

advice-07c79f389bb0e0ebf4eb835b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-07c79f389bb0e0ebf4eb835b.body:
(Natural needs and social conventions) Being once reproached for drinking in a vintner’s shop, he said, “I have my hair cut, too, in a barber’s.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 43, excerpt 8

advice-a4045f46e085bfcd657e1112.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a4045f46e085bfcd657e1112.body:
(Outward beauty and inner worth) Seeing a man reeking all over with unguents, he said to him, “Have a care, lest the fragrance of your head give a bad odour to your life.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 46, excerpt 1

advice-b7ec06af03d9a3908640c0e0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b7ec06af03d9a3908640c0e0.body:
(The rule of passions over the soul) One of his sayings was, that servants serve their masters, and that wicked men are the slaves of their appetites.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 46, excerpt 2

advice-e85226ef3f5ce7cfc62c4510.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e85226ef3f5ce7cfc62c4510.body:
(Asking a spendthrift for help) He once asked a profligate fellow for a mina; and when he put the question to him, why he asked others for an obol, and him for a mina, he said, “Because I hope to get something from the others another time, but the Gods alone know whether I shall ever extract anything from you again.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 46, excerpt 3

advice-e07e873228f4bc02c0c6743b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e07e873228f4bc02c0c6743b.body:
(Mocking an unskilled archer) One day he saw an unskilful archer shooting; so he went and sat down by the target, saying, “Now I shall be out of harm’s way.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 48, excerpt 1

advice-32ed525b1686566de0b07224.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-32ed525b1686566de0b07224.body:
