(Love, desires, and character) He used to say, that those who were in love were disappointed in regard of the pleasure they expected.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 48, excerpt 2

advice-9721f416f003903887c1e3a9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9721f416f003903887c1e3a9.body:
(Death and the fate of consciousness) When he was asked whether death was an evil, he replied, “How can that be an evil which we do not feel when it is present?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 48, excerpt 3

advice-c9e9fb2a0f3d48927649fba8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c9e9fb2a0f3d48927649fba8.body:
(Diogenes’s independence from rulers) When Alexander was once standing by him, and saying, “Do not you fear me?” He replied, “No; for what are you, a good or an evil?” And as he said that he was good, “Who, then,” said Diogenes, “fears the good?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 48, excerpt 4

advice-a98bdc5563774eea2f02b141.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a98bdc5563774eea2f02b141.body:
(Learning, experience, and wise guidance) He used to say, that education was, for the young sobriety, for the old comfort, for the poor riches, and for the rich an ornament.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 48, excerpt 5

advice-8c5fbe6e2f4d32c4cd1c9fa0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8c5fbe6e2f4d32c4cd1c9fa0.body:
(True friendship and how it is tested) A man once said to him, that his friends laid plots against him; “What then,” said he, “are you to do, if you must look upon both your friends and enemies in the same light?”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 48, excerpt 6

advice-ff2470add64193a02c54722d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ff2470add64193a02c54722d.body:
(Free and frank speech) On one occasion he was asked, what was the most excellent thing among men; and he said, “Freedom of speech.”
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 49, excerpt 1

advice-46c9c337c48a5d59102d1b5b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-46c9c337c48a5d59102d1b5b.body:
(Training the body and the soul) He used to say, that there were two kinds of exercise: that, namely, of the mind and that of the body; and that the latter of these created in the mind such quick and agile phantasies at the time of its performance, as very much facilitated the practice of virtue; but that one was imperfect without the other, since the health and vigour necessary for the practice of what is good, depend equally on both mind and body.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 50, excerpt 1

advice-f4cb6c63ff1c6e3dadc3b807.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f4cb6c63ff1c6e3dadc3b807.body:
(Practice, effort, and perseverance) He used to say also, that there was nothing whatever in life which could be brought to perfection without practice, and that that alone was able to overcome every obstacle; that, therefore, as we ought to repudiate all useless toils, and to apply ourselves to useful labours, and to live happily, we are only unhappy in consequence of most exceeding folly.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 50, excerpt 2

advice-ca595370b3e1e513026ac9e0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ca595370b3e1e513026ac9e0.body:
(The habit of a simple life without luxury) For the very contempt of pleasure, if we only inure ourselves to it, is very pleasant; and just as they who are accustomed to live luxuriously, are brought very unwillingly to adopt the contrary system; so they who have been originally inured to that opposite system, feel a sort of pleasure in the contempt of pleasure.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 50, excerpt 3

advice-f7ccc08608939acbe01f9575.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f7ccc08608939acbe01f9575.body:
(The common good and the order of the state) He also argued about the law, that without it there is no possibility of a constitution being maintained; for without a city there can be nothing orderly, but a city is an orderly thing; and without a city there can be no law; therefore law is order.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 51, excerpt 1

advice-394f27c1cb72c203e19c4e78.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-394f27c1cb72c203e19c4e78.body:
(Noble birth, reputation, and civic order) And he played in the same manner with the topics of noble birth, and reputation, and all things of that kind, saying that they were all veils, as it were, for wickedness; and that that was the only proper constitution which consisted in order.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §VI; source paragraph 51, excerpt 2

advice-20ddd468349ae9681d3980a8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-20ddd468349ae9681d3980a8.body:
(Diogenes in captivity: the sage’s inner freedom) Cleomenes relates that Diogenes’s friends wished to ransom him, but Diogenes called them foolish: lions do not become the slaves of those who keep them; rather, their keepers become the lions’ slaves. Fear is the mark of a slave, whereas wild beasts make people afraid.
Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)

sources.author: Diogenes of Sinope (attributed)
sources.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, Life of Diogenes, Yonge §IX; source paragraph 54, excerpt 1

advice-1dad45e0ebb49d4c8aca2faa.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1dad45e0ebb49d4c8aca2faa.body:
The same sound judgment becomes self-control in pleasure, endurance in hardship, and justice in our dealings with others.
Plutarch

advice-91fcb5a17fff259054fe4865.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-91fcb5a17fff259054fe4865.body:
(On vices mistaken for virtues) For no one ever yet called a fever health, or consumption a good condition of body, or gout swift-footedness, or paleness a good colour; but many call anger manliness, and love friendship, and envy competition, and cowardice prudence.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether The Disorders Of Mind Or Body Are Worse
sources.reference: Whether The Disorders Of Mind Or Body Are Worse, section III, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-bc82302d22452a0f9def43fa.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bc82302d22452a0f9def43fa.body:
(On the benefit of a friend's correction) For we ought to give our friend pain if it will benefit him, but not to the extent of breaking off our friendship; but just as we make use of some biting medicine, that will save and preserve the life of the patient.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XI, paragraph 7 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-5a666a55441cdfe9086358ed.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5a666a55441cdfe9086358ed.body:
(On improving oneself through one's enemies) If you say your enemy is uneducated, increase your own love of learning and industry; if you call him coward, stir up the more your own spirit and manliness; and if you say he is wanton and licentious, erase from your own soul any secret trace of the love of pleasure.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies
sources.reference: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies, section IV, paragraph 3 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-4cd2382a48a52bc36bc26c19.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4cd2382a48a52bc36bc26c19.body:
(On philosophy and contentment with life) By the aid of philosophy you will live not unpleasantly, for you will learn to extract pleasure from all places and things: wealth will make you happy, because it will enable you to benefit many; and poverty, as you will not then have many anxieties; and glory, for it will make you honoured; and obscurity, for you will then be safe from envy.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Virtue And Vice, section IV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-9a9115563d09d3c42e570331.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9a9115563d09d3c42e570331.body:
(On the constant exercise of reason) For the power of reason is not like physic, but wholesome food, which co-operates with good health in producing a good habit of body in those by whom it is taken.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section II, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-08c1c8ea16aba14fd06438bc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-08c1c8ea16aba14fd06438bc.body:
(On loyalty and constancy in friendship) For not to find friends at a time when you want them is hard, as also not to be able to exchange an inconstant and bad friend for a constant and good one.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section II, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-ccc59479b7648f0880d1867b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ccc59479b7648f0880d1867b.body:
(On envy of another's virtue) For as insects attack most ripe corn and roses in their bloom, so envy fastens most on the good and on those who are growing in virtue and good repute for moral character.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Envy And Hatred, section VI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-bd5001475e56507cb06145c6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bd5001475e56507cb06145c6.body:
(On happiness and one's inner disposition) You have often heard that happiness consists in right calculations resulting in a healthy state of mind, and that the changes which Fortune brings about need not upset it, and introduce confusion into our life.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Consolatory Letter To His Wife, section IX, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-6b5f33cb1f6ed702e2f8a23b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6b5f33cb1f6ed702e2f8a23b.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) For reasoning without passion has a direct tendency to justice, while if passion is infused, a contest and difference is excited between pleasure and pain on the one hand, and judgement and justice on the other.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section VII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-b83e3b795bf2acb333a3ec37.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b83e3b795bf2acb333a3ec37.body:
(On choosing the time for friendly frankness) And yet, just as in the case of any other medicine, to employ freedom of speech unseasonably is only to give needless pain and trouble, and in a manner to do so as to produce vexation the very thing the flatterer does so as to produce pleasure.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-df47ee7257e6644b62433dee.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-df47ee7257e6644b62433dee.body:
(On irritation over trifles) For as small writing strains the eyes, so small matters even more strain and bother people, and stir up their anger, which carries this evil habit to greater matters.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section XVI, paragraph 4 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-df737e32574fc120c8d4ebea.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-df737e32574fc120c8d4ebea.body:
(On reluctance to admit one's envy) But people deny that they are envious, and, if they are charged with being so, they put forward ten thousand pleas, saying they are angry with the man or fear him or hate him, suggesting any other passion than envy, and concealing it as the only disorder of the soul which is abominable.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Envy And Hatred, section V, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-0e2f467b59419857cabff41c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0e2f467b59419857cabff41c.body:
(On restraining anger at its onset) But when the judgement checks and suppresses at once the rising anger, it not only cures the soul for the moment, but restores its tone and balance for the future.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section III, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-2ad7aa084e872c170aea8ee3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2ad7aa084e872c170aea8ee3.body:
(On praise that makes friendly correction acceptable) Indeed peevishness and querulousness are altogether alien to friendship and social life: but when goodwill bestows praise ungrudgingly and readily upon good actions, people endure also easily and without pain admonition and plainspeaking, believing and continuing to love the person who took such pleasure in praising, as if now he only blamed out of necessity.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section II, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-4f79b3bb0e219b5742b54c00.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4f79b3bb0e219b5742b54c00.body:
(On envy and malicious joy) For envy is pain at another's blessings, and malignity is joy at another's misfortunes: and both proceed from the same savage and brutish vice, ill-nature.
Plutarch

advice-2f6aa5a20aaed1092dcbd3a1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2f6aa5a20aaed1092dcbd3a1.body:
(On the pain of public reproach) For people are beside themselves with pain and rage if reproached before those with whom they desire to be held in good repute.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXXII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-27077f11d3cf7ad0cf781c7c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-27077f11d3cf7ad0cf781c7c.body:
(On tact and moderation in friendly frankness) And so we ought to employ tact in our freedom of speech, as it is the greatest and most powerful remedy in friendship, and always needs a well-chosen occasion, and moderation in applying it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXXVI, paragraph 4 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-fafaa83809f2a613434eef0d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fafaa83809f2a613434eef0d.body:
(On envy of another's virtue) But whoever is steeped in contentiousness and envy against his betters, let him know that he may be pricked on by a jealous desire for glory or power, but that he neither honours nor admires virtue.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section XIV, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-c0b4146a1bff6f0dfdb8bed2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c0b4146a1bff6f0dfdb8bed2.body:
(On humility in good fortune) For there are few who are sensible in prosperity, most need to borrow wisdom from others, and such considerations as shall keep them lowly when puffed up and giving themselves airs owing to their good fortune.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXVIII, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-f0525087cf8d520e01efa0c1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f0525087cf8d520e01efa0c1.body:
(On happiness and one's inner disposition) But a happy and cheerful life is not from without, on the contrary, a man adds the pleasure and gratification to the things that surround him, his temperament being as it were the source of his feelings.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Virtue And Vice, section I, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-c2caa975b5e585ae1374411e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c2caa975b5e585ae1374411e.body:
(On remorse after wrongdoing) For reason banishes all other griefs, but itself creates regret when the soul is vexed with shame and self-tormented.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XIX, paragraph 4 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-1b6b32d83546787103d66661.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1b6b32d83546787103d66661.body:
(On remaining blessings amid adversity) And so, if we fall into any real trouble or evil, we ought to get cheerfulness and ease of mind from the consideration of the actual blessings that are still left to us, mitigating outward trouble by private happiness.
Plutarch

advice-bbc37a35160a6da1e44fd77c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bbc37a35160a6da1e44fd77c.body:
(On improving oneself through one's enemies) Similarly whoever knows that his enemy is antagonistic to his life and character, pays more attention to himself, and watches his behaviour more carefully, and regulates his life.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies
sources.reference: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies, section III, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-757b0f0b78bb08e3e48f2c3e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-757b0f0b78bb08e3e48f2c3e.body:
(On peace of mind without abandoning duties) And indeed stupor is a bad remedy for the body against despair, nor is he any better physician of the soul who removes its trouble and anxiety by recommending a lazy and soft life and a leaving our friends and relations and country in the lurch.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section II, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-8fc17ba26d1c5d1081f9ac3d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8fc17ba26d1c5d1081f9ac3d.body:
(On calmness and goodwill in debate) For in such cases moderation and mildness, and to commence arguing without quarrelsomeness and to finish without getting into a rage, and neither to be insolent if you come off best in the argument, nor dejected if you come off worst, is a sufficient sign of progress in virtue.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section IX, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-8e8092db3ec06a5bd328f866.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8e8092db3ec06a5bd328f866.body:
(On flattery for wealth and status) For just as lice leave dying persons, and abandon bodies when the blood on which they feed is drying up, so one never yet saw flatterers dancing attendance on dry and cold poverty, but they fasten on wealth and position and there get fat, but speedily decamp if reverses come.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section II, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-1c835788ce412d78a21d9673.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1c835788ce412d78a21d9673.body:
(On comfort from memories of past happiness) For as perfume gives pleasure to the nose, and is a remedy against disagreeable smells, so the remembrance of past happiness in present trouble gives all the relief they require to those who do not shut out of their memory the blessings of the past, or always and everywhere rail against Fortune.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Consolatory Letter To His Wife, section VIII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-d203038e2035bd9a32a27fe4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d203038e2035bd9a32a27fe4.body:
(On learning virtue from every source) So much does attention and assiduous practice make people perceptive and receptive of what contributes to virtue from any source.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section VIII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-60debfd07b36489bc113e531.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-60debfd07b36489bc113e531.body:
(On anger over disappointed expectations) For nothing swells the anger more, than when a good man is detected of villainy, or one who we thought loved us falls out and jangles with us.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section XVI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-149c49efb2d56e00ea276f12.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-149c49efb2d56e00ea276f12.body:
(On self-love as a cause of self-praise) For there is a wonderful incentive to talking about oneself in self-love, which is frequently strongly implanted in those who seem to have only moderate aspirations for fame.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy
sources.reference: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy, section XVIII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-69d541ac3a93a89a4da9cbdb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-69d541ac3a93a89a4da9cbdb.body:
(On talkativeness that prevents listening and learning) But the talkative person acts just contrary, for if any subject is introduced from which he might learn something he did not know, this he rejects and refuses, not being able to earn a good deal by a short silence, but he rambles round the subject and babbles out stale and commonplace rhapsodies.
Plutarch

advice-f99ab3ac4d67e09228d589b3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f99ab3ac4d67e09228d589b3.body:
(On overcoming anger through one's own reason) For anger being haughty and self-willed and hard to be worked upon by another, like a fortified tyranny, must have someone born and bred within it to overthrow it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section II, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-b43aab10de83443e1904e55b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b43aab10de83443e1904e55b.body:
(On practical wisdom in choosing actions) And there is this difference between prudence and knowledge, prudence consists in applying the contemplative to the practical and emotional so as to make reason paramount.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section V, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-f2b12613ceac1bc18aa1195c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f2b12613ceac1bc18aa1195c.body:
(On pausing before punishment in anger) For the interval of time gives a pause to passion, and a delay that mitigates it, and so judgement finds out both the fit manner and adequate amount of punishment.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section XI, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-e440ec8b0356d9d9c063a621.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e440ec8b0356d9d9c063a621.body:
(On being known and thereby benefiting others) And as light, I take it, makes us not only visible but useful to one another, so being known gives not only glory but impetus to virtue.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether "Live Unknown" Be A Wise Precept
sources.reference: Whether "Live Unknown" Be A Wise Precept, section IV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-1093496a4e44ad68007a87b6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1093496a4e44ad68007a87b6.body:
(On rejecting excessive and false praise) For even envy is not reluctant to give moderate praise to one that deprecates excessive praise, and true panegyric is not lost by people refusing to accept idle and false praise.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy
sources.reference: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy, section XII, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-b094393a7af447b59a7f161f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b094393a7af447b59a7f161f.body:
(On wisdom as distinct from external goods) So wisdom is neither gold, nor silver, nor fame, nor wealth, nor health, nor strength, nor beauty.
Plutarch

advice-00c01a697eae5732230f73d7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-00c01a697eae5732230f73d7.body:
(On the benefit of a friend's correction) And so the friend, like a musician, in bringing about an improvement to what is good and expedient, sometimes slackens the chords, sometimes tightens them, and is often pleasant, but always useful.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XI, paragraph 7 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-89d47f14a2eed3a0f8e3d01b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-89d47f14a2eed3a0f8e3d01b.body:
(On frankness while sober) And generally speaking it is not noble or brave but cowardly to conceal your ideas when people are sober and to give free vent to them at table, snarling like cowardly dogs.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXVII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-3502a23f37c67f28d7aac9da.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3502a23f37c67f28d7aac9da.body:
(On idle curiosity about others' secrets) For curiosity desires to know what is hidden and secret; but no one conceals his good fortune, nay sometimes people even pretend to have such advantages as they do not really possess.
Plutarch

advice-869998e4c9a8ecda3f8e06c6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-869998e4c9a8ecda3f8e06c6.body:
(On acknowledging one's own weaknesses) But agreeable and graceful is that man who mentions his own forgetfulness, or ignorance, or ambition, or eager desire for knowledge and conversation.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy
sources.reference: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy, section XIII, paragraph 3 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-b4d5b843a640ce07e1a3a457.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b4d5b843a640ce07e1a3a457.body:
(On happiness and one's inner disposition) So, too, wealth is pleasanter, and fame and power more splendid, when a man has joy in his heart, seeing that men can bear easily and quietly poverty and exile and old age if their character is a contented and mild one.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Virtue And Vice, section I, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-7d1d682930c6c2300aa4c6fa.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7d1d682930c6c2300aa4c6fa.body:
(On envy of another's virtue) For we hate people more as they grow worse, but they are envied only the more the more they advance in virtue.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Envy And Hatred, section VI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-e19d7082d9ec271af4bde538.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e19d7082d9ec271af4bde538.body:
(On friends sharing life, thoughts and conversation) For intimacy is the full enjoyment of friendship, and most pleasant is companying with and spending the day with a friend.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Abundance Of Friends, section V, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-d8535bfaee74ac4fa930f9d8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d8535bfaee74ac4fa930f9d8.body:
(On exile and the world as a shared home) For nature makes us free and unrestrained, but we bind and confine immure and force ourselves into small and scanty space.
Plutarch

advice-92c0f85f2250e44febb5682c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-92c0f85f2250e44febb5682c.body:
(On rational willingness to revise one's beliefs) And so reason gladly inclines to the truth, when it is evident, and abandons error; for in it, and not in passion, lies a willingness to listen to conviction and to change one's opinions on conviction.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section VII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-56973514520dbaeeef45855e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-56973514520dbaeeef45855e.body:
(On choosing worthy friends) We ought not, therefore, lightly to welcome or strike up an intimate friendship with any chance comers, or love those who attach themselves to us, but attach ourselves to those who are worthy of our friendship.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Abundance Of Friends, section IV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-642b884390bf4552e87ced68.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-642b884390bf4552e87ced68.body:
(On the benefit of a friend's correction) For true and friendly outspokenness attacks wrong-doers, bringing pain that is salutary and likely to make them more careful, like honey biting but cleansing ulcerated parts of the body, but in other respects serviceable and sweet.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XVII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-eea178113b66cee723d257d6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-eea178113b66cee723d257d6.body:
(On meddling as an escape from one's faults) But some men cannot bear to look upon their own life, so unlovely a spectacle is it, nor to throw and flash on themselves, like a lantern, the reflection of reason; but their soul being burdened with all manner of vices, and dreading and shuddering at its own interior, sallies forth and wanders abroad, feeding and fattening its malignity there.
Plutarch

advice-3bc2ca09956448bbff05df7a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-3bc2ca09956448bbff05df7a.body:
(On inner goods preserved in exile) But although one soil is more suitable to a plant than another, and it thrives and grows better on such a soil, yet no situation can rob a man of his happiness or virtue or sense.
Plutarch

advice-756eed94c93d529a8bb002c2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-756eed94c93d529a8bb002c2.body:
(On reproach without personal resentment or self-love) As then we see that much trouble arises from excessive freedom of speech, let us first of all detach from it any element of self-love, being carefully on our guard that we may not appear to upbraid on account of any private hurt or injury.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXVI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-2a7af3b51dec6776d622fcbb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2a7af3b51dec6776d622fcbb.body:
(On loyalty and constancy in friendship) But friendship requires a steady constant and unchangeable character, a person that is uniform in his intimacy.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Abundance Of Friends, section IX, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-7d98acff025af746c253927a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7d98acff025af746c253927a.body:
(On the value of a life known to others) For my part I should say, Even if your life be bad do not live unknown, but be known, reform, repent; if you have virtue, be not utterly useless in life; if you are vicious, do not continue unreformed.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether "Live Unknown" Be A Wise Precept
sources.reference: Whether "Live Unknown" Be A Wise Precept, section II, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-de4e0d2322ea868e872062e9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-de4e0d2322ea868e872062e9.body:
(On preparing in advance to resist anger) But as those who expect a siege get together and store up supplies, when they despair of relief from without, so ought we by all means to scour the country far and wide to derive aids against anger from philosophy, and store them up in the soul: for, when the time of need comes, we shall find it no easy task to import them.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section II, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-252625348045cd9876fb2ab3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-252625348045cd9876fb2ab3.body:
(On actions and words that intensify one's anger) But anger on the contrary is much more fanned by what angry persons do and say.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section V, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-63bb3435ae028c4fde168f5d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-63bb3435ae028c4fde168f5d.body:
(On choosing worthy friends) We ought not therefore to be too lavish with our virtue, binding it together and implicating it in various people's fortunes, but we ought to preserve our friendship for those who are worthy of it, and are capable of reciprocating it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Abundance Of Friends, section VIII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-8d8fef93f1339757e10cdd48.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8d8fef93f1339757e10cdd48.body:
(On matching desires to one's means) Another thing, which is a great hindrance to peace of mind, is not to proportion our desires to our means, but to carry too much sail, as it were, in our hopes of great things and then, if unsuccessful, to blame destiny and fortune, and not our own folly.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-1e351a1bf6a5e4df33b1fd85.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1e351a1bf6a5e4df33b1fd85.body:
(On gradual moral improvement) For indeed a wise man cannot in a moment of time change from absolute badness to perfect goodness, and suddenly abandon for ever all that vice, of which he could not during a long period of time divest himself of any portion.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section I, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-ac77016f861589ff1de2bba6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ac77016f861589ff1de2bba6.body:
(On flattery imitating the pleasantness of friendship) But just as spurious and mock gold only imitates the brightness and glitter of real gold, so the flatterer seems to imitate the pleasantness and agreeableness of the real friend, and to exhibit himself ever merry and bright, contradicting and opposing nothing.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section II, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-1d9c94be52d0237aa2b0c230.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1d9c94be52d0237aa2b0c230.body:
(On being known and thereby benefiting others) For the statesman does not ask for reputation as a reward or consolation, nor is he merely pleased at its attending upon his actions, but he values it because credit and character give him opportunities to do good on a larger scale.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy
sources.reference: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy, section II, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-106b09c8070a20ac902631b0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-106b09c8070a20ac902631b0.body:
(On philosophy and contentment with life) You will be contented, if you have learned what is good and honourable.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Virtue And Vice, section IV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-ed54d14af7ef12d57576f112.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ed54d14af7ef12d57576f112.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) Similarly with oxen and horses people try to restrain their mad bounds and restiveness, not their movements and powers of work, and so reason makes use of the passions when they have become tame and docile, not by cutting out the sinews or altogether mutilating the serviceable part of the soul.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section XII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-971694f81f12ad20045e9160.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-971694f81f12ad20045e9160.body:
(On the limits of close friendship) And so to love or be loved very much cannot find place with many persons; for as rivers that have many channels and cuttings have a weak and thin stream, so excessive love in the soul if divided out among many is weakened.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Abundance Of Friends, section II, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-c968d617457de32e69b75d81.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c968d617457de32e69b75d81.body:
(On acknowledging fortune and divine help in success) But those that are compelled to praise themselves do so less offensively if they do not ascribe all the honour to themselves, but, being aware that their glory will be tiresome to others, set it down partly to fortune, partly to the deity.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy
sources.reference: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy, section XI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-11eb4628d52994952ab5bfe9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-11eb4628d52994952ab5bfe9.body:
(On tact and moderation in friendly frankness) Seeing then, that it is equally disgraceful to become a flatterer through trying only to please, as in avoiding flattery to destroy all friendship and intimacy by excessive freedom of speech, we must avoid both these extremes, and, as in any other case, make our freedom of speech agreeable by its moderation.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-840af4e3d8d51bc3b3f757ae.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-840af4e3d8d51bc3b3f757ae.body:
(On overcoming anger through one's own reason) And so an empty ship in a storm at open sea would sooner admit on board a pilot from without, than a man in a tempest of rage and anger would listen to another's advice, unless his own reason was first prepared to hearken.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section II, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-e81dfbaf1377ce5529d8ebec.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e81dfbaf1377ce5529d8ebec.body:
(On conceit that makes one vulnerable to flatterers) For lofty heights are difficult of approach and hard to reach for those who endeavour to scale them, but the highmindedness and conceit of a person thrown off his balance by good fortune or good natural parts is easily reached by mean and petty people.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXIV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-c7b00d67a65581dec6f1b68e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c7b00d67a65581dec6f1b68e.body:
(On mildness and measured anger) Good temper on the other hand is useful in some circumstances, adorns and sweetens others, and gets the better of all peevishness and anger by its gentleness.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section XIV, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-cdcc54063b29ee1137e7e7c7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cdcc54063b29ee1137e7e7c7.body:
(On frankness without mockery or insults) In the next place, let us clear away as it were and remove all insolence, and jeering, and mocking, and ribaldry, which are the evil seasonings of freedom of speech.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXVII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-410c2b8453bf6c9c4c67e195.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-410c2b8453bf6c9c4c67e195.body:
(On facing adversity with reason) But the soul that accustoms itself to face steadily sickness and grief and exile, and calls in reason to its help in each case, will find in what appears so sore and dreadful much that is false, empty, and rotten, as reason will show in each case.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XVIII, paragraph 3 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-c192187264b8ae33ad6f77dc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c192187264b8ae33ad6f77dc.body:
(On the right measure between excess and deficiency) And so everything we do may be a success from one point of view, but a failure from many points of view; as to hit the mark one thing only is requisite, but one may miss it in various ways, as one may shoot beyond or too short.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section V, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-7789ceb9aa7533076686f321.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7789ceb9aa7533076686f321.body:
(On public speaking for a worthy purpose) Much more then ought those who aim at virtue and what is noble to lose no opportunity of public speaking, paying very little attention to either uproar or applause at their speeches.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section IX, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-0612333fa56241d72d136366.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0612333fa56241d72d136366.body:
(On envy of other people's lives) For not only do people envy those of the same trade and manner of life, but the rich envy the learned, and the famous the rich, and advocates sophists, aye, and freemen and patricians admire and think happy comedians starring it at the theatres, and dancers, and the attendants at kings' courts, and by all this envy give themselves no small trouble and annoyance.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XIII, paragraph 3 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-6a76fb122cedff51bdad0ecc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6a76fb122cedff51bdad0ecc.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) Now temperance is a state, wherein reason holds the reins, and manages the passions as a quiet and well-broken-in animal, finding them obedient and submissive to the reins and masters over their desires.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section VI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-9ce7105757b0cdc5b1fb82d3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9ce7105757b0cdc5b1fb82d3.body:
(On the ambition to excel in everything) Self-love is mainly to blame, making people fond of being first and aspiring in all matters, and insatiably desirous to engage in everything.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-d33ed0bbea9d8bcbd3415c76.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d33ed0bbea9d8bcbd3415c76.body:
(On weakness of will despite rational knowledge) Incontinence, therefore, is a mark of a sophistical soul, endued with reason which cannot abide by what it knows to be right.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section VI, paragraph 6 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-c9e7631a794ea1e2e1721fc6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c9e7631a794ea1e2e1721fc6.body:
(On the harm of words spoken in anger) For if the tongue of people in a fever be unnatural, it is a bad sign, but not the cause of their malady; but the tongue of angry people, being rough and foul, and breaking out into unseemly speeches, produces insults that work irremediable mischief, and argue deep-rooted malevolence within.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section VII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-874bae0da641a2c83db9b587.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-874bae0da641a2c83db9b587.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) For the function of reason is no Thracian or Lycurgean one to root up and destroy all the good elements in passion indiscriminately with the bad, but, as some genial and mild god, to prune what is wild, and to correct disproportion, and after that to train and cultivate the useful part.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section XII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-8f8c2a6778bfa1210a977baa.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8f8c2a6778bfa1210a977baa.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) For as in sounds music does not create melody by the banishment of sharps and flats, and as in bodies the art of the physician procures health not by the doing away of cold and heat but by their being blended in due proportions and quantities, so is victory won in the soul by the powers and motions of the passions being reduced by reason to moderation and due proportion.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section XII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-e3250a35db2e20916a135af8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e3250a35db2e20916a135af8.body:
(On mental burdens added to real troubles) For the body is weighed down by the burden of what presses on it, but the soul often adds to the real load a burden of its own.
Plutarch

advice-96e29896713040b87d0974a5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-96e29896713040b87d0974a5.body:
(On feelings inseparable from goodwill) And no one if they wished could pluck away or sever natural affection from friendship, or pity from philanthropy, or sympathy both in joy and grief from genuine goodwill.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section XII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-e683e9b0ec200b18324fb83d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e683e9b0ec200b18324fb83d.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) But if the passions were entirely removed, supposing that to be possible, reason would become in many duller and blunter, like the pilot in the absence of a storm.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section XII, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-cd61ae8dc20e4dc01d5b222e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cd61ae8dc20e4dc01d5b222e.body:
(On usefulness and truth over display) And not only ought each to see to his discourses but also to his actions whether he regards utility more than show, and truth more than display.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section X, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-9672343278ee4d0235ab09bb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9672343278ee4d0235ab09bb.body:
(On integrity in the face of dishonest success) But if our enemies seem to us to have got either by flattery, or fraud, or bribery, or venal services, ill-got and discreditable power at court or in state, it ought not to trouble us but rather inspire pleasure in us, when we compare our own liberty and purity and independence of life.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies
sources.reference: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies, section XI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-90b090037cc65a56d4b84757.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-90b090037cc65a56d4b84757.body:
(On happiness and one's inner disposition) For those who live at random and without judgement, like those sickly people who can stand neither heat nor cold, are unduly elated by prosperity, and cast down by adversity; and in either case suffer from unrest, but 'tis their own fault, and perhaps they suffer most in what are called good circumstances.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section V, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-d4df2f79b907c74cb3fe9507.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d4df2f79b907c74cb3fe9507.body:
(On recognizing present and past blessings) For the foolish overlook and neglect present blessings, through their thoughts being ever intent on the future; but the wise make the past clearly present to them through memory.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XIV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-bb942f03d091cb4f222d49eb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bb942f03d091cb4f222d49eb.body:
(On happiness and one's inner disposition) Let us cleanse therefore the fountain of contentedness, which is within us, that so external things may turn out for our good, through our putting the best face on them.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section IV, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-dd1c6a35d0ab86aad69e681e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-dd1c6a35d0ab86aad69e681e.body:
(On consolation that does not intensify grief) For when people see their friends' houses on fire they put it out as quickly and energetically as they can, but when their souls are on fire they themselves bring fuel.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Consolatory Letter To His Wife, section VII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-2b72adfc9ebec53e45b347c3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2b72adfc9ebec53e45b347c3.body:
(On refusing wrongdoing under pressure from others) In like manner, if a man of good repute tries to force and importune us to something bad, let us tell him that he is acting in an ignoble way, and not as his birth and virtue would warrant.
Plutarch

advice-f4dd4b1e98e759e5f5b2f03d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f4dd4b1e98e759e5f5b2f03d.body:
(On reproach without personal resentment or self-love) For people do not regard a speech on the speaker's own behalf as arising from goodwill, but from anger, and reproach rather than admonition.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXVI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-0a60d9a5bcdd0e8ad515af44.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0a60d9a5bcdd0e8ad515af44.body:
(On choosing the time for friendly frankness) And on all occasions to let an opportunity slip by is very injurious, but especially does it destroy the usefulness of freedom of speech.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXVII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-51ade2c33b12e8c671582433.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-51ade2c33b12e8c671582433.body:
(On bashfulness that prevents saying no) But bashfulness is not only a bad and inconsiderate manager of money, but also in more important matters makes us reject expediency and reason.
Plutarch

advice-333b94e007441347d7709e3b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-333b94e007441347d7709e3b.body:
(On envy of praise given to others) For as hungry people have their appetite more inflamed and sharpened by seeing others eat, so the praise of one's neighbours makes those who eagerly desire fame to blaze out into jealousy.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy
sources.reference: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy, section XVIII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-8a1013206bf32b198e3eb92c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8a1013206bf32b198e3eb92c.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) For so he that makes the baser element subject to the better has self-control and is a superior man, whereas he who allows the nobler element of the soul to follow and be subservient to the incorrigible and unreasoning element, is inferior to what he might be, and is called incontinent, and is in an unnatural condition.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section XI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-533f5cc33d0caf8920e8a2f5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-533f5cc33d0caf8920e8a2f5.body:
(On peace of mind and the morality of actions) But we ought not to estimate ease or unrest of mind by our many or few actions, but by their fairness or foulness.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section II, paragraph 6 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-e1134f46983e3722c0d42fc6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e1134f46983e3722c0d42fc6.body:
(On the mixture of good and bad in life) For, as the strings of the bow and lyre are alternately tightened and relaxed, so is it with the order of the world; in human affairs there is nothing pure and without alloy.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-a02367f6e44b43b1282edb50.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a02367f6e44b43b1282edb50.body:
(On tact and moderation in friendly frankness) For nothing makes rebuke less painful or more beneficial than to refrain from anger, and to inveigh against wrong-doing mildly and kindly.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXXVI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-4ee12d2e06aa1a8da2c8b472.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4ee12d2e06aa1a8da2c8b472.body:
(On improving oneself through one's enemies) For the cautiousness that thus represses the passions and follows reason implants a care and determination to live well and without reproach.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies
sources.reference: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies, section III, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-4df2d93ec0b9e9a53ff72922.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4df2d93ec0b9e9a53ff72922.body:
(On recognizing the harm of talkativeness and other passions) And we dislike the passions only when we discern by reason the harm and shame that results to us by indulging them.
Plutarch

advice-5399baacedb8ca2922722914.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5399baacedb8ca2922722914.body:
(On refusing to drink more than one needs) For example, if anyone pledge you to drink with him at a dinner when you have had enough, do not be bashful, or do violence to nature, but put the cup down without drinking.
Plutarch

advice-e632cb15639293618d56c2cf.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e632cb15639293618d56c2cf.body:
(On bashfulness that prevents saying no) For the bashful, not venturing to say No to those that press them hard, afterwards feel shame at just rebuke, and, through standing in awe of slight blame, frequently in the end incur open disgrace.
Plutarch

advice-506b6afffdd3845db7ec3eb7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-506b6afffdd3845db7ec3eb7.body:
(On restraining anger at its onset) For the first way, my friend, to overcome anger, like the putting down of some tyrant, is not to obey or listen to it when it bids you speak loud, and look fierce, and beat yourself, but to remain quiet, and not to make the passion more intense, as one would a disease, by tossing about and crying out.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section V, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-2141c40f4d00f80b9a29c9f9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2141c40f4d00f80b9a29c9f9.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) Not that reason wishes to expel passion altogether (that is neither possible, nor advisable), but only to keep it within bounds and order, and to engender the moral virtues, which are not apathetic, but hold the due proportion and mean in regard to passion.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section IV, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-dd8abca1866f792bc211278b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-dd8abca1866f792bc211278b.body:
(On flattery imitating the pleasantness of friendship) For as wild grains mixed up with wheat, if very similar in size and appearance, are not easily kept apart, for if the sieve have small holes they don't pass through, and if large holes they pass with the corn, so flattery is not easily distinguished from friendship, being mixed up with it in feeling and emotion, habit and custom.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section IV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-d79604d75fe227cfaf50253d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d79604d75fe227cfaf50253d.body:
(On directing curiosity wisely) For you will gain no advantage by mixing yourself up with curious people: but you will derive the greatest benefit from putting a force upon your inclinations, and bridling your curiosity, and accustoming it to obey reason.
Plutarch

advice-4b6c46ed3cea00f16a868730.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4b6c46ed3cea00f16a868730.body:
(On remaining blessings amid adversity) For the sensible make their life pleasanter and more endurable by mitigating their sorrows with the consideration of their blessings, while most people, like sieves, let the worst things stick to them while the best pass through.
Plutarch

advice-73c327653478f0917ac26ab6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-73c327653478f0917ac26ab6.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) And if those err who wish to banish love because of erotic madness, neither are they right who blame all desire because of love of money, but they act like people who refuse to run because they might stumble, or to throw because they might throw wide of the mark, or object to sing altogether because they might make a false note.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section XII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-97cf2451fa70f4d25a16c43d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-97cf2451fa70f4d25a16c43d.body:
(On valuing virtue above external goods) Whenever then, by thus comparing the advantages of virtue with external things, you get rid of envies and jealousies and those things which fret and depress the minds of many who are novices in philosophy, this also is a great indication of your progress in virtue.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section VII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-ed0268c3340c87e8a7c316df.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ed0268c3340c87e8a7c316df.body:
(On consolation that does not intensify grief) For many who come forward do more harm than good in the remarks they make to the unfortunate, as people unable to swim trying to rescue the drowning get entangled with them and sink to the bottom together.
Plutarch

advice-e020750cf8768ec63bc6d90f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e020750cf8768ec63bc6d90f.body:
(On perseverance in pursuing virtue) For the enthusiasm that can go so far as not to be discouraged at the sure prospect of trouble, but admires and emulates what is good even so, could never be turned away from what is noble by anybody.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section XV, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-70f53c2851660f91bccb72d1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-70f53c2851660f91bccb72d1.body:
(On trust between proven friends) For a friend should be like money tried before being required, not found faulty in our need.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section II, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-ea87665b747e41dd61b73109.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ea87665b747e41dd61b73109.body:
(On helping a friend without display) For the favour done by a friend, as the principal strength of an animal is within, is not for display or ostentation, but frequently as a doctor cures his patient imperceptibly, so a friend benefits by his intervention, or by paying off creditors, or by managing his friend's affairs, even though the person who receives the benefit may not be aware of it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXII, paragraph 6 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-4d45c1ec384353c60f808166.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4d45c1ec384353c60f808166.body:
(On frankness while sober) For wine makes people easily slip into rage, and oftentimes freedom of speech in liquor makes enemies.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXVII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-38afa9c56215b1e6fd35ad2b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-38afa9c56215b1e6fd35ad2b.body:
(On recognizing the harm of talkativeness and other passions) For no one is wont to shun, and eradicate from his soul, what he does not dislike.
Plutarch

advice-d28daca5b5cd1f59c3b486fd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d28daca5b5cd1f59c3b486fd.body:
(On simple living and contentment with little) We must therefore train the body to contentment by plain living, that it may be easily satisfied: for they that require little do not miss much; and it is no great hardship to begin with our food, and take it silently whatever it is, and not by being choleric and peevish to thrust upon ourselves and friends the worst sauce to meat, anger.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section XIII, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-d597ae98a7d8ac766d548f12.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d597ae98a7d8ac766d548f12.body:
(On incompatible pursuits and ambitions) And indeed there are some pursuits which cannot exist together, but are by their very nature opposed.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XIII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-7a232a9bf5c7863e00c0a5a6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7a232a9bf5c7863e00c0a5a6.body:
(On choosing pursuits suited to one's abilities) So that all things are not within any one's power, and we must obey that saying inscribed in the temple of Apollo at Delphi, Know thyself, and adapt ourselves to our natural bent, and not drag and force nature to some other kind of life or pursuit.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XIII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-c56ac176531d65ef0d77cc4e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c56ac176531d65ef0d77cc4e.body:
(On talkativeness that prevents listening and learning) And the first evil this inability to keep silence produces is an inability to listen.
Plutarch

advice-7ec1c4b601c2537ff2a4360d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7ec1c4b601c2537ff2a4360d.body:
(On restraining anger at its onset) For as a person puts out a fire by bringing no fuel to it, so with respect to anger, he that does not in the beginning fan it, and stir up its rage in himself, keeps it off and destroys it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section IV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-7fe718ca78366a226ef7e19d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7fe718ca78366a226ef7e19d.body:
(On anger reflected in one's own face) For to behold oneself unnaturally distorted in countenance will condemn anger in no small degree.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section VI, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-726877e93e2c663577b62925.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-726877e93e2c663577b62925.body:
(On reasons for ending hostility) Men put an end to their enmity and hatred, either if persuaded they have not been wronged, or if they come round to the view that those they hated are good men and not bad, or thirdly if they receive a kindness.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Envy And Hatred, section VII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-77de02ff8334506f7f25fdd4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-77de02ff8334506f7f25fdd4.body:
(On arguments learned in advance to restrain passions) For as savage dogs are excited at every sound, and are only soothed by a familiar voice, so also it is not easy to quiet the wild passions of the soul, unless familiar and well-known arguments be at hand to check its excitement.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section I, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-1732b348a6bd046504754bd4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1732b348a6bd046504754bd4.body:
(On remaining blessings amid adversity) But, as we use our brightest colours in a picture, so in the mind we ought to look at the cheerful and bright side of things, and hide and keep down the gloomy, for we cannot altogether obliterate or get rid of it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-5424ae614c9ae96c85788b5c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5424ae614c9ae96c85788b5c.body:
(On gradual moral improvement) Just as mariners sailing with full sail over the gaping ocean measure the course they have made by the time they have taken and the force of the wind, and compute their progress accordingly, so anyone can compute his progress in philosophy by his continuous and unceasing course, by his not making many halts on the road, and then again advancing by leaps and bounds, but by his quiet and even and steady march forward guided by reason.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section III, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-f9e2d63eb525fda7e1e92dc2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f9e2d63eb525fda7e1e92dc2.body:
(On praise that makes friendly correction acceptable) For friendship requires praise as much as censure on the proper occasion.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section II, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-1a2e4124a99eb861b409cf4e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1a2e4124a99eb861b409cf4e.body:
(On seriousness in a friend's admonition) We may on other occasions jest and laugh with our friends, but let our outspokenness be coupled with seriousness and gravity, and if it be on important matters, let our speech be trustworthy and moving from its pathos, and animation, and tone of voice.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXVII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-fbca93e29caf15a2a4657afd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fbca93e29caf15a2a4657afd.body:
(On reputation earned through effort and risk) For as it is with house and farm, so also is it with glory and reputation, people for the most part envy those who have got them easily or for nothing, not those who have bought them at the cost of much toil and danger.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy
sources.reference: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy, section XIV, paragraph 3 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-a3668c95f4179f3325e3906c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a3668c95f4179f3325e3906c.body:
(On consolation that does not intensify grief) Now the discourse that ought to come from friends and people disposed to be helpful should be consolation, and not mere assent with a man's sad feelings.
Plutarch

advice-edeafacc39694ec761db0987.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-edeafacc39694ec761db0987.body:
(On the reciprocal duties of friends) But most people in friendship regard only, it seems, what can be got out of it, overlooking what will be asked in return, and not remembering that he, who has had many of his own requests granted, must oblige others in turn by granting their requests.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Abundance Of Friends, section VI, paragraph 3 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-960d3a840f0be4d9bdad1c72.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-960d3a840f0be4d9bdad1c72.body:
(On friendship without envy or rivalry) Whereas among real friends there is no rivalry or jealousy of one another, but they are satisfied and contented alike whether they are equal or one of them is superior.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section X, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-b84d55ecba795972c21ce5a9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b84d55ecba795972c21ce5a9.body:
(On the moral limits of helping a friend) For one must indeed assist one's friend but not do anything wrong for him, one must advise with him but not plot with him, one must bear witness for him but not join him in fraud, one must certainly share adversity with him but not crime.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXIII, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-4c6a6fe6d94b22dfb08d73fc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4c6a6fe6d94b22dfb08d73fc.body:
(On directing curiosity wisely) For as eagles and lions on the prowl keep their claws sheathed that they may not lose their edge and sharpness, so, when we remember that curiosity for learning has also its edge and keenness, let us not entirely expend or blunt it on inferior objects.
Plutarch

advice-b70808cfaa0cafc344ab603b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b70808cfaa0cafc344ab603b.body:
(On choosing pursuits suited to one's abilities) For not to be able to do everything carries no disgrace with it, but to undertake and try and force your way to what you are unable to do, or unqualified by nature for, is in addition to the disgrace incurred a task full of trouble.
Plutarch

advice-47af7ad20b6f3dd34d5ea676.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-47af7ad20b6f3dd34d5ea676.body:
(On happiness and one's inner disposition) As therefore the shoe is shaped by the foot, and not the foot by the shoe, so does the disposition make the life similar to itself.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section IV, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-c69feae2e579b0b2f90cc89c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c69feae2e579b0b2f90cc89c.body:
(On incompatible pursuits and ambitions) We do not expect a vine to bear figs, nor an olive grapes, yet now-a-days, with regard to ourselves, if we have not at one and the same time the privilege of being accounted rich and learned, generals and philosophers, flatterers and outspoken, stingy and extravagant, we slander ourselves and are dissatisfied, and despise ourselves as living a maimed and imperfect life.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section XIII, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-eb281c8796451f1b6d27c25f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-eb281c8796451f1b6d27c25f.body:
(On admitting one's faults in order to improve) Now, when one has done what is wrong, to offer oneself for reproof, to expose the case and reveal one's wrongdoing, and not to rejoice if it lies hid, or be satisfied if it is not known, but to make confession of it and ask for interference and admonishment, is no small indication of progress in virtue.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section XI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-7a35b2e7e4c552ba81de6ea9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7a35b2e7e4c552ba81de6ea9.body:
(On the difference between envy and hatred) So envy seems illimitable, being, like ophthalmia, troubled at everything bright, whereas hatred is limited, since it settles only on what seems hostile.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Envy And Hatred, section II, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-9927f5f8c2a45f84c5c2ba29.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9927f5f8c2a45f84c5c2ba29.body:
(On self-love as a cause of self-praise) For as those who cannot obtain food are forced to feed on their own flesh against nature, and that is the end of famine, so those that hunger after praise, if they get no one else to praise them, disgrace themselves by their anxiety to feed their own vanity.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy
sources.reference: How One Can Praise Oneself Without Exciting Envy, section III, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-6935b9c68a000d643418827f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6935b9c68a000d643418827f.body:
(On emulating worthy actions) Small, therefore, can we think the progress we have made, as long as our admiration for those who have done noble things is barren, and does not of itself incite us to imitate them.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section XIV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-6cf894451aa088fc9baa3586.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6cf894451aa088fc9baa3586.body:
(On contentment with one's lot and comparison with others) And yet it makes much for contentedness of mind to look for the most part at home and to our own condition, or if not, to look at the case of people worse off than ourselves, and not, as most people do, to compare ourselves with those who are better off.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section X, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-52c8c1903270c22c61d681d7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-52c8c1903270c22c61d681d7.body:
(On happiness and one's inner disposition) A healthy and sound constitution does indeed augment the pleasures of the body, but for the soul there can be no lasting joy or gratification, unless cheerfulness and fearlessness and courage supply a calm serenity free from storms; for otherwise, even if hope or delight smile on the soul, it is soon confused and disturbed by care lifting up its head again, so that it is but the calm of a sunken rock.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Virtue And Vice, section III, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-80ce8d822759e666ad508645.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-80ce8d822759e666ad508645.body:
(On bashfulness that prevents saying no) Yet we oftentimes pass over our friends who are both deserving and in need, and give to others who continually and impudently importune us, not from the wish to give but from the inability to say No.
Plutarch

advice-70fb0cb6cc934e8873df42fe.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-70fb0cb6cc934e8873df42fe.body:
(On admitting one's faults in order to improve) We ought certainly to be ashamed of and shun every appearance of vice, but he who is more put about by his vice itself than by the bad reputation that ensues upon it, will not mind either hearing it spoken against or even speaking against it himself if it make him a better man.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue
sources.reference: How One May Be Aware Of One'S Progress In Virtue, section XI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-b3b77f6f58d9815af2b0ccb7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b3b77f6f58d9815af2b0ccb7.body:
(On peace of mind without abandoning duties) In the next place, it is false that those that have little to do are easy in mind.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section II, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-88988a06a38c0df69eb7458c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-88988a06a38c0df69eb7458c.body:
(On the habit of dwelling on unpleasant things) When our eyes are dazzled with things too bright we turn them away, and ease them by looking at flowers or grass, while we keep the eyes of our mind strained on disagreeable things, and force them to dwell on bitter ideas, well-nigh tearing them away by force from the consideration of pleasanter things.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section VIII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-1b7e34d441ae433cf7b9d003.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1b7e34d441ae433cf7b9d003.body:
(On refusing to give praise against one's judgment) For example, if a friend's harper sings badly at a drinking party, or an actor hired at great cost murders Menander, and most of the party clap and applaud, I find it by no means hard, or bad manners, to listen silently, and not to be so illiberal as to praise contrary to one's convictions.
Plutarch

advice-24b0baecf99192a6642eebf2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-24b0baecf99192a6642eebf2.body:
(On anger caused by feeling disregarded) Now when I contemplated the origin of anger itself, I observed that, though different persons fell into it for different reasons, yet in nearly all of them was the idea of their being despised and neglected to be found.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section XII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-ea25aaa8fe525deccadcbeaa.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ea25aaa8fe525deccadcbeaa.body:
(On praise that makes friendly correction acceptable) For as iron receives its consistency and temper by first being submitted to fire and so made soft and then dipped into cold water, so when friends have been first warmed and melted with praises we can afterwards use gentle remonstrance, which has a similar effect to that of dipping in the case of the metal.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXXVI, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-abf56046c2171a5e4cf79105.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-abf56046c2171a5e4cf79105.body:
(On idle curiosity about others' secrets) So if anyone were to open occasionally the stores that curiosity had amassed, and observe what a cargo there was of useless and idle and unlovely things, perhaps the sight of all this poor stuff would inspire him with disgust.
Plutarch

advice-a655916591ed8387c9a4c803.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a655916591ed8387c9a4c803.body:
