(On fear of a bad reputation that prevents action) However we must avoid too much timidity and fear of censure, since many have played the coward, and abandoned noble ventures, more from fear of a bad name than of the dangers to be undergone, not being able to bear a bad reputation.
Plutarch

advice-6647926564541dead59982ff.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6647926564541dead59982ff.body:
(On vice as a cause of unhappiness) Fortune therefore does not produce perfect infelicity, unless Vice co-operate.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether Vice Is Sufficient To Cause Unhappiness
sources.reference: Whether Vice Is Sufficient To Cause Unhappiness, section IV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-b9487def9d147875244a3381.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b9487def9d147875244a3381.body:
(On the need to teach sound judgment) Still more ridiculous is he who asserts that good sense alone need not be taught, without which all other arts are useless and profitless, seeing that she is the mistress and orderer and arranger of all of them, and puts each of them to their proper use.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: That Virtue May Be Taught, section III, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-dd7100062c664a8cc6ffc043.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-dd7100062c664a8cc6ffc043.body:
(On the benefit of a friend's correction) So we, if we observe the blots, blemishes, shortcomings, and imperfections of our private selves, shall perceive clearly that we do not need a friend who shall bestow upon us praise and panegyric, but one that will reprove us, and speak plainly to us, aye, by Zeus, and censure us if we have done amiss.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-0be98eb17832da3625813c0d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0be98eb17832da3625813c0d.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) As for those who wonder that what is unreasoning should obey reason, they do not seem to me to recognize the power of reason, how great it is, and how far-reaching its dominion is—a power not gained by harsh and repelling methods, but by attractive ones, as mild persuasion which always accomplishes more than compulsion or violence.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Moral Virtue, section IV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-ee7c1e768bb96f80b20df09f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ee7c1e768bb96f80b20df09f.body:
(On the flatterer who adapts to another's character) But the flatterer having no fixed character of his own, and not seeking to lead the life suitable for him, but shaping and modelling himself after another's pattern, is neither simple nor uniform, but complex and unstable, assuming different appearances, like water poured from vessel to vessel, ever in a state of flux and accommodating himself entirely to the fashion of those who entertain him.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section VII, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-0adc817629d940f5bfb273fa.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0adc817629d940f5bfb273fa.body:
(On tact and moderation in friendly frankness) And so outspokenness ought to be tempered with kindness, and reason ought to be called in to correct its excessive tartness, (as we tone down the too powerful glare of a lamp), that people may not, by being troubled and grieved at continual blame and rebuke, fly for refuge to the shade of the flatterer, and turn aside to him to free themselves from annoyance.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend
sources.reference: How One May Discern A Flatterer From A Friend, section XXV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-67047c4148b8d75a2eef4132.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-67047c4148b8d75a2eef4132.body:
(On choosing worthy friends) For what is easily got is not always desirable: and we pass over and trample upon heather and brambles that stick to us on our road to the olive and vine: so also is it good not always to make a friend of the person who is expert in twining himself around us, but after testing them to attach ourselves to those who are worthy of our affection and likely to be serviceable to us.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Abundance Of Friends, section IV, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-e7c7ae4d0917efdedbad0e97.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e7c7ae4d0917efdedbad0e97.body:
(On improving oneself through one's enemies) For as those animals that have the strongest and healthiest stomachs eat and digest serpents and scorpions, and some even feed on stones and shells, which they convert into nourishment by the strength and heat of their stomachs, while fastidious people out of health almost vomit if offered bread and wine, so foolish people spoil even their friendships, while the wise know how to turn to account even their enmities.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies
sources.reference: How A Man May Be Benefited By His Enemies, section II, paragraph 3 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-59ac58f1695582c87a139958.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-59ac58f1695582c87a139958.body:
(On preparing in advance for adversity) And as Xenophon advised that we should remember and honour the gods most especially in prosperity, that so, when we should be in any strait, we might confidently call upon them as already our well-wishers and friends; so sensible men would do well before trouble comes to meditate on remedies how to bear it, that they may be the more efficacious from being ready for use long before.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section I, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-9f793d498b98c1f35a2a77b6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9f793d498b98c1f35a2a77b6.body:
(On enjoying goods without constant fear of loss) Nor ought we to amass things we regard as valuable, and always be on the tremble and afraid of losing them as valuable things, and yet, when we have them, ignore them and think little of them; but we ought to use them for our pleasure and enjoyment, that we may bear their loss, if that should happen, with more equanimity.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section IX, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-e3f6f33938434cc31c4079b2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e3f6f33938434cc31c4079b2.body:
(On recognizing present and past blessings) So we should not overlook, but take account of everyday blessings, and rejoice that we live, and are well, and see the sun, and that no war or sedition plagues our country, but that the earth is open to cultivation, the sea secure to mariners, and that we can speak or be silent, lead a busy or an idle life, as we choose.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section IX, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-b21f6a806ed694a68d90bf4d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b21f6a806ed694a68d90bf4d.body:
(On the merits of silence and concise speech) In the next place we must consider the opposite virtue to talkativeness, always listening to and having on our lips the encomiums passed upon reserve, and remembering the decorum sanctity and mysterious power of silence, and ever bearing in mind that terse and brief speakers, who put the maximum of matter into the minimum of words, are more admired and esteemed and thought wiser than unbridled windbags.
Plutarch

advice-7912d0463f3423a4c6cde97b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7912d0463f3423a4c6cde97b.body:
(On the ineffectiveness of revenge driven by anger) For, indeed, when I consider revenge, I find its angry method to be for the most part ineffectual, since it spends itself in biting the lips and gnashing the teeth, and in vain attacks, and in railings coupled with foolish threats, and eventually resembles children running races, who from feebleness ridiculously tumble down before they reach the goal they are hastening to.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Restraining Anger, section X, paragraph 1 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-6f982d5c24459ec80ba19a72.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6f982d5c24459ec80ba19a72.body:
(On calmly accepting others' shortcomings) But if you take people as they are, as the surgeon uses his bandages and instruments for drawing teeth, and with cheerfulness and serenity welcome all that happens, as you would look upon barking dogs as only following their nature, you will be happier in the disposition you will then have than you will be distressed at other people's disagreeableness and shortcomings.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: On Contentedness Of Mind, section VII, paragraph 2 (Shilleto 1898)

advice-66ea75c8c59610ad1aa00c56.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-66ea75c8c59610ad1aa00c56.body:
(On contributing appropriately to a conversation) For in a race the victory belongs to him who gets in first, but in company, if anyone has given a satisfactory answer, it is sufficient by assenting and agreeing to his view to get the reputation of being a pleasant fellow; and if no satisfactory answer is given, then to enlighten ignorance and supply the necessary information is well-timed and does not excite envy.
Plutarch

advice-a6aa6a831909e37e661a9acd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a6aa6a831909e37e661a9acd.body:
(On pausing before answering the questioner) When it seems that he really desires information, we should accustom ourselves to pause, and interpose some interval between the question and answer; during which time the questioner can add anything if he chooses, and the other can reflect on his answer, and not be in too great a hurry about it, nor bury it in obscurity, nor, as is frequently the case in too great haste, answer some other question than that which was asked.
Plutarch

advice-d1c2b8bd7b9ff77935c24d6b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d1c2b8bd7b9ff77935c24d6b.body:
(On generously acknowledging others' merits) And those who are truly good take it for their greatest honor and commendation to be just in paying honor and commendation where it is due to others; and for a man to adorn another is a most glorious ornament, proceeding from a generous abundance of glory and honor in himself; while those who are niggardly in praising others only betray how poor and bare they are of praises at home.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 13, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-bdd7ec615ba992b610e87ec5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bdd7ec615ba992b610e87ec5.body:
(On peace of mind and the morality of actions) For he that hath attained to virtue by the methods of philosophy hath his mind all in tune and good temper; he is not struck with those reproaches of conscience, which cause the acutest sense of pain and are the natural punishments of our follies; but he enjoys (the great prerogative of a good man) to be always easy and in amity with himself.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: That a Philosopher Ought Chiefly to Converse with Great Men
sources.reference: That a Philosopher Ought Chiefly to Converse with Great Men, section 2, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-1f2fb4077712c1354d98faed.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1f2fb4077712c1354d98faed.body:
(On thinking for oneself while listening to a teacher) For the mind requires not like an earthen vessel to be filled up; convenient fuel and aliment only will inflame it with a desire of knowledge and ardent love of truth.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 18, paragraph 5 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-54385e3529bf82365bfd7687.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-54385e3529bf82365bfd7687.body:
(On choosing wise and cooperative political allies) But when some great and useful matter, yet such as requires much struggling and industry, is to be taken in hand, endeavor to choose the most powerful of your friends, or rather the mildest of the most powerful; for they will least thwart you and most co-operate with you, having wisdom without a contentious humor.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 26, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-0bc2b147fe6b27262f25ce95.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0bc2b147fe6b27262f25ce95.body:
(On avarice that prevents enjoying wealth) There is also this particular mischief in the love of wealth, that this desire hinders and opposes its own satisfaction, which other desires do procure.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 4, paragraph 3 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-c016915905b11b7fb547d6d9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c016915905b11b7fb547d6d9.body:
(On envy that prevents learning from a speaker) Yet he that grieves at the wealth, glory, or beauty of any is but simply envious, for he repines only at the good of others; but he that is ill-natured to a good speaker is an enemy to his own happiness.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 5, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-29435574cf68048deb311661.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-29435574cf68048deb311661.body:
(On power that magnifies a person's vices) Vice, being furnished with wheels by power, sets all the faculties of the soul in a violent fermentation; of anger it makes murder, of love adultery, and of covetousness the confiscation of other men’s goods.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince
sources.reference: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince, section 6, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 4)

advice-6f419cedbb1e8ace6ec84837.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6f419cedbb1e8ace6ec84837.body:
(On a ruler's reluctance to accept sound advice) Wherefore it is very difficult to give counsel to princes in matters of government; for they fear to receive advice as a thing seeming to command them, lest the force of reason should seem to lessen their power, by obliging it to submit to truth.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince
sources.reference: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 4)

advice-0fe9ca6d46507fe9b5e7d018.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0fe9ca6d46507fe9b5e7d018.body:
(On respect for the elderly) For to no honor is it so incident to grace the honorer more than the honored, as to that which is given to persons in years.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 7, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-bcc0963b12e1a8ef4fe06711.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bcc0963b12e1a8ef4fe06711.body:
(On preferring wealth to happiness) You may see indeed many persons that choose rather to be rich and at the same time very miserable, than to part with their money and become happy.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-48fbc9ed4adef2679d870b71.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-48fbc9ed4adef2679d870b71.body:
(On thinking for oneself while listening to a teacher) In fine, if there is any other precept concerning hearing, it is briefly this, to be careful in observing the last exhortation,—that is, to join the exercise of our invention to our hearing; that so, while we lay down the rule that hearing well is the first step to living well, we may not content ourselves with a superficial commonplace knowledge, but endeavor after such a philosophical habit as shall be deeply imprinted on the mind.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 18, paragraph 5 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-34206fba3f8817b0f2c93262.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-34206fba3f8817b0f2c93262.body:
(On moral education through listening) For there are many organs and other parts of the body which serve as avenues and inlets to the soul to give admission to vice; there is but one passage of virtue into young minds, and that is by the ears, provided they be preserved all along free from the corruptions of flattery and untainted with lewd discourses.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 2, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-43066d29e7c17ef256140e03.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-43066d29e7c17ef256140e03.body:
(On shared friends and harmony between brothers) Wherefore neither the common table nor the common recreations nor any other sort of intimacy comprehends so much of amity betwixt brothers, as to be united in their interest and to have the same common friends and enemies; for ordinary friendship suffers neither calumnies nor clashings, but if there be any anger or discontent, honest and impartial friends make an end of it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 20, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-c65e3c30f97ea708881ec019.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c65e3c30f97ea708881ec019.body:
(On love for parents and between brothers) Now I would persuade the son to show all possible honor and reverence to his parents, but not with that greedy design of engrossing all their love to himself,—of which too many have been guilty, working their brethren out of favor, on purpose to make way for their own interest,—a fault which they are apt to palliate with specious, but unjust pretences.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 9, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-db6687e4ba0354df8674e92f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-db6687e4ba0354df8674e92f.body:
(On a statesman refusing a friend's dishonest request) But he must reject the dishonest and unreasonable request of his friends, yet not churlishly but mildly, teaching and showing them that they are not beseeming their virtue and honor.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 13, paragraph 8 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-d73721a62b8c24c2d77b39a1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d73721a62b8c24c2d77b39a1.body:
(On modest public honors for service) A moderation in the expense is therefore the best and surest preservative of honors; for such as are great, immense, and ponderous are like to unproportioned statues, soon overthrown.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 27, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-c83ce5e5b5537162e0fe2f91.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c83ce5e5b5537162e0fe2f91.body:
(On avarice that prevents enjoying wealth) But it is otherwise in the love of wealth, which, like a hard and severe mistress, compels us to get what it forbids us to enjoy, and excites an appetite but denies the pleasure of its gratification.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 5, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-ce38ae22277d0e0a95525cdb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ce38ae22277d0e0a95525cdb.body:
(On faith as a support for courage) For God is the brave man’s hope, and not the coward’s excuse.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Superstition, section 8, paragraph 5 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-cb4966c60e05530157dbac2d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cb4966c60e05530157dbac2d.body:
(On health as a condition of enjoying life) For diseases do not either rob or spoil us of so much business, hope, journeys, or exercise, as they do of pleasure; so that it is no way convenient for those who would follow their pleasure to neglect their health.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Rules for the Preservation of Health
sources.reference: Rules for the Preservation of Health, section 8, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-fb415b1b6bdbf1922062a35b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fb415b1b6bdbf1922062a35b.body:
(On an uncle encouraging his nephews' worthy achievements) For it is prudence in a brother, when he beholds with joy the brave and worthy actions of his nephews growing great and honorable by their own deserts, to prompt and encourage them on by congratulation and applause.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 21, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-9e40bc63cd226cd39fe368ae.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9e40bc63cd226cd39fe368ae.body:
(On finding reasons for praise through goodwill) Thus love, like ivy, must needs find something or other to lay hold on.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 13, paragraph 3 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-065d66b44d0ff6d18824a5db.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-065d66b44d0ff6d18824a5db.body:
(On individual variations in virtue) Moreover, virtues do admit some other differences, like peculiar colors, by reason of men’s dispositions, and are assimilated to the manners and temperaments of the bodies wherein they are, yea, to the education and manner of diet.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Concerning the Virtues of Women, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-effbcc69f9790f7c5339104e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-effbcc69f9790f7c5339104e.body:
(On love for parents and between brothers) To parents therefore the love of brothers is a plain argument of their children’s love to themselves.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 6, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-25c6c41e7e78cfe45e5c593d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-25c6c41e7e78cfe45e5c593d.body:
(On mental and bodily strain in debate) For disputes bring with them a vehemence and contention, adding the labor of the mind to that of the body.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Rules for the Preservation of Health
sources.reference: Rules for the Preservation of Health, section 16, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-fadb6c1aec8799e7072c6743.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fadb6c1aec8799e7072c6743.body:
(On being known and thereby benefiting others) But a wise man, if he design to engage in business and matters of state, will so far aim at fame and popularity as that he may be better enabled to benefit others; for it is a difficult and very unpleasant task to do good to those who are disaffected to our persons.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: That a Philosopher Ought Chiefly to Converse with Great Men
sources.reference: That a Philosopher Ought Chiefly to Converse with Great Men, section 2, paragraph 3 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-193068ff6bbade2f79d63ec6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-193068ff6bbade2f79d63ec6.body:
(On possessing wealth versus being independent of it) Being wealthy is not despising wealth; nor is possessing things superfluous the same as not needing things superfluous.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-17e8dad151dda624247b9957.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-17e8dad151dda624247b9957.body:
(On the caring ruler and the fearful tyrant) For indeed good princes are possessed with fear for their subjects, but tyrants with fear of them; insomuch that their timorousness increaseth with their power, since the more people they have under their dominion, so much the more objects they see of dread and terror.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince
sources.reference: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince, section 4, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 4)

advice-26d79f6a39c79b8a57343bc2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-26d79f6a39c79b8a57343bc2.body:
(On the insatiable pursuit of wealth) But the love of money is not abated by having silver and gold; neither do covetous desires cease by possessing still more.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 2, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-0441b39b4c95fcf56ab0deba.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0441b39b4c95fcf56ab0deba.body:
(On the constant exercise of reason) For the habit of prudence does not continue the same in those who give themselves to their ease; but by little and little diminishes and is dissolved by sloth, as always requiring some exercise of the thought to rouse up and purify the rational, active faculty of the soul.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 8, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-cbfc5cd5a19da07728965a1b.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cbfc5cd5a19da07728965a1b.body:
(On luxury displacing useful applications of wealth) And just thus the things that are necessary and useful in riches are swallowed up by those that are unprofitable and superfluous.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 8, paragraph 6 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-611efa12318478012e0c6521.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-611efa12318478012e0c6521.body:
(On fear that disables action) Fear alone, being equally destitute of reason and audacity, renders our whole irrational part stupid, distracted, and unserviceable.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Superstition, section 3, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-bc63cb5ee123c52acdca99df.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bc63cb5ee123c52acdca99df.body:
(On unexplained anxiety as a sign of ill health) For there are despondencies of mind and fears that are without reason or any apparent cause, which extinguish our hopes on a sudden.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Rules for the Preservation of Health
sources.reference: Rules for the Preservation of Health, section 14, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-e7fc90210e76e431fee0c8c0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e7fc90210e76e431fee0c8c0.body:
(On goods of the soul that money cannot buy) But, alas! freedom from distress and repose of spirit, magnanimity, constancy, resolution, and contentment of mind,—these are not a money-purchase.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-e356892750fac5ff52d10bf4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e356892750fac5ff52d10bf4.body:
(On care for the body and its limits) But still the body is very much more inconvenienced by the soul, when it is used beyond reason and there is not care enough taken of it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Rules for the Preservation of Health
sources.reference: Rules for the Preservation of Health, section 24, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-ca01f1973c45c3ae2a13a686.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ca01f1973c45c3ae2a13a686.body:
(On the desires of a ruler with unlimited power) But herein lies the greatest danger, lest he that is able to do all things that he desires should desire those things that he ought not.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince
sources.reference: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince, section 6, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 4)

advice-67fa04e7dc3bd906656de8d4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-67fa04e7dc3bd906656de8d4.body:
(On political disagreements without personal hostility) But contentions about public matters, where private grudges are taken away, are soon appeased, and bring no difficult or fatal mischiefs.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 32, paragraph 3 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-4c78440f9a5d77c62b3545b6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4c78440f9a5d77c62b3545b6.body:
(On an active life and care for health) We ought to preserve the natural constitution of our bodies by other means, knowing every part of our life is capable of sickness and health.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Rules for the Preservation of Health
sources.reference: Rules for the Preservation of Health, section 24, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-99ff44264f9faaffbaccc316.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-99ff44264f9faaffbaccc316.body:
(On torturing and killing animals) For my part I cannot think him a worse criminal that torments a poor creature while living, than a man that shall take away its life and murder it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Eating of Flesh, section 7, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-1a79fb7115c586ad2612a0b3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1a79fb7115c586ad2612a0b3.body:
(On willingness to accept correction of one's faults) On the contrary, men commonly flatter themselves, and admire the philosopher so long as he discourses of indifferent things; but if he come home to themselves and deal freely with them about their real interests, this they think is beyond all enduring, or at best a needless piece of supererogation.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 12, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-814df821f739ddcd03728a17.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-814df821f739ddcd03728a17.body:
(On envy that prevents learning from a speaker) Thus again, envy and detraction and prejudice are in no case good, but always a great impediment to what is so; yet nowhere worse than when they are made the bosom friends and counsellors of a hearer, because they represent the best things to him as unpleasant and impertinent, and men in such circumstances are pleased with any thing rather than what deserves their applause.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 5, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-065efa4e4af6dbc449f2c1a2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-065efa4e4af6dbc449f2c1a2.body:
(On alternating work with excessive pleasures) But an intemperate and slavish mind, so soon as it is free from labor, like a sailor, runs insolently into pleasures and delights, and again falls upon business, so that nature can have no rest or leave to enjoy that temper and calmness which it does desire, but is troubled and tormented by all this irregularity.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Rules for the Preservation of Health
sources.reference: Rules for the Preservation of Health, section 25, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-480c9aa987473cb6972124bc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-480c9aa987473cb6972124bc.body:
(On philosophy that inspires worthy action) The true philosophy is of a quite different nature; it is a spring and principle of motion wherever it comes; it makes men active and industrious, it sets every wheel and faculty a going, it stores our minds with axioms and rules by which to make a sound judgment, it determines the will to the choice of what is honorable and just; and it wings all our faculties to the swiftest prosecution of it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: That a Philosopher Ought Chiefly to Converse with Great Men
sources.reference: That a Philosopher Ought Chiefly to Converse with Great Men, section 1, paragraph 3 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-478c7908feb543ea436a6be3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-478c7908feb543ea436a6be3.body:
(On peace of mind and the morality of actions) But the very joys of wicked men are tumultuary and confused, like those who dwell in the borders of two great empires at variance, always insecure, and in perpetual alarms; whilst a good man enjoys an uninterrupted peace and serenity of mind, which excels the other not only in duration, but in sense of pleasure too.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: That a Philosopher Ought Chiefly to Converse with Great Men
sources.reference: That a Philosopher Ought Chiefly to Converse with Great Men, section 2, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-c1d45d289910859f3970c8fc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c1d45d289910859f3970c8fc.body:
(On preparing in advance to resist anger) For it is a piece of admirable prudence for a man so prone to anger, as being by nature hasty and furious, to understand himself so well as to set a guard upon his own inclinations, and by avoiding provocations to keep his passion at due distance by the use of reason, lest he should be unawares surprised by it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 11, paragraph 8 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-911fdd963d21038432e3faf6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-911fdd963d21038432e3faf6.body:
(On unfair reproaches about birth or misfortune) For as they who scourge a man’s garments do not touch the body, so those that turn other men’s evil fortunes or mean births to matter of reproach do only with vanity and folly enough lash their external circumstances, but touch not their internal part, the soul, nor those things which truly need correction and reproof.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 13, paragraph 16 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-9c6a73854dde2041cde8c00f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9c6a73854dde2041cde8c00f.body:
(On kinship and the human need for company) For the ordinary inclinations and desires of men, being after some sort of society or other, sufficiently admonish them to set the highest value upon relations, to pay them all becoming respects, and to have a tender regard for their persons, nothing being more irksome to nature than to live in that destitution and solitude that denies them the happiness of a friend and the privilege of communication.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 3, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-1bb29179def40667decbf9e9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1bb29179def40667decbf9e9.body:
(On love for parents and between brothers) Now those who are truly noble in character do not only love one another the more entirely for the sake of their common parents, but they love their very parents for the sake of one another; always owning themselves bound to their parents especially for the mutual happiness that they enjoy in each other, and looking upon their brethren as the dearest and the most valuable treasure they could have received from their parents.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 6, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-22de776c7da7973a120e5ec8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-22de776c7da7973a120e5ec8.body:
(On harmony among public officials) Now the mutual concord and friendship of magistrates with one another is a far greater honor of magistracy than their diadems and purple-garded robes.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 20, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-bbe6bb3c84b8bf14de01d2e8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bbe6bb3c84b8bf14de01d2e8.body:
(On entering public service with preparation and purpose) Now I am of opinion, that those who by chance and without foresight stumble upon policy, falling as it were into a pit, cannot but be troubled and repent; whereas they that go leisurely into it, with preparation and a good resolution, comfort themselves moderately in all occurrences, as having no other end of their actions but the discharging of their duty with honor.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 2, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-4a2cfc58be39596cf1982db2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4a2cfc58be39596cf1982db2.body:
(On constant care that preserves public trust) For neither does a friend, when he is once had, require many and great services that he may so continue, but assiduity does by small signs preserve his good-will; nor do the friendship and confidence of the people expect to have a man always bestowing largesses, defending their causes, or executing of magistracy, but they are maintained by a readiness, and by not failing or being weary of carefulness and solicitude for the public.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 6, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-12121a8dda130a654b693f06.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-12121a8dda130a654b693f06.body:
(On honors as an expression of public gratitude) For the honor should not be a recompense of the action, but an acknowledgment of gratitude, that it may continue also long, as those did which we have mentioned.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 27, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-1726c1cbc702dba0a0edfad2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1726c1cbc702dba0a0edfad2.body:
(On trust in a person's goodwill and integrity) But there is nothing which renders one man so obsequious and submissive to another, as the confidence of his good-will, and the opinion of his integrity and justice.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 28, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-5fc2165323c8c9e4395c8fec.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5fc2165323c8c9e4395c8fec.body:
(On avarice that prevents enjoying wealth) For no man abstains from a good morsel because he loves dainties, nor from wine because he thirsts after wine, as these men abstain from using money because they love money.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 4, paragraph 3 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-62fb4c5bae96731a72c68329.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-62fb4c5bae96731a72c68329.body:
(On rational persuasion rather than gifts and spectacles) For to lead a people is to persuade them by reason and eloquence; but such allurements of the multitude nothing differ from the baits laid for the taking of irrational animals.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 5, paragraph 8 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-909e3fc843b8011fa8f06e6a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-909e3fc843b8011fa8f06e6a.body:
(On a worthy mentor for a new statesman) Now he that begins to enter upon the administration of state affairs should choose himself a guide, who is not only a man of credit and authority but is also such for his virtue.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 12, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-cc3613dc2f5466a5dd993f11.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cc3613dc2f5466a5dd993f11.body:
(On the imperfection of human relationships) For, if you examine the love of relations, the love of associates, or the more sensual passion of fond lovers, you will find none of them all clear, pure, and free from all faults.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 8, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-022deca3f3cf62cbf0325a95.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-022deca3f3cf62cbf0325a95.body:
(On a pupil accepting unpleasant but useful instruction) But let him learn to be thankful to him that purges away the darkness and stupidity of his mind, though (as we clear beehives by smoking) with an offensive or unpalatable discourse.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 9, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-ff294310dd306859933685b6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ff294310dd306859933685b6.body:
(On wealth within the limits of natural needs) To those indeed that are wise, the riches that Nature requires are limited, and confined within the compass of their real needs, as within a circle drawn from a centre at a certain distance.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 4, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-0e20f82d6b7f1a420182a29a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0e20f82d6b7f1a420182a29a.body:
(On listening with goodwill and discernment) For although such as are contemptuous and self-conceited receive but little good from what they hear, yet the good-natured and such as are given to admire every thing take a great deal of harm.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 7, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-4c452e3b90c18e893b444cf0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4c452e3b90c18e893b444cf0.body:
(On envy of one's brother's success) But if he envies all that are so happy, or is the only one in the world that repines at his own brother’s felicity, his malicious temper speaks him one of the most wretched creatures in the world.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 14, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-7c782039d3025d7d736798cb.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7c782039d3025d7d736798cb.body:
(On joy in one's brother's success) But to a prudent and ingenious brother, it would be as great a satisfaction to see his brother an excellent orator, a person of great wealth or authority, as if he had been any or all these himself.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 16, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-94a8a2e59760e0fcbf15b0f8.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-94a8a2e59760e0fcbf15b0f8.body:
(On patience and gentleness with those close to us) For, except nature has bestowed those virtues of meekness and patience upon us in vain and to no purpose, we have certainly the greatest reason to exercise them towards our intimate friends and kindred.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 18, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-9174d794c3e11f5b30c185a6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9174d794c3e11f5b30c185a6.body:
(On the insatiable pursuit of wealth) But as for him that, having more than enough, yet still desires to have more, it is not gold nor silver, not horses, sheep, or oxen, that can cure him of this disease, but he needs evacuation and purgation.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 3, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-57a066ba8de79433b5adc26d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-57a066ba8de79433b5adc26d.body:
(On supporting a brother through one's merits and success) You then are a happy man, one would think, that can oblige your brother at a cheaper rate, illustrate him with the honor of your virtues, and make him great like yourself, without any damage or derogation.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 12, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-5742d49f9718a20093c5dc05.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5742d49f9718a20093c5dc05.body:
(On civic responsibility during civil strife) Yet does it not become you in the time of a sedition to sit as if you were neither sensible nor sorry, praising your own unconcernedness as a quiet and happy life, and taking delight in the error of others.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 32, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-fd3055c23e0799854ca4acd1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fd3055c23e0799854ca4acd1.body:
(On the difficulty of changing the people's character) For the changing of a multitude is a difficult and laborious work.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 4, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-39caccc1f7242415a6a92408.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-39caccc1f7242415a6a92408.body:
(On trust that makes a person vulnerable to deception) For the part of the soul by which we believe is most apt to be caught.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 28, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-e92591c402ba8d2271fecb5f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e92591c402ba8d2271fecb5f.body:
(On reason replacing a guardian in adulthood) But you, who have often heard that to follow God and to obey reason are all one, cannot but believe that men of best sense in passing from minority to manhood do not throw off the government, but simply change their governor.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-93e3bf54a3850f850e58a1a0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-93e3bf54a3850f850e58a1a0.body:
(On supporting a brother through one's merits and success) I would persuade that brother therefore that excels his fellows in any accomplishments, in those very things to communicate and impart to them the utmost he can, that they may shine in his honor, and flourish with his interest.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 12, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-e31046c7998a53d3d429ae20.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e31046c7998a53d3d429ae20.body:
(On an uncle encouraging his nephews' worthy achievements) For to praise his own son may be absurd and offensive, but to commend the good actions of a brother’s son, is an excellent thing, and one which proceeds from no self-interest, nor any other principle but a true veneration for virtue.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 21, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-054a0d1dc40611274983fc01.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-054a0d1dc40611274983fc01.body:
(On a new statesman improving civic practices) There are also in the cities many good and laudable usages neglected, which may be restored, and many ill practices brought in by custom, to the disgrace or damage of the city, which may be redressed, to gain him the esteem of the people.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 10, paragraph 4 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-54ca3bbf13b8cc14d5220f72.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-54ca3bbf13b8cc14d5220f72.body:
(On the reciprocity of sincere friendship) For every sincere substantial friend joins in affection with one that approves himself such to him.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 19, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-e8d5e6e53f3b6356316b94e1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e8d5e6e53f3b6356316b94e1.body:
(On health as a condition of enjoying life) Health is to pleasure as still weather to the halcyon, giving it a safe and commodious birth and nest.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Rules for the Preservation of Health
sources.reference: Rules for the Preservation of Health, section 8, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-e4dda82c9435232042ae20d6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e4dda82c9435232042ae20d6.body:
(On respect for the elderly) Moreover, all men do not expect to gain themselves authority from wealth, eloquence, or wisdom; but as for the reverence and glory to which old age brings men, there is not any one of those who act in the management of the state but hopes to attain it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 7, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-7c245b8850dd66ac0b59113c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7c245b8850dd66ac0b59113c.body:
(On apparent freedom under the rule of one's vices) For that libertinism which some wild young fellows, for want of more happy education, mistake for liberty, subjects them to harder tyrants than their late tutors and masters, even to their own vicious inclinations, which, as it were, break loose upon them.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-6801f8388bc6cabf08e9d0ae.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6801f8388bc6cabf08e9d0ae.body:
(On moral education through listening) For discourse to an hearer, like light to the eye, is a great benefit, if he will make the best use of it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 5, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-894375886370da14dd156cfc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-894375886370da14dd156cfc.body:
(On awareness of one's true worth) For it is the part of a wise man to value himself upon the consciousness of his own true worth and excellency.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 11, paragraph 18 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-380d991feb5b32df7ed97351.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-380d991feb5b32df7ed97351.body:
(On testing poetic teachings by reason) But poets are not to be obeyed as pedagogues and lawgivers are, except they have reason to back what they say.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 9, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-4fd986218f90704fee502871.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-4fd986218f90704fee502871.body:
(On envy that prevents learning from a speaker) Envy in all other instances carries this pretence with it, that it is to be referred to the depraved and ungovernable affections of the mind, but that which is conceived against a speaker arises from an unjust presumption and vain-glorious affectation of praise.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 5, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-fe468368d5b2a8bac765ed97.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-fe468368d5b2a8bac765ed97.body:
(On the merits of even an imperfect brother) But, however, the vilest, the most despicable things have some proportion of good, or natural disposition to it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 13, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-867ee136e72af8ebe97583c7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-867ee136e72af8ebe97583c7.body:
(On finding reasons for praise through goodwill) But much more will a studious hearer and scholar be sure to find some not unworthy reason for praising every speaker.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 13, paragraph 3 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-9fad469542e4de67fc276f6a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-9fad469542e4de67fc276f6a.body:
(On restraint before tempting food) Therefore when any rare or noble dish is before you, you will get more honor by refraining from it than partaking of it.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Rules for the Preservation of Health
sources.reference: Rules for the Preservation of Health, section 7, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-745ebb547c62f7c6edb2750e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-745ebb547c62f7c6edb2750e.body:
(On public service in old age) But we ought to turn to a better purpose the saying of Thucydides, and believe that it is not the desire of honor only that never grows old, but much more also the inclinations to society and affection to the state, which continue even in ants and bees to the very last.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 1, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-0d1fdd3d4b3a674b3dad7bf9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0d1fdd3d4b3a674b3dad7bf9.body:
(On praise for men and women after death) For the Roman law seems exceeding good, which permits due praises to be given publicly both to men and women after death.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Concerning the Virtues of Women, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-46705a16e4e30218b4d68c3f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-46705a16e4e30218b4d68c3f.body:
(On understanding human dispositions in politics) For the ignorance of men’s humors brings no less disorders and obstacles in commonweals than in the friendships of kings.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 3, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-583c4c89735d59e66327b921.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-583c4c89735d59e66327b921.body:
(On fulfilled desires that can cause harm) For it is an unhappy thing and not to be wished, for a man to obtain and be master of what he desires if it be inexpedient.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 12, paragraph 11 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-456c5ed50310104cd16184da.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-456c5ed50310104cd16184da.body:
(On wealth used for display) The happiness riches pretend to is such that it depends upon spectators and witnesses; else it would signify nothing at all.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 10, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-7c0ad164981fe462f9de0754.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-7c0ad164981fe462f9de0754.body:
(On rational speech as a means of moral influence) For virtue hath no instrument so suitable and agreeable to human nature to work on men withal, as that of rational discourse.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 12, paragraph 15 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-d7289b2d1eb0278fbee776e1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d7289b2d1eb0278fbee776e1.body:
(On a friend reconciling two brothers) For as tin unites and solders up broken brass, being put to the ends and attempered to the nature of the broken pieces; so it is the part of a friend betwixt two brothers, to suit and accommodate himself to the humors of both, that he may confirm and secure their friendship.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 20, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-bcec1b383f9373d238ac5714.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-bcec1b383f9373d238ac5714.body:
(On reason and the direction of passions) But the common charge upon all sorts of passions is, that they excite and urge the reason, forcing it by their violent stings.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Superstition, section 3, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-8e6a3e84a47ec4a138a315fd.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8e6a3e84a47ec4a138a315fd.body:
(On respect for the elderly) And as the law places the diadem and crown, so does Nature the hoariness of the head, as an honorable sign of princely dignity.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 10, paragraph 5 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-b7f02088ffc47915ccfdcdee.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b7f02088ffc47915ccfdcdee.body:
(On superstition giving rise and excuse to atheism) Moreover, atheism hath no hand at all in causing superstition; but superstition not only gave atheism its first birth, but serves it ever since by giving it its best apology for existing, which, although it be neither a good nor a fair one, is yet the most specious and colorable.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Superstition, section 12, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-6216381248f1b73bb24311d6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6216381248f1b73bb24311d6.body:
(On public service in old age) For never did any one know a bee to become by age a drone, as some think it requisite of statesmen, of whom they expect that, when the vigor of their youth is past, they should retire and sit mouldy at home, suffering their active virtue to be consumed by idleness, as iron is by rust.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 1, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-a084118e0cde35e43978b186.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a084118e0cde35e43978b186.body:
(On self-interest degrading the dignity of public service) For the dignity and greatness of political virtue is overthrown, when it is debased to such mean administrations and traffics for gain.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 4, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-0a4297b46cdc1e77fa5bd56e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-0a4297b46cdc1e77fa5bd56e.body:
(On moral education through listening) And in this particular we may observe many to have been mistaken, that they practise speaking before they have been used enough to hearing.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 3, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-5d9a6ccdab84e0312581c23a.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5d9a6ccdab84e0312581c23a.body:
(On listening with goodwill and discernment) But he that brings along with him a modest and unwearied attention has this advantage, that whatever is beneficial in the discourse he makes his own, and he more readily discovers what is false or impertinent, appearing all the while a friend to truth rather than to squabbling or rashness.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 4, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-24c047fa0d536ddd003f937c.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-24c047fa0d536ddd003f937c.body:
(On a pupil accepting unpleasant but useful instruction) Let then a young man be pleased and entertained with a discourse; but let him not make his pleasure the only end of hearing, nor think he may come from the school of a philosopher singing and sportive; nor let him call for perfumes and essences when he has need of a poultice and fomentations.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 9, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-a8bf141f42914d6d3262e007.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a8bf141f42914d6d3262e007.body:
(On prepared and substantive speech before the people) Let your chief endeavor therefore be, to use to the multitude a premeditated and not empty speech, and that with safety, knowing that Pericles himself, before he made any discourse to the people, was wont to pray that there might not a word pass from him foreign to the business he was to treat of.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 8, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-a94b5bd9eb8be79cd1c93a47.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a94b5bd9eb8be79cd1c93a47.body:
(On public service within the limits of one's ability) For a readiness and good will to serve the public ought not to fail, whilst ability lasts; but when that is once gone, it is no longer to be forced.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 27, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-b6688d35f45c629d76cc3a90.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b6688d35f45c629d76cc3a90.body:
(On a pupil accepting unpleasant but useful instruction) For such as carry off a disgrace from a philosopher carelessly and without due concern, so as to grin at his reprehensions or scoffingly to praise him for them, as sharping parasites applaud the scurrilous reflection of their cullies,—such, I say, are shameless and insolent, and betray only their invincible impudence, which is no good or true argument of courage.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 16, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-27f17d09c90fc1a33011d846.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-27f17d09c90fc1a33011d846.body:
(On listening with goodwill and discernment) We ought indeed to use all the candor imaginable in praising the speaker, yet withal as great caution in yielding our assent to what he says; to look upon his expression and action with a favorable construction, but to inspect the usefulness and truth of his doctrine with the nicest and most critical judgment; that speakers may cease to be malicious, and that what they say may do no mischief.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 7, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-f552ee7d9f01f1defba071c1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-f552ee7d9f01f1defba071c1.body:
(On examining the moral effect of one's learning) For it becomes us but ill, when we rise from the barber’s chair, to be so long in consulting the mirror, or to stroke our heads and examine so curiously the style in which our hair is trimmed and dressed, and then, at our return from hearing in the schools, to think it needless to look into ourselves, or examine whether our own mind has discharged any turbulent or unprofitable affections and is grown more sedate and serene.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 8, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-ede1c25213cbfcd8c2c0d46e.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-ede1c25213cbfcd8c2c0d46e.body:
(On educating young readers and listeners) Wherefore we are not only to govern their appetites in the delights of eating and drinking, but also (and much more) to inure them to a like temperance in reading and hearing, that, while they make use of pleasure as a sauce, they may pursue that which is wholesome and profitable in those things which they read.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-1b6040b2bb9e82c89d6ff592.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-1b6040b2bb9e82c89d6ff592.body:
(On the young reader and morally imperfect poetic characters) But we should teach him rather to judge that poetry is an imitation of the manners and lives of such men as are not perfectly pure and unblamable, but such as are tinctured with passions, misled by false opinions, and muffled with ignorance; though oftentimes they may, by the help of a good natural temper, change them for better qualities.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 8, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-676b3fbf32debd98e038a680.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-676b3fbf32debd98e038a680.body:
(On envy of one's brother's success) But some are so unlucky in estimating of virtuous and worthy actions that, whereas they are overjoyed to see their friends grow in esteem, and are not a little proud of entertaining persons of honor or great opulency, their brother’s worth and eminency is in the mean time looked upon with a jealous eye, as though it threatened to cloud and eclipse the splendor of their condition.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 14, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-aa878750f9dd9285052c8f51.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-aa878750f9dd9285052c8f51.body:
(On brothers pursuing success through different paths without rivalry) Therefore, where the disposition of brothers is such that they cannot agree in prosecuting the same methods of becoming great, it is convenient that one of them should so command himself as to assume the most different inclinations and designs from his brother; that, if they both aim at honor, they may serve their ambition by different means, and that they may cheerfully congratulate each other on the success of their designs, and so enjoy at once their honor and themselves.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 15, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-37017015999f1066841a44b9.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-37017015999f1066841a44b9.body:
(On the difficulty of restoring broken brotherly bonds) For, as those things which are joined together by art, being parted, may by the same art be compacted again, but if there be a fracture in a natural body, there is much difficulty in setting and uniting the broken parts; so, if friendships that through a long tract of time have been firmly and closely contracted come once to be violated, no endeavors will bring them together any more.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 7, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-c6ac600475a3c3ea6303fba2.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-c6ac600475a3c3ea6303fba2.body:
(On a ruler beginning by governing himself) For, as it is necessary at first that the rule itself should be right and straight, before those things that are applied to it can be rectified and made like unto it; so a potentate ought in the first place to learn how to govern his own passions and to endue his mind with a tincture of princely virtues, and afterwards to make his subjects conformable to his example.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince
sources.reference: A Discourse to an Unlearned Prince, section 2, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 4)

advice-48f7b374a9d946052f7066b7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-48f7b374a9d946052f7066b7.body:
(On the habit of killing wild beasts, birds and fish) And the love of slaughter, being first experimented and exercised in these, at last passed even to the laboring ox, and the sheep that clothes us, and to the poor cock that keeps the house; until by little and little, unsatiableness being strengthened by use, men came to the slaughter of men, to bloodshed and wars.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Eating of Flesh, section 4, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-2cb40a148fcb71cb08f9e63d.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-2cb40a148fcb71cb08f9e63d.body:
(On allies who complement one's abilities) Nevertheless, thoroughly understanding your own nature, you ought, in that for which you are naturally less fit, rather to make choice of such as are of suitable abilities, than of such as are like yourself; as Diomedes, when he went forth to spy, passing by the valiant, took for his companion one that was prudent and cautious.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 26, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-5e9226b5eb402de7a7da6c82.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5e9226b5eb402de7a7da6c82.body:
(On trust in a statesman for integrity and service) But the multitude, though they may at the beginning reject a good and prudent man, yet coming afterwards to understand his veracity and the sincerity of his disposition, esteem him a public-spirited person and a magistrate; and of the others, they think and call one a maintainer of choruses, a second a feaster, and a third a master of the exercises.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 31, paragraph 4 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-79e3cb269a02ffe6a9a50f7f.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-79e3cb269a02ffe6a9a50f7f.body:
(On preserving harmony among fellow citizens) There remains therefore to a statesman, of all those things that are subject to his charge, this alone, which is inferior to none of the other benefits, the keeping of those who are co-inhabitants of the same city in perpetual concord and friendship, and the taking away of all contentions, animosities, and heart-burnings.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 32, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-b3864e66ebab5cc921fb2f00.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b3864e66ebab5cc921fb2f00.body:
(On seeking to monopolize all public responsibilities) Since even that man is not commended who, in the vigor and strength of his years, imposing all public affairs in general on himself, and unwilling to leave any thing for another (as the Stoics say of Jupiter), thrusts himself into all employs, and intermeddles in every business, through an insatiable desire of glory, or through envy against those who are in some measure partakers of honor and authority in the state.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 18, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-6e0e58fa72e60cfdbf1c16a0.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-6e0e58fa72e60cfdbf1c16a0.body:
(On remembering a shared childhood during brothers' quarrels) But rather, far be it from us that the feuds of that day should bury the memory of all that happier time wherein we were educated and conversed together.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 18, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-d7c6fbaa1cfdfd0ecd88e7ae.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d7c6fbaa1cfdfd0ecd88e7ae.body:
(On willingness to kill an animal oneself for meat) But if you will contend that yourself was born to an inclination to such food as you have now a mind to eat, do you then yourself kill what you would eat.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Eating of Flesh, section 5, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-b250ca424aa87c2744892eb6.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-b250ca424aa87c2744892eb6.body:
(On outward honors paid to a hated tyrant) For the very worst of tyrants are complimented and attended, yea, have statues of gold erected to them, by those who in private hate them and wag their heads.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Superstition, section 11, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-74dbc97e974ba8389cdd2d83.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-74dbc97e974ba8389cdd2d83.body:
(On friends who disrupt harmony between brothers) But those of different and uncomplying tempers are like improper notes in music, that serve only to spoil the consort, and offend the ear with a harsh noise.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 20, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-accae80afa26dbecde984ddf.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-accae80afa26dbecde984ddf.body:
(On instability before the attractions of pleasure and beauty) For it is no commendation of a man’s dexterity to be tossed up and down as pleasure and beauty move him, but an argument rather of a weak and unstable disposition.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 12, paragraph 17 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-514a140c78a8e5d64de8d8fa.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-514a140c78a8e5d64de8d8fa.body:
(On brotherly harmony strengthened by worthy people's approval) And the satisfaction you have from well-doing will give the more firm durance to your judgment, when you shall find yourselves approved by wise and judicious spectators.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 1, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-d472b5eba887c60514e7e623.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-d472b5eba887c60514e7e623.body:
(On avarice that prevents enjoying wealth) So covetous men seem to be profuse by what they possess, when they are sordid wretches if you consider what they use and enjoy; for they endure labor, but taste no pleasure.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 5, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-dca37871c3a9533ca7fc23a7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-dca37871c3a9533ca7fc23a7.body:
(On the value of depicting the consequences of wrongdoing) For the fiction and representation of evil acts, when it withal acquaints us with the shame and damage befalling the doers, hurts not but rather profits him that reads them.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 4, paragraph 14 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-8ad9cc368fbe50ec30d979fc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8ad9cc368fbe50ec30d979fc.body:
(On taking harmless jokes calmly) Yet to bear handsomely without passion an innocent jest in raillery is not unbecoming the breeding of a gentleman, but a good accomplishment and altogether worthy of a Spartan.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 16, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-93efc031aec022e264666df1.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-93efc031aec022e264666df1.body:
(On poetic laments over death and lack of burial) To fortify us therefore against expressions of this nature, let this principle continually ring in our ears, that poetry is not at all solicitous to keep to the strict measure of truth.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 2, paragraph 14 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-8cb13475b3bfda37d3032630.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-8cb13475b3bfda37d3032630.body:
(On seeking excellence in what is most worthy) For, in truth, a man that designs to excel ought to endeavor it in those things that are in themselves most excellent, and to become chief in the chiefest, and great in the greatest things.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems
sources.reference: How a Young Man Ought to Hear Poems, section 13, paragraph 10 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-eea1c8476b4a3a8a1c9790b4.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-eea1c8476b4a3a8a1c9790b4.body:
(On peacefully dividing an inheritance between brothers) And when they come to dividing their parents’ goods, let them take heed that they come not with prejudice and contentious resolutions, giving defiance and shouting the warcry, as so many do.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 11, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-e02fdccdff7a8a17227d68bc.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e02fdccdff7a8a17227d68bc.body:
(On correcting oneself through others' mistakes) For there is nothing in the world more easy than to discover the faults of others; but it is done to no effect if we do not make it useful to ourselves in correcting and avoiding the like failures.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 6, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-5b45efa6b001cf6210936728.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-5b45efa6b001cf6210936728.body:
(On philosophical understanding that preserves goodwill) Philosophy indeed removes that foolish admiration and surprise which proceeds from doubt or ignorance, by laying open to us the causes of things, but endeavors not to destroy all good-nature and humanity.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 13, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-651a24579b270771527235e3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-651a24579b270771527235e3.body:
(On public scrutiny of a statesman's private life) For statesmen are not only liable to give an account of what they say or do in public; but there is a busy enquiry made into their very meals, beds, marriages, and every either sportive or serious action.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Political Precepts, section 4, paragraph 2 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-a9e93bea7724a34780423fba.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-a9e93bea7724a34780423fba.body:
(On accepting an honorable office in old age) And yet old men ought not ambitiously to affect even these honors, but accept them with refusal, not seeking but being sought; nor as taking government on themselves, but bestowing themselves on government.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 20, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-e857b2247de518d5ac7298e5.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-e857b2247de518d5ac7298e5.body:
(On self-interest degrading the dignity of public service) For the managing of state affairs is not a ministry which has profit for its end; but the life of gentle, civil, and sociable animals, framed by nature to live civilly, honestly, and for the benefit of mankind.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs
sources.reference: Whether an Aged Man Ought to Meddle in State Affairs, section 14, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 5)

advice-cfe517ddac2d90e52e80b880.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-cfe517ddac2d90e52e80b880.body:
(On an active life and care for health) Nor is it true that they are the most healthful that do least.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.work: Rules for the Preservation of Health
sources.reference: Rules for the Preservation of Health, section 24, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-90d3e2afc1a2df3b4f6cbd11.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-90d3e2afc1a2df3b4f6cbd11.body:
(On parents passing avarice to their children) The purse indeed becomes foul and musty after money is put up in it; but the children of the covetous, before they are enriched by their parents, are replenished with covetous desires which they derive from them.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of the Love of Wealth, section 7, paragraph 3 (Goodwin edition, vol. 2)

advice-43bf98ab0eff6a6902b44720.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-43bf98ab0eff6a6902b44720.body:
(On avoiding injustice toward others) We are therefore enjoined to take heed of doing any one wrong.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Brotherly Love, section 4, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 3)

advice-042a22838637c6dd9bb792c7.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-042a22838637c6dd9bb792c7.body:
(On choosing appropriate expressions of praise) Neither ought we to use any expressions of praise indifferently.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 15, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-79b322da80548ccc3c8a11f3.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-79b322da80548ccc3c8a11f3.body:
(On empty eloquence that gives only brief pleasure) The hearers admire as long as they are pleased and tickled, but the satisfaction on one hand and glory on the other conclude with the oration; and the hearers lose their time idly, and the speakers their whole life.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
sources.reference: Of Hearing, section 7, paragraph 1 (Goodwin edition, vol. 1)

advice-de5c0600fa09a253c42aa914.title: Philosophers’ aphorisms
advice-de5c0600fa09a253c42aa914.body:
(On eating meat for hunger rather than indulgence) Let us eat flesh; but let it be for hunger and not for wantonness.
Plutarch

sources.author: Plutarch
